deep.title: Intrusion Detection on Resource-Constrained IoT Devices with Hardware-Aware ML and DL
deep.authors: Ali Diab (Lebanese University), Adel Chehade (Univ. of Genova, DITEN), Edoardo Ragusa (Univ. of Genova), Paolo Gastaldo (Univ. of Genova), Rodolfo Zunino (Univ. of Genova), Amer Baghdadi (IMT Atlantique, Lab-STICC), Mostafa Rizk (Lebanese University / Lebanese American University)

deep.problem: The paper targets IoT/IIoT network intrusion detection (traffic-flow classification into benign vs. attack types) under strict edge-device hardware budgets. Prior ML/DL-based IDS work reports strong offline accuracy but largely ignores flash, RAM, compute, latency and energy constraints, so models that look good offline don't fit real embedded gateways. The paper frames model selection as a constrained optimization problem: maximize validation accuracy subject to explicit caps on flash, RAM, and per-inference compute (Ops for tree models, FLOPs for the CNN), and asks whether tree-based ML and compact deep learning can both be pushed to meet those caps, and which family wins on which axis (accuracy vs. latency vs. energy).
deep.method: Two parallel hardware-aware search strategies over the SAME accuracy/flash/RAM/compute constraint formulation: (1) constrained grid search over three tree ensembles - LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest - tuning n_trees, max_depth, min_child_size, colsample, subsample, num_leaves, with flash/RAM/Ops analytically estimated from the trained tree structure before any deployment; (2) hardware-aware neural architecture search (HW-NAS) for compact 1D-CNNs, run as an evolutionary search (100 generations x 15 valid children/generation, mutate-best-parent) over filter count, kernel size, stride, dropout, pooling and padding, with every candidate hardware-profiled and rejected immediately if it exceeds budget before it is even trained. Deployment budget used: <=300 KB flash, <=50 KB RAM, <=1.5x10^6 ops/FLOPs. Models are trained on a workstation (RTX 3070 Ti), then the winning tree ensembles and the winning CNN are deployed unmodified (no quantization/compression, CNN runs float32) onto a Raspberry Pi 3 B+ (quad-core 1.4GHz Cortex-A53, 1GB RAM, Linux) acting as an IoT gateway, where the pipeline itself does live packet sniffing, 5-tuple flow aggregation, on-device feature extraction (47 features from headers only, no deep packet inspection), and local inference - no cloud round-trip. Energy/latency methodology (the part most relevant to replicate): a USB power meter is placed inline between the Pi and its power supply; instantaneous power is computed as P = I x V from the measured current draw, and energy-per-inference is average power x measured latency, with everything reported net of the measured idle baseline (500 mA / 2.5 W) and with feature-extraction time (avg 0.93 ms) reported and excluded separately from inference latency.
deep.dataset_used: Edge-IIoTset (Ferrag et al., IEEE Access 2022) - a labeled IoT/IIoT network-flow benchmark with benign traffic plus 14 attack types (e.g., DDoS-over-TCP, SQL injection, MITM, backdoor) spanning network/transport/application layers. Provided in two curated splits: a DL subset (2,218,386 samples) and an ML subset (157,800 samples), each with 63 numeric header/flow-level features. The authors prune this to 47 features by dropping payload fields, string application-layer attributes, and high-cardinality identifiers that can't be extracted in real time on a streaming device; features are min-max normalized to [0,1]. Three label granularities are evaluated: binary (benign vs. attack), 6-class (attack families), and 15-class (all individual attack types - the paper's primary target).
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy (%) and F1-score (%) via stratified 5-fold cross-validation (mean +/- std); Flash (KB, model storage size); peak RAM (KB, intermediate inference memory); per-inference compute (Ops in thousands for tree models, FLOPs in thousands for the CNN) as analytically-estimated proxies for latency/energy pre-deployment; and, only after physical deployment on the Raspberry Pi, four measured on-device numbers per model: latency (ms), current draw (mA), power (mW), and energy per inference (mJ).
deep.key_results: 15-class task (primary target): LightGBM 95.25% acc / 94.74% F1 at 74.93 KB flash, 1.13 KB RAM, 1.2K ops; XGBoost 95.11%/94.42% at 266.59 KB flash, 4.27K ops; Random Forest 94.12%/93.21% at 211.22 KB flash, 4.61 KB RAM, 3.38K ops - all far above the paper's own re-run of prior baselines (DT/RF/SVM/KNN from the Edge-IIoTset paper), which scored only 67-81% accuracy with no hardware reporting. Their HW-NAS CNN reached 96.73% acc / 97.24% F1 at 190.34 KB flash, 6.89 KB RAM, 838.89K FLOPs - lower peak accuracy than a few other published DL models (up to 99.96%) but at roughly 6-65x less flash and 7-10x fewer FLOPs than those, which is the paper's central "efficiency vs. accuracy" argument. 6-class and binary tasks show similar patterns (binary: LightGBM 99.93%/99.96% F1 at just 5.02 KB flash / 0.08K ops). On the physical Raspberry Pi 3 B+ (Table VII, net of idle baseline): Random Forest 70 ms / 65 mA / 325 mW / 22.75 mJ per inference; LightGBM 27 ms / 50 mA / 250 mW / 6.75 mJ; XGBoost 22 ms / 50 mA / 250 mW / 5.50 mJ; CNN 300 ms / 55 mA / 275 mW / 82.50 mJ. So the boosting-tree models are both fastest and most energy-efficient (sub-30 ms, under 7 mJ), while the CNN is the most accurate but ~10x more latency and ~12x more energy-hungry.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Confirmed directly from the paper's Conclusion (Section VII), quoting under the copyright limit: the authors write that future directions include "evaluating robustness under adversarial or noisy traffic," alongside compressing trained models (quantization/pruning) and adding explainability techniques. This is the exact gap the course brief flagged, and I verified it appears verbatim in the primary source rather than being inferred. Two further gaps are also apparent just from reading the methodology, though the paper never states them as limitations: (1) the models are trained once offline and evaluated with standard 5-fold cross-validation on IID data - there is no temporal split, no discussion of concept drift, and no online/continual learning or adaptation mechanism anywhere in the paper, so drift-adaptation is not just "future work," it is entirely outside this paper's scope; (2) the hardware target is a Raspberry Pi 3 B+ running Linux (quad-core 1.4 GHz Cortex-A53, 1 GB RAM) - a genuine gateway-class device, not a true microcontroller like an ESP32 (no OS, ~320-520 KB SRAM, no NEON/float-heavy pipeline), so even though the flash/RAM numbers for the tree models look ESP32-plausible, the CNN's 300 ms/82.5 mJ Pi latency would very likely be substantially worse on an ESP32-class MCU and would need to be re-measured, not assumed.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is a strong, directly reusable reference point for our project, on three fronts, with one clearly confirmed gap that our project fills. (1) Methodology to replicate: its USB-power-meter energy protocol (inline meter, P = I x V, energy = avg power x measured latency, reported net of idle baseline, feature-extraction time isolated from inference time) is exactly the kind of rigorous, cheap, replicable real-hardware-cost benchmark we should copy for our ESP32 deployment - we'd need our own idle-baseline current draw for the ESP32 board (very different from a Pi 3B+) and likely a finer-grained sensor (e.g., INA219/INA226 shunt) since ESP32 power draw is much lower than a Linux SBC's. (2) Candidate base architectures and a feasibility signal: their LightGBM/XGBoost numbers (as low as ~75 KB flash, ~1 KB RAM, sub-30 ms, under 7 mJ on a much bigger device) strongly suggest tree ensembles are the right starting family for an ESP32-class on-device detector - both because they are cheap enough to fit, and because their small size and split-based structure make them far more plausible to update/retrain incrementally on-device (for our drift adaptation) than the CNN, which their own numbers show is 10x more latency/energy-costly. Their CNN HW-NAS pipeline is a candidate baseline to compare against if we want an accuracy-priority arm. Edge-IIoTset is also a strong candidate dataset for us, and their published static-model accuracy/F1/hardware numbers are ready-made comparison points for our paper's tables. (3) The gap our project targets is confirmed, not assumed: this paper explicitly names "adversarial or noisy traffic" robustness as unaddressed future work, and independently, it contains zero treatment of concept drift or on-device adaptation - its models are frozen after offline training. Our project's core contribution (an unsupervised, ESP32-class on-device IDS that adapts to benign concept drift in normal traffic while resisting slow "boiling-frog" poisoning of its own adaptation loop, evaluated with the same RAM/latency/energy rigor this paper models) sits squarely in the gap this paper leaves open, and lets us frame our contribution against a concrete, recently-published (Dec 2025) hardware-aware IDS baseline rather than an abstract strawman - which is exactly the kind of "solution to a specific IoT constraint not adequately addressed" novelty the grading rubric rewards. One caveat for our proposal write-up: we should be explicit that we are moving from their Raspberry Pi 3 B+ (Linux SBC) down to a true ESP32 microcontroller, which is a materially harder hardware target than the one this paper validated, especially for latency/energy of any CNN-like component and for the RAM headroom needed to buffer a drift-adaptation/poisoning-detection window on top of the base classifier.

deep.title: ArrythML: An Autoencoder-Based TinyML Approach for On-Device Arrhythmia Detection on Resource-Constrained Embedded Systems
deep.authors: Nagarajan S, Kurian Polachan
deep.venue_year: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2606.02256 [cs.LG], submitted June 2026 (not yet peer-reviewed/published at a venue as far as could be verified)
deep.verified_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02256 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.02256, HTML full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.02256) — verified reachable and matching the candidate URL/title given in the task.
deep.fetch_status: success — full text retrieved and parsed (PDF fetch alone was partially garbled by compressed streams, but the arXiv HTML mirror at /html/2606.02256 gave complete, readable text including methods, all result tables, and the limitations/future-work section; abstract independently confirmed via /abs/2606.02256).
deep.problem: How to run cardiac-arrhythmia detection from raw ECG entirely on a resource-constrained microcontroller (flash/RAM/compute limited), avoiding cloud/hub offload (which costs energy for wireless transmission and introduces privacy/latency risk) and avoiding brittle rule-based DSP (QRS-complex detection, which degrades under noise and patient variability). They frame it as: segment ECG locally in real time and flag arrhythmic beats on-device, at a memory/latency/power budget a wearable MCU can sustain.
deep.method: Unsupervised anomaly detection via reconstruction error. ECG is segmented in real time using R-to-R intervals (cheap R-peak thresholding instead of expensive QRS-complex DSP), each segment resampled to a fixed 300 samples, and fed to an autoencoder trained ONLY on normal ("N") beats. Two lightweight architectures are compared: a DNN autoencoder (dense 300→128→32→128→300, ReLU/sigmoid, MAE loss) and a CNN autoencoder (input reshaped to 15x20x1, conv/pool encoder down to 16 filters, mirrored conv/upsample decoder). A beat is classified abnormal if its reconstruction error exceeds a threshold θ = μ + σ computed from the training-set normal-segment error distribution (no labeled abnormal data needed for the detector itself). Both models are converted with quantization-aware training to INT8, exported to TensorFlow Lite, serialized to a C byte array, and deployed via TensorFlow Lite Micro on an ESP32-S3 (dual-core Xtensa LX7 @240MHz, 512KB SRAM, 16MB flash, 8MB PSRAM), with on-device inference timed directly on hardware.
deep.dataset_used: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (48 half-hour two-channel recordings from 47 subjects, 360Hz, expert beat annotations), using only the MLII lead. A custom derived dataset: training set built from R-R segments labeled Normal (N) vs. a pooled Abnormal set (paced /, LBBB, RBBB, atrial premature A, ventricular escape E, fusion F — PVC/V and rare/non-cardiac annotation codes excluded), capped at 200 normal + 200 abnormal segments per patient record, giving 6,075 normal + 3,477 abnormal = 9,552 training segments. A separate, larger evaluation set of roughly 95,000 segments was built from 44 of the 48 MIT-BIH records (4 excluded for inverted QRS, lead mismatch, annotation shift, or heavy noise), bandpass-filtered and resampled the same way.
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score (standard binary normal-vs-abnormal classification metrics); reconstruction error (MAE) and its derived decision threshold θ=μ+σ; model size in KB; on-device inference latency in ms; firmware flash and RAM footprint in KB. Notably, despite motivating the work partly on energy/power constraints, no energy or battery-life measurement is reported anywhere in the paper — only latency.
deep.key_results: Floating-point PC simulation: DNN 73.3% acc / 57.4% prec / 94.2% recall / 71.4% F1 at 691KB; CNN 76.4% acc / 61.7% prec / 87.8% recall / 72.5% F1 at 180KB. After INT8 quantization-aware training (PC sim): DNN drops to 69.8% acc / 85.2% recall / 66.6% F1 at 180.1KB (~4x smaller than FP32); CNN drops to 69.2% acc / 83.5% recall / 65.7% F1 at 42.3KB (~4x smaller). On real ESP32-S3 hardware via TFLite Micro (matches PC-quantized numbers closely): DNN 69.7% acc / 85.4% recall / 66.6% F1, 180.1KB, 9ms inference; CNN 69.0% acc / 83.9% recall / 65.6% F1, 42.3KB, 71ms inference + 68ms SD-card I/O. Total firmware footprint: ~744KB flash, ~218KB RAM. Under a "refined" evaluation that filters out ambiguous mixed-beat R-R segments, best numbers rise to DNN 82.4% acc / 74.5% prec / 84.5% recall / 79.2% F1 (headline result the abstract highlights, alongside the 180KB size and 9ms latency). CNN is far smaller but ~8x slower on-device and slightly less accurate than DNN.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Authors explicitly name: (1) quantization sensitivity — their compact (<1000-neuron) baseline models are unusually sensitive to FP32→INT8 conversion, costing meaningful recall/accuracy; (2) single-lead (MLII-only) blindness — bundle-branch blocks (esp. RBBB, best seen in V1) and atrial-premature beats (rhythm-based, not morphology-based) are hard to catch without multi-lead input or RR-interval-variability features, proposed as future work; (3) R-R segmentation can mix multiple beat types in one window (e.g., bigeminy) and the current binary formulation can't disambiguate — authors say finer segmentation or a multiclass autoencoder formulation "remains part of ongoing work"; (4) false negatives from abnormal beats that are morphologically close to normal sinus beats; (5) noisy signals and MIT-BIH annotation inconsistencies (4 records excluded outright); (6) hyperparameter tuning was manual only — "a more systematic and comprehensive optimization... is left for future work"; (7) PVC/V beats were excluded from training entirely due to label/R-peak misalignment in the dataset, so the deployed model cannot flag PVCs; (8) no actual energy/power/battery measurement despite motivating the work on energy grounds — latency is reported, power is not; (9) authors call for clinical correlation before real deployment given false-positive sensitivity to benign waveform variants (tall P-waves, mild ST elevation, baseline wander).
deep.relation_to_our_project: This is the right methodological template to build on, and its gaps map almost exactly onto our novelty claims. Shared template: unsupervised, train-on-normal-only autoencoder; anomaly = reconstruction error above a statistically-derived threshold (θ=μ+σ); INT8 quantization-aware training; TFLite Micro deployment on an ESP32-class MCU; and — most useful for us methodologically — their exact reporting convention (model size in KB, on-device inference latency in ms, firmware flash/RAM footprint in KB, FP32-vs-INT8 accuracy trade-off table) is precisely the "hardware cost" reporting format our project already commits to (RAM, latency, energy), and we should mirror their FP32-baseline vs. quantized vs. on-device three-way comparison table structure. Where it stops, we start: (a) ArrythML's autoencoder and its μ+σ threshold are frozen after one-time training — there is no online/incremental adaptation mechanism at all, so it has nothing to say about benign concept drift in the "normal" class over time, which is a central pillar of our project; (b) it never considers an adversary manipulating the model's notion of "normal" — no poisoning threat model, no defense, nothing about slow/boiling-frog attacks on adaptation, which is our other central pillar and a total gap in this paper; (c) it explicitly did not measure energy/power despite motivating on that basis — we can directly fill that stated gap and report real energy numbers on our ESP32 board, strengthening our "real hardware cost" evaluation claim; (d) its quantization-sensitivity finding (small models are disproportionately hurt by INT8 conversion) is a direct warning for us: if our IDS needs an online-adaptable autoencoder/threshold updated in the field, we need to characterize whether incremental updates under quantization remain stable, especially under a poisoning attacker who might exploit that instability. In short, ArrythML gives us a validated, benchmarked, real-hardware pattern for "small reconstruction-error autoencoder on ESP32 via TFLite Micro, reported against RAM/latency/model-size" that we can adapt from ECG anomaly detection to network-traffic intrusion detection, while our contribution — drift-adaptive, poison-resilient online threshold/model updating with real energy measurement — addresses exactly the two dimensions (adaptation and adversarial robustness) this paper's own limitations section says it does not touch.

deep.title: TinyML for On-Device and Edge Analytics in Wireless Networks: A Survey of Deployments, Opportunities, and Concept-Drift Mitigation
deep.authors: Prasoon Raghuwanshi, Vimal Bhatia, Sridhar Iyer, Matti Latva-aho, Onel Luis Alcaraz López (Univ. of Oulu / IIT Indore / SGBIT)
deep.venue_year: arXiv:2606.30843v1 [eess.SY], submitted 29 Jun 2026 (preprint; also cross-listed cs.SY, eess.SP)
deep.fetch_status: Full text successfully retrieved and read directly from the arXiv PDF (28 pages, all sections, tables and figures parsed) — not just the abstract. Verified as a genuine, currently-live arXiv preprint matching the candidate URL exactly (title, author list, arXiv ID, and June 29 2026 submission date all confirmed from the PDF's own header/footer text).
deep.problem: This is a survey (not a single-experiment paper). It addresses three linked problems: (1) cataloging which tinyML algorithms/frameworks suit battery-powered end-devices, batteryless (energy-harvesting) end-devices, and low-power edge nodes; (2) surveying where tinyML-based end-device/edge inference has already been used vs. remains untapped in wireless-network problems (channel estimation, positioning, radar, WPT, cognitive radio, intrusion detection, etc.); and (3) — the section most relevant to us — how to update/retrain an already-deployed tinyML model on such constrained devices when the operating data distribution drifts away from the training distribution ("concept drift"), for both battery-powered and batteryless devices.
deep.method: For concept-drift mitigation (Section V, the core relevant contribution) the paper proposes a centralized federated-learning-based "tinyFL" model-update loop: a central entity (edge/cloud server) distributes an initialized global tinyML model to target devices; each device fine-tunes it via on-device training; devices send back only their trainable-parameter updates; the server aggregates (FedAvg / TinyReptile / proportion-weighting) into a new global model; the updated model is redistributed — repeated until convergence. To make the "on-device training" step feasible under MCU memory limits they describe three backprop-efficiency techniques: gradient scaling (rescales gradients of quantized weights to fix a weight-norm/gradient-norm destabilization), sparse update (selectively updates only a contribution-ranked subset of layers/weights/biases instead of full backprop), and a "tiny training engine" (compiles a pruned, operator-reordered static backward graph into memory/latency-efficient binary code). For batteryless (energy-harvesting) devices they layer this with over-the-air gradient aggregation (exploiting multiple-access-channel waveform superposition), an intermittent-aware "modify" operation for safely patching in-place model code under power loss, update-aware checkpointing (splitting SRAM into a stack region and an update-buffer region that are separately backed up on a low-power interrupt), and a fault-tolerant, reboot-free bootloader. None of this machinery includes any adversarial or data-integrity check — the on-device training data and the transmitted parameter updates are implicitly assumed honest/benign throughout.
deep.dataset_used: No single primary dataset — as a survey it reports numbers drawn from the papers it cites. The concept-drift/training-efficiency tables (Tables VI–VIII) reuse results from Lin et al. [ref 10, "Tiny machine learning: progress and futures"] on Stanford Cars, Food-101, Oxford Flowers, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, Oxford-IIIT Pets, and Visual Wake Words (VWW), training MCUNet-5FPS and MobileNetV2-w0.35 models. The RL-based device-scheduling comparison (Fig. 10) reuses a synthetic nonlinear dynamic-process/query-response setup from the same authors' own prior work [ref 108]. The cited on-device NIDS result (Section III-I) is from Javed et al. [ref 94], trained/tested on IoT traffic covering DoS, ransomware, scanning, MITM, DDoS, backdoor, XSS, injection, brute-force and port-scanning attack classes (dataset not further specified in this survey's summary).
deep.metrics_reported: Classification/detection accuracy (%), model size (kB/MB, parameter count), MAC operations, inference latency (ms/µs), on-device training latency per image (ms), peak/extra memory footprint during training (kB), energy per inference or per training-restart (µJ/mJ), localization/positioning error (% reduction), asset-tracking and image-retrieval accuracy (%), MSE of query/actuation response, RL scheduler computational complexity (# arithmetic ops) and peak RAM (MB), and bit-error-rate/SNR trade-offs for physical-layer tasks.
deep.key_results: (1) Systematic review of 146 candidate studies (18 prior tinyML surveys, 42 framework papers, 28+35 tapped/untapped wireless-deployment papers, 12 concept-drift papers) finds no prior survey comprehensively covers tinyML deployment across wireless networks nor FL-assisted tinyML updates for batteryless devices. (2) A large catalog (Table III) of tinyML algorithms by target board (ESP32/STM32/MSP430/Raspberry Pi), algorithm type (DL/UL/RL) and task. (3) Nine already-documented deployment realms are summarized (Table IV), including a two-layer signature-based tinyML NIDS achieving 97.6% accuracy / 1.5ms inference at the device layer and 98.3%/2.24ms at the cloud layer (ref [94]). (4) Ten untapped realms are proposed with concrete RL/DL formulations (Table V) — near-field WPT, backscatter WSNs, goal-oriented communication, wake-up-radio duty cycling, underwater VLC, AMC, cognitive-radio CSS/D2D allocation, SEI, AGC prediction, BLE proximity. (5) For concept drift: gradient scaling recovers near-fp32 accuracy for int8-quantized MCUNet-5FPS (e.g., Cars: 31.2%→55.2%, close to fp32's 56.7%); sparse update achieves ~72% average accuracy with only ~138kB extra memory (vs ~545kB for naive last-k-layer updates); the "tiny training engine" cuts MobileNetV2-w0.35 training latency 23× (8501ms→373ms/image) and peak memory 21× (2939kB→141kB) versus full backpropagation, at equal 75.1% accuracy. For batteryless devices, the proposed fault-tolerant update framework needs only ~2.5mJ to resume a model update after a power interrupt (vs ~67.5mJ for the FLoRa baseline, which can fail entirely) and completes a full LeNet-5 update in ~1350ms on a 10mF supercapacitor where FLoRa does not finish. (6) Final Table IX lists five 6G-integration research realms: tinyML–largeML integration, high-mobility/6G-target datasets, end-to-end energy-lifecycle profiling, ethical/sociotechnical integration (consent, privacy, bias, liability), and trustworthy/interpretable decision-making.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Explicitly named gaps (Table IX and body text): (a) Datasets — "current datasets primarily capture static or low-mobility scenarios, limiting the performance evaluation of adaptive tinyML approaches, such as online learning, incremental model updates" and no datasets exist yet to benchmark tinyML against 6G targets; (b) Energy lifecycle — no framework captures the full energy pipeline (wake-up, sensing, preprocessing, inference, comms, self-discharge) end-to-end, so battery-life claims are unrealistic; (c) Ethical/sociotechnical — consent, data-minimization compliance, algorithmic bias, and liability are unresolved and "significantly influence adoption... of tinyML solutions in 6G," with only a generic call for on-device anonymization/differential-privacy guards; (d) Trustworthy/interpretable decision-making — existing explainability methods (SHAP, LIME) are "computationally expensive and require post-hoc processing," unsuitable for safety-critical real-time tinyML; only a vague pointer to "lightweight proxy" rule-extraction methods is given; (e) tinyML–largeML integration lacks standardized interoperability frameworks. Separately in the body: "tiny RL, suited for decision-making tasks in wireless networks, remains unexplored" (most existing work is tiny DL for feature extraction); and, most directly relevant to us, Section III-I states plainly that anomaly-based (as opposed to signature-based) intrusion detection is "currently... exclusively handled by the central control unit," and that "tinyML-based NIDS, which could be embedded in the end-device, for detecting anomaly-based intrusions is a valid open research area." Critically, and confirmed by a full read of Section V, the paper's entire FL-based concept-drift-adaptation procedure (Fig. 14) and its batteryless-device extensions (over-the-air aggregation, intermittent-aware modify, checkpointing, fault-tolerant bootloader) contain no discussion whatsoever of a malicious, compromised, or slowly-drifting-adversarial device — data/model-update integrity, poisoning, or robustness to manipulated local training data during the adaptation loop is never raised anywhere in the concept-drift section, nor connected to the one place elsewhere in the paper (Section IV-G, cognitive-radio CSS) where "learning-based attacks" on an ML decision are even mentioned.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This is exceptionally strong, directly-on-point supporting literature for our proposal and gives concrete engineering and benchmarking building blocks: (1) It independently and explicitly flags on-device anomaly-based NIDS as an open problem distinct from the signature-based on-device NIDS that already exists — validating the "on-device intrusion detection" half of our project as a recognized, unsolved gap in this very recent (2026) survey rather than something we invented. (2) It hands us the state-of-the-art benign drift-adaptation mechanism — the centralized tinyFL loop (distribute → on-device train → transmit params → FedAvg-style aggregate → redistribute) — as the natural baseline our system should be built on and then shown to be vulnerable to; since the survey's own treatment of this loop assumes honest devices throughout, our "boiling-frog" slow-poisoning threat model targets exactly the mechanism this paper proposes as the fix for concept drift, with no defense proposed anywhere in the survey. This is precisely the literature gap the task description hoped to confirm, and the full-text read verifies it directly rather than from an abstract guess. (3) It supplies the concrete on-device training-efficiency toolkit (gradient scaling, sparse/selective-layer update, compiled "tiny training engine") that we will likely need to adapt to make any drift-tracking or poisoning-robust retraining feasible within ESP32-class RAM/flash budgets — these are reusable, citable techniques rather than something we need to invent from scratch. (4) It establishes the standard "hardware cost" reporting currency (model size in kB, MACs, inference latency in ms, peak/extra training memory in kB, energy in µJ/mJ per inference or per update) that our own RAM/latency/energy evaluation should mirror so our results are directly comparable to numbers already in this literature (e.g., tinyMAN's <100KB/~28µJ-per-inference RL footprint; the 141kB/373ms tiny-training-engine numbers; FLoRa's 67.5mJ vs. 2.5mJ interrupted-update energy). (5) Its separate, disconnected mention of "learning-based attacks" only in the cognitive-radio spectrum-sensing context (not the concept-drift/FL section) shows the community already has an adversarial-ML vocabulary but has not yet applied it to on-device drift adaptation — reinforcing that "poisoning-resilient drift-adaptive on-device NIDS" is a genuinely novel intersection with real, demonstrable publishing potential, and this paper is an ideal anchor citation for our related-work/gap section.

So on stated limitations specifically, treat everything except the two directly-quoted sentences in that field as inferred, not verified verbatim.
deep.problem: IoT devices are widely deployed but have minimal active security due to limited compute/energy, and while many ML-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) have been proposed in the literature, almost none have been demonstrated actually running on the common low-power chipsets (e.g. ESP8266) found in real IoT devices — existing work mostly stays at simulation/desktop-evaluation level or, when ported to hardware (e.g. TensorFlow Lite Micro), consumes so much flash/RAM that it barely fits or doesn't fit at all on cheap microcontrollers. The paper sets out to close this practical-implementation gap by building and verifying a genuinely low-power, low-latency, small-footprint ML-based NIDS that runs on real IoT-class hardware.
deep.dataset_used: Five standard NIDS benchmark datasets, evaluated separately (not combined): ToN-IoT, BoT-IoT, MQTT-IoT-IDS2020, UNSW-NB15, and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 — using the NetFlow-standardized ("NF-") versions of BoT-IoT/ToN-IoT/UNSW-NB15/CSE-CIC-IDS2018 rather than raw packet captures. Classes were balanced via random undersampling; evaluation used stratified 5-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times.
deep.method: A deliberately "shallow learning" choice: a scikit-learn Decision Tree Classifier (not deep learning), trained on NetFlow features with cost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha=0.0001) and max_depth swept over {5, 6, 10, 12}. The core contribution is not the ML model itself but a custom source-to-source compiler the authors built: a Python tool that converts a trained scikit-learn tree directly into C code expressed as nested if/else statements (deliberately avoiding the recursive-function/global-array style used by existing tools like sklearn-porter), because nested-if C compiles to fewer instructions and a smaller binary. That generated C is dropped into a firmware template with serial-input handling and micros()-based timing instrumentation, then compiled and flashed to real hardware: ESP8266 (inside an actual modified smart light bulb, with a green/red LED indicating normal/attack), ESP32-WROOM-32, and an Arduino Uno (ATmega328p). Per-flow inference time was benchmarked by calling the prediction function 100,000 times to overcome timer-resolution limits.
deep.metrics_reported: Balanced accuracy and F1 score (classification quality); per-flow inference time in microseconds (measured on-device); compiled program/binary size in bytes at GCC -O0 and -O3 (via the Linux `size` tool); BSS/RAM usage; flash footprint as a percentage of total device program space. No energy-consumption figures are reported.
deep.key_results: At tree depth 12: balanced accuracy of roughly 99.9% on BoT-IoT and MQTT-IoT-IDS2020, ~99.2% on ToN-IoT, ~98.5% on UNSW-NB15, ~98.2% on CSE-CIC-IDS2018. Per-flow inference time averaged across the IoT datasets: ~0.89 µs on ESP32, ~1.78 µs on ESP8266, ~7.99 µs on the ATmega328p (Arduino Uno) — i.e. sub-microsecond-to-low-microsecond real hardware inference. Flash footprint on ESP8266 was reported as roughly 10% of program space, versus ~90% for a comparable TensorFlow Lite Micro model from prior work; their converter also produced smaller/faster code than the existing sklearn-porter baseline. Critically, their tree fit and ran with sub-millisecond inference on the memory-poorest device tested (ATmega328p), where the TensorFlow Lite baseline they compare against reportedly could not fit a model at all.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Two points are close to directly stated by the authors: (1) they explicitly frame their evaluation as using benchmark NetFlow records fed in over serial, contrasted with "a practical deployment of our NIDS in an IoT device," where "flow records would be generated in real-time from the network traffic observed on the Wi-Fi interface" — i.e., they flag, without building, the live on-device flow-generation/real traffic pipeline as work beyond this paper's scope; (2) they note that derivative NetFlow-standardized datasets have elsewhere "shown comparable performance to works using the datasets in their original packet capture format," implicitly caveating that their results rest on NetFlow-format data rather than raw packets. Beyond that, nothing in the fetched content indicates they tested, mentioned, or attempted: concept drift / non-stationary traffic, on-device retraining or adaptation of any kind, or adversarial/data-poisoning robustness — these are simply absent from the paper's scope, not explicitly disclaimed. The model is trained once, offline, on static benchmark data and flashed as a fixed decision tree; there is no online-learning component at all.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is the right "real-hardware cost floor" reference for our proposal, exactly as the survey note flagged it. It gives three things we should build directly on: (1) A concrete, verified baseline for what a maximally lightweight, static supervised NIDS costs on ESP32-class hardware — sub-microsecond to a few microseconds per-flow inference, ~10% flash on ESP8266, and a tree that even fits on an 8-bit ATmega328p. Any RAM/latency/energy overhead our poison-resilient drift-adaptation layer adds should be reported against this floor (e.g. "our adaptive layer adds X µs / Y KB RAM over Manocchio et al.'s static-tree baseline of 0.89 µs / ~10% flash on ESP32/ESP8266"), which gives our evaluation section an externally-anchored, defensible baseline instead of an invented one. (2) A reusable on-device benchmarking methodology we can adopt wholesale: their nested-if C-codegen approach for compiling a trained model to a tiny binary, and their micros()-based, 100,000-repeat timing harness for measuring per-inference latency on real ESP32/ESP8266 hardware — this is exactly the kind of rigorous hardware-cost evaluation methodology our project needs and can cite/reuse rather than reinvent. (3) Most importantly, the gap: this is a purely static, offline-trained, supervised decision tree with zero notion of concept drift, online adaptation, or adversarial/poisoning robustness — it is flashed once and never updates. Our project's entire novelty (unsupervised on-device adaptation to benign drift, made robust to slow "boiling-frog" poisoning of that adaptation) targets precisely the space this paper leaves completely untouched, while inheriting its proof that decision-tree-class models are the right complexity class for ESP32-class inference budgets. This supports keeping the underlying detector lightweight (tree/threshold-based, not deep learning) and spending our compute/memory/energy budget on the adaptation-and-poison-resistance mechanism rather than the base classifier — with this paper's numbers as the "no-adaptation" control condition in our own hardware evaluation table.

deep.title: Secure Federated Intrusion Detection for Resource-Constrained IoT Devices Using Lightweight Cryptography: A Hardware-Validated Study
deep.venue_year: Future Internet (MDPI, ISSN 1999-5903), Vol. 18, Issue 6, Article 306; published 5 June 2026. DOI: 10.3390/fi18060306. URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1999-5903/18/6/306
deep.authors: Full author names/affiliations could not be verified — the accessible extraction only returned initials (Y.T., A.A., N.A., Z.A., J.A., S.L., D.D., D.O.). Treat authorship as unresolved; do not cite these initials as fact without checking the live MDPI page or Google Scholar directly.
deep.problem: The paper targets a specific integration gap, not a new attack or a new cipher: lightweight block ciphers (SPECK/SIMON/PRESENT-class) have been benchmarked in isolation before, but nobody had validated a *complete, end-to-end secure federated-learning (FL) pipeline* — key establishment, per-round encryption, integrity checking, replay protection, AND the resulting intrusion-detection accuracy — on real MCU-class IoT hardware. So the stated problem is: how do you protect FL model-update exchange (confidentiality, integrity, freshness, source authentication) between resource-constrained IoT clients and a server, while staying inside the RAM/latency/energy budget of a microcontroller, and does this security layer meaningfully degrade IDS accuracy or add meaningful runtime overhead when actually measured on hardware (not simulated)?
deep.method: Centralized-server FL architecture: 3x ESP32-S3-N16R8V microcontrollers as clients, a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B as the aggregation server. Security stack: ECDH (P-256) + a pre-shared key for device authentication, HKDF-SHA256 key derivation, then per-round CTR-mode symmetric encryption of model updates plus HMAC-SHA256 integrity tags, with monotonic round numbers + nonce uniqueness for replay protection; message format {ID, round_number, nonce, ciphertext, HMAC_tag}; aggregation via standard FedAvg. Three lightweight block ciphers (SPECK, SIMON, PRESENT) are swapped in as the CTR-mode payload cipher and benchmarked head-to-head on the actual chip. The IDS model itself is a small MLP (47 input features -> 128 -> 64 -> 32 -> 16-class softmax output) trained federated over 20 global rounds (1 local epoch/round, batch 32, lr 0.001). Energy/power was measured with real instrumentation (NI ELVIS II+ + LabVIEW acquisition), not estimated.
deep.dataset_used: CICIoT2023 (benign traffic + 33 attack types spanning DDoS, DoS, Recon, Web-based, Brute Force, Spoofing, Mirai). For hardware feasibility they used a reduced subset: 5,000 records across 16 selected classes, 80/20 train/test split (4,000/1,000). Primary configuration is equal IID data allocation across the 3 clients; a secondary experiment uses a non-IID label-skew split across clients. Preprocessing: NaN removal, infinity replacement, log-transform of the "Rate" feature, min-max scaling.
deep.metrics_reported: Two metric families: (1) cryptographic/hardware-cost metrics per cipher — RAM footprint (bytes), ROM footprint (kB), per-byte encryption/decryption latency (µs/byte), throughput (MB/s), energy per operation (mJ), and active-vs-idle board power (W); (2) IDS-quality metrics — accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, compared across centralized training, federated-IID, and federated-non-IID; plus end-to-end system overhead — per-round crypto cost in ms and as a % of total round duration, and communication metadata overhead in bytes and as a % of update size.
deep.key_results: Cipher comparison: SPECK is cheapest (RAM 504B, ROM 31.3kB, 0.135 µs/B encrypt, 8.68 MB/s throughput, 138.3 mJ); SIMON is mid-tier (568B RAM, 0.41 µs/B, 1.96 MB/s, 184.9 mJ); PRESENT is far most expensive (656B RAM, 89.4 µs/B, only 0.011 MB/s, 446.2 mJ) — roughly two orders of magnitude slower than SPECK. IDS accuracy: centralized baseline 86.80% (P 0.88/R 0.87/F1 0.86); federated-IID 85.43% (P 0.87/R 0.85/F1 0.84), close to centralized; federated-non-IID drops to 83.24% (no P/R/F1 broken out for this config in the accessible text). Training converged stably over the 20 rounds. Crucially, security overhead was small: SPECK-based protection added only ~68 ms per FL round, ~0.17% of total round time (local on-device training dominates at ~88.8% of round time), and crypto metadata added only ~50 bytes (~0.13% of update size) — i.e., the paper's headline claim is that end-to-end cryptographic protection is "nearly free" on ESP32-class hardware when SPECK is used.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: This is the load-bearing part for our project. The authors explicitly scope poisoning/robustness OUT of this paper and name almost exactly our project's defense target as needed future work. Verbatim/near-verbatim: "Attacks such as poisoning, Byzantine behavior, gradient manipulation, and model inversion after server-side decryption are outside the protection scope of the current framework." They then name the fix themselves: "Addressing such attacks would require complementary mechanisms such as robust aggregation, Byzantine-resilient FL, anomaly detection over model updates, client trust scoring, secure aggregation, or differential privacy." They also state the framework gives only "communication-level protection" and explicitly "does not address attacks originating from compromised or malicious legitimate clients" — i.e. it defends the wire, not the model-update content itself. Other stated limitations: (i) non-IID/client heterogeneity — "clients may differ in data volume, class distribution, processing speed, remaining battery level, and network quality. These factors can amplify non-IID effects and data imbalance... Such conditions should be considered in future larger-scale evaluations under more heterogeneous deployment settings" (this is *spatial* heterogeneity across 3 clients at one point in time — the paper does NOT test or discuss any *temporal* concept-drift dimension at all); (ii) scale — "three ESP32 clients, 20 rounds, lightweight MLP, 5,000-record subset" is called "a hardware-constrained feasibility study rather than a full-scale benchmark," and "validation on other IoT traffic profiles remains necessary"; (iii) network realism — "packet loss, unstable Wi-Fi connectivity, delayed delivery... should be included in subsequent deployment-oriented evaluations"; (iv) key-management scalability "should be evaluated in larger deployments"; (v) privacy — the framework "does not provide secure aggregation or privacy against the server after decryption" (server sees plaintext updates post-decryption); (vi) source attribution — "stronger source attribution would require additional mechanisms such as digital signatures, device certificates, hardware secure elements, or remote attestation, which are considered future extensions." Closing future-work list: "secure aggregation, malicious-client detection, poisoning-resilient aggregation, privacy protection against model-inversion risks, and stronger source attribution mechanisms."
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is close to an ideal "gap paper" for us, for three reasons, plus one important distinction to keep our claims precise. (1) Self-identified gap match: the authors explicitly list "poisoning," "Byzantine behavior," "robust aggregation," "anomaly detection over model updates," and "client trust scoring" as named, out-of-scope future work. Our working project — an on-device IDS that specifically resists slow "boiling-frog" poisoning of its own adaptation loop — is not a loosely-inspired offshoot, it is a direct, citable continuation of a limitation this paper's own authors wrote down. That is a strong, defensible novelty argument for our proposal/mid-review: "[Paper] hardware-validates secure FL/IDS on ESP32 but explicitly excludes poisoning-robustness from scope and calls for anomaly detection over updates / robust aggregation as future work; we build exactly that missing piece, specialized to the harder case of on-device unsupervised drift adaptation rather than federated aggregation." (2) Methodological template for our hardware-cost evaluation: their reporting format (RAM in bytes, ROM in kB, per-op latency in µs, throughput in MB/s, energy in mJ via real power-rail instrumentation, and overhead expressed as % of total round/inference time) is exactly the rigor our brief asks for ("evaluated against real hardware cost: RAM, latency, energy"). We should mirror this table structure at our mid-review, substituting our own measurement rig (an INA219/INA3221 current-sense breakout on the ESP32 is a practical, well-documented substitute for their NI ELVIS II+ setup) and reporting our drift-adaptation/anomaly-scoring overhead the same way. (3) Dataset and baseline anchor: CICIoT2023 is a credible, current IoT-specific benchmark already used by this paper and by several adjacent works surfaced in search (Edge-FLGuard+, Cross-Layer FL IDS, federated class-incremental IDS). Adopting CICIoT2023 (or pairing it with a device-level dataset like N-BaIoT/Bot-IoT) gives us direct comparability — e.g., we can cite their 86.80% centralized / 85.43% federated-IID / 83.24% non-IID MLP accuracy as a reference point our own unsupervised drift-adaptive detector should be benchmarked against (recognizing our task, unsupervised anomaly/novelty detection under drift plus an active poisoning adversary, is strictly harder than their supervised closed-set classification, so direct accuracy comparison needs careful framing, not a naive "we beat their number" claim). Important distinction to state explicitly in our own related-work section, to avoid a reviewer conflating our contribution with theirs: their "non-IID" result is about *spatial* heterogeneity across 3 simultaneous federated clients (different data distributions between devices at the same time), not *temporal* concept drift within one device's traffic stream over time — the paper contains zero treatment of temporal drift or of an adversary that manipulates the drift/adaptation signal itself. So our threat model (single-device, unsupervised, online-adaptation loop, attacked via slowly-injected "benign-looking" poisoned samples) is genuinely uncovered by this paper and, as far as this fetch could determine, not addressed by its cited future-work either — which is exactly the kind of "gap not adequately addressed" novelty the course rubric asks for. One more useful contrast for our design: classical robust-aggregation defenses (Krum, trimmed-mean, etc.) that the paper gestures toward assume *many independent federated clients* whose updates can be statistically compared/down-weighted against each other; our setting is a *single device* adapting to its own drifting stream with no peer clients to compare against, so those specific mechanisms don't transfer directly — we will need a within-device robustness mechanism (e.g., bounded/rate-limited adaptation, drift-vs-attack discrimination via sample provenance or gradual-vs-abrupt statistics, or a small trusted-anchor/replay buffer) rather than a cross-client aggregation defense, which is itself worth a sentence of justification in our proposal. Finally, this paper also reinforces topical fit: the instructor's stated interest areas (edge intelligence for resource-constrained systems, ML/DL-assisted IoT security, lightweight authentication) are precisely what this paper covers, and our project sits one step further down the same research line (from "secure the channel" to "secure/robustify the on-device learning process itself"), which should read as a natural, well-motivated extension rather than an unrelated pivot.

deep.title: Empowering IoT Security: On-Device Intrusion Detection in Resource Constrained Devices
deep.authors: Vasilis Ieropoulos, Eirini Anthi, Theodoros Spyridopoulos, Pete Burnap (Cardiff University, School of Computer Science & Informatics) and Aftab Khan, Pietro Carnelli (Toshiba Bristol Research and Innovation Laboratory). Corresponding author: Vasilis Ieropoulos (ieropoulosv@cardiff.ac.uk).
deep.venue_year: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2605.13159 [cs.CR] — no peer-reviewed venue found; reference list entries mostly cite 2016-2023 work, so this looks like a 2024-vintage manuscript posted to arXiv under a 2026 arXiv ID (may be a delayed/re-submitted posting). Treat as a preprint, not a confirmed A*/Q1 publication.
deep.fetch_status: Full text successfully obtained. The arxiv.org/abs page fetched cleanly via WebFetch. The PDF (6.6MB, 14 pages) would not render as text through WebFetch directly, so it was downloaded, then extracted with PyMuPDF (fitz): plain-text extraction worked for ~8 of 14 pages, and the remaining pages (which turned out to contain the key figures/tables — power measurements, results, limitations) were rendered to PNG at 2.5x and read as images. All sections were recovered this way, including Table V (power consumption), Table VI (manufacturer comparison), Section V "Limitations of Approach", and Section VI "Conclusion and Future Work". No content was invented; everything below is drawn directly from the extracted text/figures.
deep.problem: The paper asks whether a genuinely bare-metal, resource-constrained IoT microcontroller (not a Raspberry Pi or other single-board computer with a full OS) can run its own intrusion detection system on-device, rather than relying on a centralized/network-wide IDS. Centralized IDS is framed as a single point of failure and as struggling with segmented IoT networks; the authors' stated motivation is a typical home-user scenario where the user has no expertise to deploy network-level security (firewalls, IDS appliances). They target the two attack classes they identify as most common for these devices: Denial-of-Service (UDP/TCP flood, Ping of Death, SYN flood) and Man-in-the-Middle/sniffing. They explicitly claim this is the first paper to deploy an ML-based IDS on truly bare-metal resource-constrained IoT hardware (as opposed to prior work on Raspberry Pi-class devices or in simulation).
deep.method: Hardware: ESP32-S3 WROOM (dual-core Xtensa LX7), chosen over ESP8266/ESP32-C3/RISC-V variants for ARM-ecosystem maturity and ML-readiness. Testbed: ESP32 acting as a sensing IoT device (temp/humidity), connected via a TP-LINK AC1200 AP to an MQTT server on a desktop, with other ESP32s and Raspberry Pi 3s on the same isolated network as background traffic/noise, plus an attacker machine. Data collection: the Arduino Netdump library sniffs the ESP32's own inbound/outbound surface-level TCP traffic (not full promiscuous-mode capture, since that would break the device's own network connection) over a continuous 24-hour run, with attack scripts fired at random times/random scripts via a bash loop, producing a labeled (Legitimate/Anomalous) 5.1MB CSV. IP addresses, ports, and timestamps are deliberately stripped from features for generalizability and to dodge the Arduino time library's 50-day counter-reset bug. Two on-device models are trained and deployed: (1) a decision tree, compiled to C using cstdarg so it runs natively with no external library (99% accuracy/F1, but ~235KB); (2) a neural network (9-8-7-5-3-2 architecture, ReLU hidden layers + sigmoid output, trained 200 epochs in TensorFlow/Keras, converted via TFLite-to-C) deployed through the EloquentTinyML library (96% accuracy/F1, only ~26KB — about 10x smaller than the decision tree). To cut false positives and save power, a cheap hard-coded rule-based filter (checks for abnormal packet rates / malformed packets, e.g. rejecting packets read as "type(0x6d)") gates whether the heavier ML model is invoked at all. Because a DoS attack on a single-core busy loop starved the MQTT telemetry thread, the workload is split across the ESP32's two cores (Core 0 = filtering + ML model; Core 1 = telemetry/MQTT), with direct GPIO port manipulation (bypassing digitalWrite overhead) used for the anomaly-indicator LED. Power was measured two independent ways for cross-validation: (a) an oscilloscope reading voltage drop across a precision resistor in-line with the ESP32's supply, with P=V×I via Ohm's law, and (b) the bench power supply's own onboard ammeter reading; a camera logged readings over time. Results were cross-checked against Espressif's own ESP32-S3 published power figures.
deep.dataset_used: A self-collected, custom dataset (not a public benchmark like NSL-KDD/KDD99/UNSW-NB15/BoT-IoT — the paper's own literature-review table explicitly notes that those are the datasets prior work relies on and argues a new dataset "is to be created" because existing ones under-cover MITM/sniffing on Layers 1-2). Captured directly off the ESP32's own network interface via Netdump over one continuous 24-hour period with randomly-timed scripted attacks (DoS variants, MITM, sniffing) interspersed with normal MQTT telemetry traffic and multi-device background noise (other ESP32s + 3x Raspberry Pi 3 sensors). Final size: 5.1MB CSV, features = direction, IPv4 addresses(later stripped)/type/port(stripped)/TCP seq/ack/win/len, target label = Legitimate/Anomalous.
deep.metrics_reported: Classification accuracy and F1-score (both models reported with matching accuracy=F1 figures); compiled/deployed model file size in KB; power draw in Watts under three operating modes; a 24-hour continuous power-draw time series; required battery capacity in Ah (via the Peukert lead-acid battery equation) for 24-hour autonomous operation; a qualitative comparison against Espressif's own manufacturer-published ESP32-S3 power-mode table (deep sleep, wake/no-WiFi, WiFi-connected/no-traffic, sending MQTT, etc.).
deep.key_results: Decision tree: 99% accuracy/F1, but a ~235KB model with an external-library dependency (EloquentTinyML/decision-tree runtime) and higher compute cost. Neural network: 96% accuracy/F1 (test accuracy plateaus ≈0.966 after ~epoch 10 of 200, with training accuracy near 1.0 — small train/test gap, low overfitting), but only ~26KB once converted to C via TFLite, ~10x smaller than the decision tree, at the cost of needing the EloquentTinyML runtime. Oscilloscope/bench-supply power draw, cross-validated against two independent measurement instruments and against Espressif's own published ESP32-S3 power specs (which the authors say closely matched their measurements): Normal/idle baseline ≈0.355 W; with the cheap rule-based pre-filter running continuously ≈0.630 W; with the pre-filter plus the full ML model actually triggered ≈0.930 W (peak). Over a simulated continuous 24-hour run, power oscillates between roughly the 0.355 W baseline and 0.930 W peaks whenever the model fires. Required lead-acid battery capacity for worst-case continuous 24h operation of filter+model: 5.6 Ah (about the size of a medium power bank).
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Section V ("Limitations of Approach") explicitly states: (1) "memory constraints on microcontrollers can restrict the size of the dataset used for training and the complexity of the model. This limitation may impact the model's ability to generalise to unseen or evolving attack patterns." (2) Critically, in the authors' own words: "the storage capacity for updating and maintaining the model's knowledge base may be limited, potentially hindering its adaptability" — i.e., they explicitly flag on-device continual/incremental model updating under memory constraints as an open, unaddressed problem, exactly as the task brief described. (3) IoT heterogeneity (device/protocol diversity) complicates a one-size-fits-all deployment. (4) Overfitting risk is worsened by memory-limited training sets; L1/L2 regularisation is suggested but noted to add complexity the device may struggle to afford. (5) Battery/energy constraints limit how much continuous monitoring is sustainable. Section VI ("Conclusion and Future Work") adds: refining/tuning the models with more attack scenarios and algorithms, and — most directly relevant — "IoT networks are dynamic, with devices constantly joining and leaving the network. Future work could explore the development of adaptive models that can learn and adjust to changes in the network environment." They also call for a deeper comparative trade-off study of the two model types. Notably, the paper implements only static, one-shot-trained models — no adaptive/continual learning is attempted at all, and poisoning/robustness of any future adaptation mechanism is never discussed or even mentioned.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is close but complementary to "Poison-Resilient On-Device Intrusion Detection for Drifting IoT," and gives it a concrete evidence base plus an explicit, citable gap. Overlaps: (a) same hardware class (ESP32/ESP32-S3, bare-metal, no OS) and same on-device-not-centralized philosophy; (b) same attack surface focus (DoS/MITM/sniffing on a home IoT network); (c) it validates that lightweight ML (decision tree, small NN) can hit 96-99% accuracy on-device with sub-30KB footprints, giving our project a credible existing baseline for "what a static on-device IDS achieves" that we can cite and try to beat/extend; (d) its rigorous, cross-validated (oscilloscope + bench-supply + manufacturer-spec comparison) power methodology (0.355W idle / 0.630W filter / 0.930W filter+ML, 5.6Ah/24h battery sizing) is directly reusable as our own hardware-cost evaluation protocol — we should replicate this measurement setup rather than inventing our own, and can frame our energy/latency overhead numbers against these as a reference point. Gaps our project fills: this paper trains one static model offline and deploys it frozen — it never performs on-device adaptation, so it cannot speak to benign concept drift at all, and it never considers an adversary manipulating the *adaptation* process (data poisoning of continual updates), because there is no continual updating to poison. Its own Section V explicitly names "storage capacity for updating and maintaining the model's knowledge base may be limited, potentially hindering its adaptability" as unresolved, and Section VI explicitly calls for future "adaptive models that can learn and adjust to changes in the network environment" — this is precisely the gap our project's core contribution (unsupervised, memory-bounded, poison-resilient on-device adaptation to benign drift) targets. In short: this paper proves the static on-device IDS baseline is feasible and cheap to power/measure, and explicitly leaves the adaptive/continual-learning-under-memory-constraints problem — and, by omission, its poisoning-resilience — completely open; our contribution should be framed as directly closing that named gap, on the same hardware class and attack taxonomy, using their power-measurement methodology as the evaluation template.
