A direct WebFetch on the PDF failed (tool reported it could not parse the binary stream), but it did save the raw PDF locally; I installed poppler (brew install poppler) and ran `pdftotext -layout` on the saved file, then read the entire extracted text — full 8-page paper including intro, related work, method (Sections 3), experiments (Section 4), Conclusion/future-work (Section 5), and references. All fields below come directly from the full text, not just the abstract.
deep.problem: The paper addresses detection of IoT botnet attacks (specifically Mirai and BASHLITE/Gafgyt) launched from IoT devices that are already compromised and enlisted into a botnet, within a large-enterprise network with many heterogeneous, often Wi-Fi-connected IoT devices. Unlike prior work that targets early botnet operational steps (propagation/scanning, infection, C&C communication), the authors deliberately target the LAST step — actual attack execution (e.g., DDoS traffic) — arguing that early-step defenses will eventually be bypassed as malware mutates, so a "last line of defense" is needed that instantly recognizes an IoT device is attacking and triggers its isolation. The core research question: given many heterogeneous IoT devices on an org network, can a centralized, automated, network-based method accurately and instantly detect which specific device has been compromised, including previously-unseen ("open world") botnet behaviors, without relying on host-side software or manual/expert labels?
deep.method: Anomaly detection via one deep autoencoder PER IoT device, trained only on that device's own benign traffic (never on attack data or on other devices' data). Pipeline: (1) Data collection — raw pcap traffic captured via port mirroring on the network switch, with each device's "clean" benign traffic gathered right after installation. (2) Feature extraction — for every incoming packet, compute a 115-dimensional statistical "behavioral snapshot": 23 statistics per time window (packet-size mean/variance, packet count, packet jitter mean/variance/count, and joint magnitude/radius/covariance/correlation of in+out packet size), aggregated over four traffic scopes (source IP, source MAC-IP, channel, socket) and 5 decaying time windows (100ms, 500ms, 1.5s, 10s, 1min), computed incrementally/online so no raw traffic needs to be stored. (3) Training — an autoencoder with input dim 115, 4 encoder layers shrinking to 75/50/33/25% of input size and a mirrored decoder, trained in Keras on a benign training split (DStrn); hyperparameters (learning rate, epoch count) tuned on a second benign optimization split (DSopt) by minimizing reconstruction MSE; an anomaly threshold tr* is set as mean+std of MSE on DSopt; a minimal majority-vote window size ws* is separately tuned on DSopt to drive false-positive rate on that set to 0%. (4) Continuous monitoring — new traffic instances are scored by reconstruction error against tr*, and a majority vote over the last ws* instances decides whether to raise an anomaly alert for that device (rather than alerting on single-packet errors, which the authors found too noisy at 5–7% FPR). Compared against three standard unsupervised baselines trained/optimized the same way: Local Outlier Factor, One-Class SVM, and Isolation Forest.
deep.dataset_used: The N-BaIoT dataset (publicly released by the authors on the UCI ML Repository as "detection_of_IoT_botnet_attacks_N_BaIoT"): real traffic from 9 commercial IoT devices in an isolated lab — Danmini Doorbell, Ennio Doorbell, Ecobee Thermostat, Philips B120N/10 Baby Monitor, Provision PT-737E Security Camera, Provision PT-838 Security Camera, SimpleHome XCS7-1002-WHT Camera, SimpleHome XCS7-1003-WHT Camera, and Samsung SNH-1011-N Webcam. Each device was infected in-lab with real, fully deployed Mirai (from leaked source) and BASHLITE/Gafgyt (via IoTPOT binaries) botnet malware and C&C infrastructure (not simulated/emulated). Attacks executed: BASHLITE — Scan, Junk, UDP flood, TCP flood, COMBO; Mirai — Scan, Ack flood, Syn flood, UDP flood, UDPplain. Per-device benign instance counts range from ~13k (Ecobee) to ~175k (Philips baby monitor). Benign data per device was split chronologically into DStrn / DSopt / benign-DStst; malicious traffic from the executed attacks was appended to DStst to build each device's test set.
deep.metrics_reported: True Positive Rate (TPR), False Positive Rate (FPR, mean ± std across devices/methods), and detection time (mean ± std, seconds/milliseconds from attack launch to alert), each compared across the 4 methods (autoencoder, LOF, One-Class SVM, Isolation Forest). Also secondary regression analysis (p-values) relating traffic-variability features to average FPR and detection time across devices.
deep.key_results: The per-device autoencoder detected every single attack instance from every compromised device: TPR = 100%, matched only loosely by LOF/SVM and clearly beating Isolation Forest (inferior, highly variable TPR). It had the lowest and most consistent FPR: 0.007 ± 0.01, versus SVM 0.026 ± 0.029, Isolation Forest 0.027 ± 0.041, and LOF 0.086 ± 0.081. Mean detection time was 174 ± 212 milliseconds — the authors contrast this with typical real-world DDoS durations of 20–90 seconds (with a long tail: 10% of attacks >1 day, 2% >1 month), arguing sub-second detection allows near-immediate isolation of the compromised device. FPR was not uniform across devices — the Philips baby-monitor (highest-traffic, most functionally diverse device) had the worst FPR, which the authors link statistically (p=0.019 for inbound-traffic variability → FPR; p=0.001 for max inbound-traffic volume → detection time) to lower traffic "predictability."
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Explicitly stated in the Conclusion (Section 5), the authors flag: (1) FPR was NOT uniform across devices — they hypothesize this varies with a device's functional diversity/complexity (the multi-sensor Philips baby monitor being the worst case) and with traffic "predictability" more generally, and state "future observations may be subject to more categorization errors" for such devices. (2) Named future work #1: "further define and investigate the subject of traffic predictability, both theoretically and empirically" — i.e., formalize/quantify IoT traffic predictability, relate it to static device features (sensor count/type, memory, OS) and dynamic features (unique destination IPs/hour, in/out traffic ratio variance), and rank which features drive predictability and thus detection performance. (3) Named future work #2 ("another extension"): evaluate TRANSFER LEARNING — apply a model trained on one instance of a device to identical device instances in other organizational networks, motivated by (a) saving the cost of re-collecting data/retraining per-deployment, and (b) catching devices that were already compromised before joining a network (so no clean benign baseline exists to train on locally). Beyond what is explicitly named, the method's own design surfaces gaps the authors do NOT discuss: the per-device model is trained ONCE on an initial benign window "immediately following installation" and then deployed as a fixed detector — there is no described mechanism for retraining, updating, or safely re-baselining "normal" as legitimate device behavior evolves after deployment (benign concept drift), and there is no discussion anywhere of adversarial manipulation of the training/adaptation data (poisoning), since the model never adapts post-deployment in the first place.
deep.relation_to_our_project: N-BaIoT is exactly the "static per-device autoencoder" archetype our proposal positions itself against, and it is the field's standard baseline/dataset, so it serves three roles for us. (1) Direct counterexample motivating adaptivity: N-BaIoT's autoencoder is trained once on a short post-install benign window and then frozen — it has zero mechanism to update "normal" as a device's legitimate behavior drifts (firmware updates, new usage routines, schedule changes). The authors' own finding that FPR correlates with a device's traffic "unpredictability" is effectively an early symptom of the same problem our project targets: a static baseline degrades (rising false alarms or masked misses) exactly when real traffic is less stable/more evolving — which is what continuous benign drift looks like over a full deployment lifetime, not just at first boot. (2) The poisoning gap is genuinely untouched: because N-BaIoT never adapts after initial training, the paper has no notion of an adaptation process to protect, so it says nothing about slow/boiling-frog poisoning of a live-updating baseline. That is precisely the novel contribution slot for us — we are not just adding drift-adaptivity (an incremental idea on top of N-BaIoT-style detectors) but adding it in a way that is provably resistant to an adversary trying to slowly walk the "benign" model toward tolerating attack traffic, a threat model the canonical paper does not consider at all. (3) On-device cost is a blank baseline we must establish, not inherit: N-BaIoT is explicitly network-based and the authors tout, as a design benefit, that it "does not consume any computation, memory, or energy resources from the (typically constrained) IoT devices" — it runs autoencoders on a central server fed by switch port-mirroring, not on the constrained device itself. Its reported "174±212ms" figure is alert latency in a lab capture pipeline, not compute latency/RAM/energy on an ESP32-class MCU — none of which N-BaIoT measures. So for our ESP32-class, on-device angle we get no numeric baseline to beat from this paper; we would need our own resource profiling, though N-BaIoT's 115-feature / 5-window incremental statistic design is a reasonable, already-published starting point for a lightweight on-device feature extractor (it's explicitly built to be computed fast and incrementally without storing raw traffic, which matters for RAM-constrained deployment). (4) Practical use as our reproducibility baseline: the public N-BaIoT dataset (9 devices, real Mirai/BASHLITE infections, the same 115-feature/TPR-FPR-detection-time protocol) is the standard comparison point in this literature; reproducing the static per-device-autoencoder result (TPR≈100%, FPR≈0.007, sub-second detection under IID benign/attack conditions) as our own "non-adaptive, non-robust" baseline, then showing (a) how its FPR degrades under injected benign drift and (b) how a naively-adaptive version of it can be poisoned by a slow attacker, while our poison-resilient adaptive method holds TPR/FPR near-baseline under both stressors — gives us a clean, well-known reference point for the novelty and evaluation-rigor a top-tier venue would expect. The authors' own named future work (cross-device/cross-org transfer learning, formalizing "traffic predictability") is complementary but distinct from ours — it is about generalizing a still-static model across contexts, not about making one deployed model safely self-update under adversarial drift over time — so it does not preempt our contribution, it reinforces that this exact gap (safe continual adaptation under a poisoning threat, on constrained hardware) was left open by the canonical paper in this space.

deep.title: A Lightweight Concept Drift Detection and Adaptation Framework for IoT Data Streams
deep.authors: Li Yang and Abdallah Shami, Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Western University, London, Ontario, Canada (emails: lyang339@uwo.ca, abdallah.shami@uwo.ca)
deep.venue_year: IEEE Internet of Things Magazine — "Accepted and to appear" (per the PDF header); arXiv preprint posted 21 Apr 2021, arXiv:2104.10529v1 [cs.LG]. (I could not independently verify final IEEE volume/issue/page numbers or the exact publication date beyond the arXiv timestamp and the "accepted" header — treat those as unconfirmed.)
deep.verified_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.10529 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10529). Code repo linked in the paper: https://github.com/Western-OC2-Lab/OASW-Concept-Drift-Detection-and-Adaptation
deep.fetch_status: Full text successfully fetched and read (8-page PDF via WebFetch/Read, all sections reviewed: intro, challenges table, proposed framework, OASW algorithm listing, experimental setup, results tables/figures, conclusion, references, author bios).
deep.problem: IoT streaming-data analytics (they use anomaly/intrusion detection as the example use case) faces two compounding constraints: (1) IoT devices are low-power/low-cost with tight time and memory budgets, ruling out heavy batch-retraining models, and (2) IoT data is non-stationary — physical events sensed, device aging/replacement, and network conditions change over time, causing "concept drift" that silently degrades a static model's detection accuracy (they show this concretely: an offline model's accuracy on NSL-KDD collapses from ~99% to 84.25% after a known drift point). Traditional offline ML can't detect or react to this drift, so the paper targets a framework that is simultaneously lightweight (fits IoT resource limits) and adaptive (detects and corrects for drift without human intervention).
deep.method: A two-stage adaptive framework: (1) Offline stage — an initial LightGBM (gradient-boosted trees, chosen for its GOSS/EFB efficiency tricks) model is trained on a historical dataset, with its 5 main hyperparameters (n_estimators, max_depth, learning_rate, num_leaves, min_data_in_leaf) tuned via Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). (2) Online stage — their core contribution, "Optimized Adaptive and Sliding Windowing" (OASW): a fixed-size sliding window (size t) continuously tracks recent-window accuracy; if accuracy drops by a threshold α relative to the prior window, a "warning" state opens and an adaptive window begins collecting new samples (up to max size t'_max); if accuracy keeps falling to a stricter threshold β, a "drift" state triggers and the model is retrained on the adaptive window's collected samples, producing an updated classifier; if accuracy recovers before hitting β, it's treated as a false alarm and the adaptive window is discarded. OASW's own four hyperparameters (α, β, t, t'_max) are in turn tuned by PSO to maximize average accuracy. Stated complexity: O(NM) training, O(N) run-time/space (N = instances, M = PSO search iterations).
deep.dataset_used: Two public IoT/network intrusion datasets, both reduced and used as binary (attack vs. normal) classification tasks: (1) IoTID20 — a real IoT-traffic anomaly dataset, highly imbalanced (94% normal / 6% attack), reduced by timestamp-subsampling to 62,578 records. (2) NSL-KDD — a balanced benchmark intrusion-detection dataset with a known sudden concept drift between its train and test partitions, reduced to 35,140 records (last 10% of training set + full test set used, to create a clean two-concept comparison). Evaluation used hold-out validation (first 10% of each dataset as offline training set) plus prequential (test-then-train) validation for the online phase.
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score (on both datasets); average online per-instance prediction/execution time in milliseconds, measured on three platforms — a Raspberry Pi 3 (BCM2837B0, 1GB RAM, used to represent "a real IoT device"), a desktop (i7-8700, 16GB RAM), and a Google Colaboratory cloud machine (Xeon); and total memory usage in MB during online learning.
deep.key_results: The proposed OASW+LightGBM beat every baseline (offline LightGBM with no drift adaptation, SAM-KNN, HATT, ARF, SRP) on both datasets. IoTID20: 99.92% accuracy / 99.93% precision / 99.98% recall / 99.96% F1 (vs. 99.01–99.27% accuracy for the four state-of-the-art baselines, and 99.78% for offline LightGBM with no adaptation). NSL-KDD (the harder case, with a severe train→test drift): 98.31% accuracy / 98.57% precision / 98.30% recall / 98.43% F1, dramatically outperforming offline LightGBM (84.25% accuracy, collapsing on the drifted test set) and the other adaptive baselines (94.11–96.58% accuracy). It also had the lowest memory footprint of all six compared methods (0.4MB on IoTID20, 1.8MB on NSL-KDD) — attributed to retraining only on the small adaptive-window subset rather than full/large replay buffers. Per-instance latency on the Raspberry Pi 3 was 7.8ms (IoTID20) / 9.1ms (NSL-KDD) — much faster than SAM-KNN (43.4/21.6ms) and SRP (67.8/35.7ms), though slower than ARF/HATT (which had markedly lower accuracy); on desktop/cloud hardware, per-sample time dropped to 1.3ms/0.9ms.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Important finding: this paper contains no dedicated "Limitations" or "Future Work" section. Section V ("Conclusion") is a short paragraph that only restates the contributions and headline accuracy numbers — the authors do not explicitly name anything they did not do. So nothing below is an author-stated limitation; it is my own inference from what the paper does and does not test, offered because the computed task asked for exactly this kind of gap-spotting. Observable gaps: (1) Hardware realism — their "real IoT device" stand-in is a Raspberry Pi 3 (quad-core 64-bit CPU, 1GB RAM, runs full Linux), which is orders of magnitude more capable than an ESP32-class microcontroller (single/dual-core, ~320–520KB RAM, no OS, no LightGBM/Python runtime); no true microcontroller-class deployment is attempted. (2) No energy/power measurements anywhere — only latency and RAM are reported. (3) Drift detection is purely performance-based (accuracy-drop thresholds α/β), which requires continuously available ground-truth labels online — this is a supervised/label-dependent design, not unsupervised. (4) No adversarial or data-poisoning consideration at all: OASW's adaptive window admits and later retrains on whatever samples arrive during a detected warning/drift state, with no check on whether those samples are genuinely benign drift versus an attacker slowly shifting the traffic distribution to get poisoned data accepted as "the new normal concept" (a boiling-frog attack on the adaptation mechanism itself). The paper neither raises nor tests this threat model.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This is the closest structural precedent to our project's core mechanism. OASW's dual-window design (a fixed sliding window for drift detection + a separate adaptive window that collects new-concept samples and is used to retrain the model) is essentially the lightweight, lookback-bounded, IoT-oriented adaptive-windowing idea our project also wants, and its results establish that such windowing can beat heavier drift-adaptive baselines (SAM-KNN, ARF, SRP, HATT) on both accuracy and memory footprint on real IoT-relevant intrusion data (IoTID20, NSL-KDD) — useful as a baseline/related-work anchor and even as a candidate starting implementation (their code is public on GitHub). However, three gaps in this paper map directly onto our project's intended contributions, giving us a defensible novelty claim: (1) Hardware realism — we would validate on an actual ESP32-class microcontroller with measured RAM, latency, AND energy, versus their Raspberry-Pi-3-as-proxy setup that reports no energy figures at all; (2) Label-free operation — our unsupervised design removes their reliance on continuously available ground-truth accuracy as the drift signal; (3) Poisoning resilience — this is the sharpest gap. OASW's own adaptation mechanism (blindly retrain on whatever the adaptive window collected once a drift/warning threshold trips) is exactly the attack surface a slow "boiling-frog" poisoning attacker would exploit: an attacker who drifts traffic gradually enough to stay under β but above α could get their samples treated as a legitimate new concept and baked into the retrained model. The paper doesn't raise, model, or defend against this at all — so a method that keeps OASW-style lightweight windowed adaptation but adds a poisoning-aware admission/trust check on what enters the adaptive window, evaluated with real embedded-hardware cost figures, is a genuine, well-scoped combination this survey-identified "closest paper" leaves fully open, and is publishable as a targeted extension rather than requiring an entirely new detection paradigm.

deep.title: Kitsune: An Ensemble of Autoencoders for Online Network Intrusion Detection
deep.authors: Yisroel Mirsky, Tomer Doitshman, Yuval Elovici, Asaf Shabtai — Ben-Gurion University of the Negev
deep.venue_year: NDSS 2018 (Network and Distributed System Security Symposium, San Diego, Feb 18–21 2018). arXiv:1802.09089v2 [cs.CR], last revised 27 May 2018. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2018.23204. Source code released at github.com/ymirsky/KitNET-py.
deep.fetch_status: Full text successfully obtained and verified. Note on process: WebFetch's own summarization pass (a small intermediate model) hallucinated several details not in the actual paper — most notably claiming the datasets were "NSL-KDD" and "UNSW-NB15" and inventing several quoted sentences. This was caught and discarded. I instead extracted the raw PDF text directly with PyMuPDF from the fetched arXiv PDF (all 15 pages, ~82,000 characters) and read it in full, so every fact below is drawn from the paper's actual text, not the unreliable summary. One caveat: several results appear in the paper as a dense multi-panel figure (Fig. 9: TPR/FNR/AUC/EER per algorithm per dataset) whose numbers, once flattened by PDF-to-text extraction, cannot be reliably re-mapped cell-by-cell to (algorithm, dataset) pairs — so exact per-dataset AUC/EER numbers are reported only qualitatively below rather than as precise fabricated figures.
deep.problem: Kitsune targets the impracticality of existing ANN-based NIDS for simple, resource-constrained network gateways/routers. The authors identify three concrete obstacles to deploying neural-network intrusion detectors in a distributed fashion directly on cheap routers: (1) "Offline Processing" — supervised training needs all labeled data available locally, infeasible when an hour of traffic is millions of packets; (2) "Supervised Learning" — expert labeling is slow/expensive, what counts as "normal" is local to each network, attack types constantly evolve, and closed-world classifiers can't cover unseen attack classes; (3) "High Complexity" — ANN computational cost grows with network size/neurons, which is impractical on hardware with no GPU. They therefore define three design requirements for a viable router-hosted NIDS: Online Processing (each instance is used once then discarded, O(1) memory), Unsupervised Learning (no labels needed), and Low Complexity (must keep up with peak packet arrival rate). Kitsune is proposed as a "plug and play NIDS which can learn to detect attacks on the local network, without supervision, and in an efficient online manner."
deep.method:
Kitsune's core algorithm, KitNET, is a two-layer ensemble-of-autoencoders anomaly detector fed by a custom streaming feature-extraction pipeline:

1) Feature Extractor (FE): on every packet, computes 115 statistical features (23 base statistics × 5 exponentially-decayed time windows: 100ms, 500ms, 1.5s, 10s, 1min) describing the traffic from the packet's source MAC-IP, source IP, the src↔dst IP "Channel," and the src↔dst TCP/UDP "Socket." Statistics (packet-rate/weight, mean, std, plus 2D magnitude/radius/covariance/correlation between paired streams) are maintained via "damped incremental statistics" — an O(1)-per-update, O(1)-memory running-statistics scheme with exponential time-decay (λ) instead of a stored sliding window, kept in a hash table so entries can be dropped once their weight decays to ~0.

2) Feature Mapper (FM): during an initial train-mode, incrementally builds an n×n correlation-distance matrix over the 115 features (O(n²) memory, computed on-site) and runs agglomerative hierarchical clustering once, at the end of train-mode, to partition the n features into k disjoint groups of at most m features each (m is Kitsune's one main tunable hyperparameter, trading detection performance against speed).

3) Anomaly Detector / KitNET: an Ensemble Layer of k small 3-layer autoencoders (one per feature group from the FM, each with inner-layer compression ratio β=3/4), each producing its own RMSE reconstruction error on its feature subspace; these k RMSE values feed as inputs to a single Output-Layer autoencoder that acts as a non-linear combiner, and its own RMSE is the final anomaly score s. All autoencoders are trained with single-pass SGD (one gradient step per instance, instance then discarded), making the whole pipeline strictly online and never storing more than one instance in memory. Complexity is shown to be O(k²) versus O(n²) for one large autoencoder over the same feature space, i.e. roughly a factor-of-m speedup in the typical case.

Important architectural nuance: training and execution are two distinct modes, not continuous online adaptation. Train-mode runs once, over the initial block of traffic assumed to be benign (build the map, fit weights, record the max RMSE seen as the alert threshold φ); the system then switches to execute-mode, in which "KitNET does not update any of its internal parameters" — it only does forward passes and scores. So, as published, Kitsune does not keep adapting/retraining after deployment; it trains once, freezes, and scores thereafter.
deep.dataset_used:
Two self-collected, real-hardware network captures (no public benchmark like NSL-KDD/CICIDS/UNSW-NB15 is used):

(1) An operational IP-camera video-surveillance network: two sites of four HD PoE Sony cameras (SNC-EM602RC, SNC-EB600, SNC-EM600, SNC-EB602R; H.264/MPEG4, 1280x720, 15fps) linked to a DVR over a site-to-site VPN, monitored at a single capture point. Eight attack datasets were captured on it: OS Scan (Nmap recon), Fuzzing (SFuzz against camera web-server CGIs), Video Injection (MitM, "Video Jack" tool), ARP MitM (Ettercap-based LAN interception), Active Wiretap (a Raspberry Pi 3B physically inserted as a covert network bridge on an exposed cable), SSDP Flood (Saddam tool, UPnP advertisement DoS against the DVR), SYN DoS (Hping3, disables a camera's web server/stream), and SSL Renegotiation (THC tool, disables a camera stream via repeated SSL renegotiation). Each dataset ranges from ~0.76M to ~6.1M packets; every algorithm is trained on the first 1,000,000 packets (assumed benign) and evaluated on the remainder.

(2) A separate, noisier Wi-Fi IoT network: 9 IoT devices (a thermostat, baby monitor, webcam, two different doorbells, four different cheap security cameras) plus 3 PCs. One security camera was infected with a real sample of Mirai botnet malware (Telnet default-credential exploitation, then scanning for new victims) to produce a ninth attack dataset, "Botnet Malware (Mirai)."

Runtime/throughput benchmarks used the same live-traffic feature stream (n=198 features noted in that section) replayed on a Raspberry Pi 3B and an Ubuntu VM on a Windows 10 PC.
deep.metrics_reported: True Positive Rate (TPR) and False Negative Rate (FNR) at two fixed operating points (FPR = 0 and FPR = 0.001), Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), and Equal Error Rate (EER) — all computed per dataset per algorithm. Separately, runtime/throughput is reported as packets-processed-per-second on a single CPU core, as a function of ensemble size k, plus qualitative statements about memory footprint (e.g., "roughly 1MB of RAM can contain approximately 1,000 network links" of incremental statistics in the C++ implementation).
deep.key_results:
Kitsune (online, single-pass, no GPU) is compared against: Suricata (signature-based NIDS, 13,465 Emerging Threats rules), two offline/batch anomaly detectors — Isolation Forest and Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) — used as an approximate upper bound since they see the whole dataset and iterate multiple times, and two other online baselines — incremental GMM and pcStream2 (a Mahalanobis-distance stream-clustering method). Kitsune was run at both m=1 and m=10.

Reported findings (paraphrased from the results text, since the underlying figure's per-cell numbers could not be reliably re-extracted): Kitsune "performed very well" relative to the offline batch methods despite being a strictly online, single-pass algorithm — on the Active Wiretap dataset it outperformed the (offline) GMM outright, and it achieved better EER than GMM on several other datasets (ARP MitM, Fuzzing, Mirai, SSL Renegotiation, SYN DoS, and Active Wiretap). Against the other online baselines (incremental GMM, pcStream2), the paper states Kitsune "clearly outperforms both algorithms in terms of AUC and EER" across the datasets. There is an explicit detection-vs-speed trade-off via m: smaller m (near 1) or very large m tend toward better detection performance at higher compute cost; a moderate m favors speed. Signature-based Suricata is used mainly to illustrate that rule-based detection cannot catch these novel/behavioral attacks, establishing the value of anomaly-based detection.

Runtime results (quoted): "With a single autoencoder in L(1), the PI and PC can handle approx. 1,000 and 7,500 packets per second respectively. However, with 35 autoencoders in L(1), the performance of both environments improve by a factor of 5 to approx. 5400 and 37,300 respectively." The ensemble structure also reduces the variance/jitter of per-packet processing time versus one large autoencoder. Hardware used: Raspberry Pi 3B (Broadcom BCM2837, 1.2GHz, 4 cores, 1GB RAM) vs. an Ubuntu VM on an Intel i7-4790 (3.6GHz) — all runtime benchmarks were single-core, C++.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work:
The paper has a dedicated Section VI, "Adversarial Attacks & Countermeasures," that is directly on-point for this project and is worth quoting closely:

1) Zero defense against training-time poisoning, stated explicitly: "an advanced adversary may attempt to perform adversarial machine learning. When first installed, Kitsune assumes that all traffic is benign while in train-mode. Therefore, a preexisting adversary may be able to evade Kitsune's detection." The authors only note that once in execute-mode "Kitsune will detect new attacks... as they present themselves," and otherwise just warn the user to "be aware of this risk when installing Kitsune on a potentially compromised network" — no mechanism, defense, or evaluation is provided.

2) An unimplemented, unevaluated idea for exactly the kind of continual/self-filtering training loop this project wants to build, offered only as future work: "it would be interesting to find a mechanism which can safely filter out potentially contaminated instances during the training process. For example, we can first execute and see if there is a high anomaly score. If there is, then we will not train from the instance (since we only want to learn from benign instances). By doing so, we can potentially remain in train-mode indefinitely." This sentence is effectively the authors gesturing at continual online adaptation with self-supervised contamination filtering — the exact mechanism the current project's title implies building and, critically, actually attacking/evaluating.

3) A named alternative mitigation that is explicitly framed as an unsatisfying trade-off rather than a solution: pairing Kitsune with a signature-based NIDS (Snort 3.0/Suricata) as "a good compromise," since signature systems have lower FPR but by nature "cannot automatically detect new or abstract threats."

4) A second, distinct threat named but not defended: a resource-exhaustion DoS against the Feature Extractor itself — "an attacker sends many packets with random IP addresses. By doing so, the FE will create many incremental statistics which eventually consume the device's memory... the system may become unstable." Their only mitigation is an informal recommendation to cap/evict the incremental-statistics table, not an implemented or evaluated defense.

5) Runtime results were single-core only, with multi-core parallelization explicitly left as future work: "we plan on parallelizing KitNET over multiple cores."

6) Not stated as a limitation by the authors, but verifiable directly from the method description (Section IV-D-3, "Execute-mode"): after the initial training window, "KitNET does not update any of its internal parameters" during execution — i.e., the published algorithm has no built-in mechanism to adapt to benign concept drift post-deployment at all; it trains once on an assumed-clean initial block and then runs frozen. The paper never uses the word "drift" and never evaluates behavior under a changing normal-traffic distribution.

7) No adversarial-evasion evaluation is performed anywhere in the paper (only the qualitative warning in Section VI); no poisoning attack is actually implemented or measured against KitNET's training loop despite the authors identifying it as a real risk.

8) Threshold/cutoff selection (φ) is left to the user's judgment ("A user of KitNET should decide the best method of selecting φ according to his/her application") rather than being solved or automated in the paper.
deep.relation_to_our_project:
Kitsune is precisely the direct methodological ancestor the survey note described, and its own text hands the project team a validated, citable novelty gap rather than requiring one to be invented from scratch:

1) Baseline to port/compress. KitNET (damped incremental statistical features + an ensemble of tiny 3-layer autoencoders + a combiner autoencoder, all trained by single-pass SGD) is exactly the algorithmic core an ESP32-class port would carry over. Kitsune already proves this recipe reaches near-offline-detector AUC/EER on real IoT/camera-network attack traffic on a Raspberry Pi 3B (1GB RAM, 1.2GHz, no GPU) at ~1,000–5,400 pkt/s single-core. An ESP32 (hundreds of KB SRAM, no MMU, far less compute) is roughly 2–3 orders of magnitude more constrained than the Pi 3B Kitsune was benchmarked on, so a legitimate, evaluable systems contribution exists even before touching poisoning/drift: reducing the 115-feature/5-window statistic set, quantizing/pruning the ensemble, and re-measuring RAM/latency/energy on real ESP32 hardware, using Kitsune's own Section V-E methodology (single-core pkt/s vs. ensemble size, RAM-per-incremental-statistic accounting) as the template to report against.

2) The poisoning-resilience novelty axis is explicitly named — but not built — by Kitsune's own authors. Section VI states plainly that Kitsune "assumes all traffic is benign while in train-mode" with no defense against a "preexisting adversary," and then proposes, as a single unimplemented sentence of future work, a self-filtering scheme to "remain in train-mode indefinitely" by rejecting high-anomaly-score instances before learning from them. That sentence is essentially a one-line sketch of exactly the continual, poison-aware online-adaptation mechanism this project's title commits to designing, implementing, and — crucially — actually attacking with a real slow/"boiling-frog" poisoning adversary and measuring detection degradation under it. Kitsune never does either of those things.

3) The drift-adaptation novelty axis follows from a structural fact about the published algorithm, not just a stated caveat: KitNET as described freezes all parameters after its one training window ("execute-mode... does not update any of its internal parameters"), so it has zero mechanism for tracking benign concept drift in normal traffic post-deployment, and the paper never evaluates or discusses drift at all. This means the project's "drift-adaptive" contribution is not incremental polish on an existing mechanism — it is building a mechanism Kitsune structurally lacks, then showing it can be added without reopening the poisoning hole Section VI flags.

4) Natural undefended baseline/ablation. Because Kitsune's own text identifies exactly the two failure modes the project studies (train-mode poisoning; no post-deployment adaptation), "vanilla frozen KitNET" and "naive continually-retraining KitNET" (i.e., simply removing the freeze) are both principled, citable baselines for the project's evaluation: the first shows the drift-adaptation gap, the second reproduces the exact undefended poisoning vulnerability the NDSS'18 authors warned about but never tested — giving the project a clean "we built and evaluated what they only speculated about" framing for novelty.

5) Reusable, already-published attack data. Kitsune's 9 released attack datasets (especially the Mirai-infected IoT/Wi-Fi network capture, which is genuinely IoT-relevant, not a camera-network artifact) can be used directly as a realistic benign/attack traffic base to synthesize benign drift and slow poisoning campaigns on top of, giving the project traceable comparability to a well-cited NDSS baseline instead of an ad hoc dataset — strengthening the "proper evaluation" bar the grading rubric asks for.

6) A secondary, related constrained-hardware threat is also worth folding in: Kitsune's own Section VI additionally flags a feature-extractor memory-exhaustion DoS (spoofed-source-IP flood growing the incremental-statistics hash table without bound), which becomes far more dangerous on an ESP32's tiny RAM than on a Pi — a second, closely related "IoT constraint not adequately addressed" that the project's resource-cost/threat-model section could reasonably scope in alongside the main poisoning-resilience contribution.

deep.title: LE3D: A Lightweight Ensemble Framework of Data Drift Detectors for Resource-Constrained Devices
deep.authors: Ioannis Mavromatis, Adrian Sanchez-Mompo, Francesco Raimondo, James Pope, Marcello Bullo, Ingram Weeks, Vijay Kumar, Pietro Carnelli, George Oikonomou, Theodoros Spyridopoulos, Aftab Khan (Toshiba Europe Ltd. Bristol Research and Innovation Laboratory; Univ. of Bristol EEE; Univ. of Bristol Engineering Mathematics; Cardiff Univ. School of Computer Science and Informatics)
deep.venue_year: IEEE CCNC 2023 (Las Vegas). arXiv:2211.01840v2, submitted 3 Nov 2022, revised 18 Nov 2022.
deep.fetch_status: Full text successfully retrieved. The arXiv abstract page (WebFetch) gave only the abstract/metadata (limitations/future work "not detailed"). The direct PDF WebFetch failed (tool could not parse binary PDF content), but WebFetch had already saved the raw PDF locally; I then used the Read tool's native PDF-page extraction (pages 1-12, the full 8-page paper) to read the actual rendered pages, which succeeded and gave complete access to every section including Related Work, Method, Implementation, Results tables/figures, Conclusion, and References. All details below are drawn from that full-text read, not invented.
deep.problem: Detecting data drift/irregularities in raw time-series IoT sensor streams (temperature, humidity, pressure, VOC/CO2, etc.) caused either by benign factors (faulty sensors, natural environmental change) or malicious action (unauthorized data tampering), while (a) running fully unsupervised and online on resource-constrained edge devices (no labels available at inference, no cloud round-trip), (b) needing only a handful of samples to initialize per new sensor stream (not thousands, unlike prior DL drift approaches), and (c) additionally classifying a detected drift as "natural" (seen consistently across multiple devices with the same sensor type) vs "abnormal/possibly-malicious" (seen on only one device) without sharing raw sensor data between devices (only voting decisions), preserving data confidentiality.
deep.method: LE3D is a two-layer hierarchical, fully unsupervised ensemble drift-detection framework. Layer 1 (per-device, per-sensor-stream): three lightweight streaming statistical drift detectors run in parallel per sample — ADWIN (ADaptive WINdowing, adaptive two-sub-window mean-difference test), PHT (Page-Hinkley Test, a two-sided CUSUM-style mean-shift detector, extended by the authors to be two-sided), and KSWIN (Kolmogorov-Smirnov Windowing, a two-sample KS test over fixed windows). Each estimator's hyperparameters are auto-tuned per sensor stream via a two-step (coarse then fine) grid search during an initialization phase using only the first ~100 received samples (justified via the Central Limit Theorem). Decisions from the three estimators are combined by an equal-weight majority vote (>=2 of 3) over an adaptive voting window W_v, whose length is itself adapted online: a non-overlapping trend window computes the slope/angle of the incoming data via linear regression, and a fitted exponential regression (per sensor type) maps that trend strength to the appropriate window length — steep/abrupt changes get a short window, subtle/incremental changes get a longer one. Layer 2 (cross-device, only for classification, not detection): each edge device shares only its per-window voting outcome plus a one-sample KS-test statistic and metadata (never raw sensor values) with neighbouring devices of the same sensor type; if the observed drift's statistical distance is insignificant across the group it is labeled "natural," otherwise "abnormal" and reported to a backend for investigation. The framework is built in Python 3.9.12 on River (online/streaming ML library), with Flask REST APIs and an MQTT (Paho client) data bus for edge-cloud/edge-edge messaging, and is open-sourced (github.com/toshiba-bril/le3dDataDriftDetector).
deep.dataset_used: (1) Real-world dataset: collected at the University of Bristol Communication Systems & Networks Laboratory, 15-22 Feb 2022 (ethics-approved), from 8 custom IoT endpoint boards (Nordic nRF52480 BLE SoC + BME680 environmental sensor for temperature/humidity/pressure/VOC-CO2, plus an ISL29125 light sensor and MMA8452Q accelerometer) spread across lab/office space with ~10-12 people present, sampled every 10s and exchanged over an IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH mesh network; publicly released at github.com/jpope8/synergia_datadrift_dataset. (2) Emulated drift streams: real streams (temperature, humidity, pressure) replayed/streamed from a desktop PC with synthetically injected abrupt and incremental drifts of varying magnitude Q in {sigma^2/3, sigma^2/2, sigma^2, 2sigma^2, 3sigma^2, 4sigma^2, 5sigma^2} across 40 randomized timeslots per experiment (~40k samples/experiment), averaged over 1000 experiments per condition. Gradual/recurring drift and categorical data are explicitly excluded from the evaluation (recurring drift is treated as independent abrupt/incremental events; gradual drift is deferred as "more suitable for categorical data").
deep.metrics_reported: F1-score (chosen for detection accuracy because drift samples outnumber normal samples in their synthetic setup, i.e. class imbalance), per-operation execution time in microseconds/milliseconds (detector initialization time; per-sample processing time), and hardware resource utilization on the target device: CPU utilization (%, normalized to the RPi's 4 cores, sampled via `ps` every 0.1s), RAM utilization (%), and average system load (via `uptime`), each measured over a 20-minute run window (captured between the 5-20 min mark) and swept across incoming sample rates from 1 Hz to 4000 Hz.
deep.key_results: LE3D achieves up to 97% detection accuracy (F1-score near/at 1.0 across nearly all drift magnitudes Q, for temperature, humidity, and pressure streams), never dropping below an F1 of ~0.83 even for the smallest tested drift (Q < sigma^2). This is far above any single constituent estimator run alone (ADWIN/PHT/KSWIN individually score roughly 0.3-0.7 F1 depending on drift size and sensor), demonstrating the value of the voting ensemble. Against the state-of-the-art baseline PWPAE (Yang et al. 2021, a 4-classifier supervised ensemble drift detector): PWPAE with continuous online retraining scores a near-perfect F1 of 0.998, but this requires true labels at every inference step, which the authors argue is infeasible in a real deployment; with online training disabled (the realistic, label-free scenario) PWPAE's F1 collapses to ~0.32 (it degenerates to always predicting "normal"). On resource cost: LE3D's detector initialization takes ~3ms vs PWPAE's ~4.5ms (with training) — roughly 20x less average time than PWPAE-with-training and 8x less than PWPAE-without-training; per-sample processing takes 150-600 microseconds for LE3D vs 2000-8500 microseconds for PWPAE. On a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 3B+ (BCM2837B0 Cortex-A53, 1.2GHz quad-core, 1GB RAM), LE3D was benchmarked up to 4000 samples/s while keeping CPU under 20% and RAM under 11.5% even at the highest tested rate (at 2000 Hz and 4000 Hz specifically CPU was ~9.85%/19.5% and RAM ~9.8%/11.4%); by contrast PWPAE was estimated to top out around only ~150 samples/s. The observed throughput ceiling (~4000 samples/s) was traced to the single-threaded Eclipse Paho MQTT client implementation, not to the detection algorithms themselves.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper does not have a single dedicated "Limitations" section, but explicitly scopes out or defers, in its own words/intent, the following (all verified in the full text): (1) Categorical (non-time-series) data drift is "considered a future extension to LE3D" — the current work is scoped to raw time-series data only. (2) Only abrupt and incremental drift types are evaluated; recurring drift is "a priori considered and reported as independent events" (not specially handled), and single-sample "blip" drift events are explicitly "considered outliers and are ignored from our framework" (i.e., LE3D does not attempt to detect single anomalous samples). (3) "In the future, more estimators are required for different use-cases can be easily integrated into LE3D" — the 3-estimator (ADWIN/PHT/KSWIN) ensemble is presented as extensible, not final. (4) Neighbour/peer discovery for the cross-device voting mechanism is explicitly "out of the scope of this work"; they assume routing/DDS-style discovery is available externally. (5) "The cross-correlation of the metadata between different sensors is outside of the scope of this work" — i.e., correlating drift across different sensor TYPES (not just same-type across devices) is left open. (6) System/large-scale scalability is explicitly not evaluated: "evaluating the scalability of our solution is out of the scope of this work" — only qualitative ideas are discussed (e.g., a future "neighbour discovery mechanism... not considered at this stage" to optimize voting-decision exchange at scale). (7) A concrete engineering bottleneck is identified and left as future work: the single-threaded Paho MQTT client library caps throughput near 4000 samples/s; the authors state "workarounds will be considered as future extensions," naming three candidates (replace the MQTT library, use a different messaging protocol, or batch/queue samples for asynchronous processing). (8) Implicit but important for our purposes: the paper never considers an adversary that specifically targets the drift-adaptation mechanism itself (i.e., no threat model for poisoning ADWIN/PHT/KSWIN's own adaptive windows over time); "abnormal" vs "natural" is decided purely by same-timestep cross-device statistical consensus, not by any temporal/robustness safeguard against a slow-drifting attacker, and the system operates on physical sensor readings (temperature/humidity/pressure), not network traffic features — it is not an intrusion-detection system.
deep.relation_to_our_project: LE3D is directly the strongest available template for two separate parts of our project. First, methodologically: it is a genuinely unsupervised, few-sample-initialized (~100 samples), online ensemble of classic streaming drift detectors (ADWIN + PHT + KSWIN) combined by adaptive-window majority voting — this is essentially the "adapt-to-benign-concept-drift" mechanism our project needs, and it is lightweight enough in principle to reimplement natively in C/C++ for an ESP32 (the paper's own River/Python implementation is edge-Linux-class, running on a Raspberry Pi CM3B+, one tier above ESP32, so porting the three statistical detectors down to a microcontroller is itself a nontrivial, well-scoped engineering contribution). Second, and more important for grading/novelty: LE3D gives us an exact template for how to report our own ESP32 hardware costs — its Table IV/V pattern (detector init time in ms, per-sample processing time in microseconds, CPU%/RAM% swept across incoming sample rate 1 Hz-4000 Hz, and an explicit root-cause analysis of the throughput bottleneck) is precisely the rigor level our project should match when reporting ESP32 RAM/latency/energy numbers, which is exactly what the course's "A/A*-level" bar (proper evaluation against real hardware cost) demands. Third, and this is the gap our project should exploit: LE3D's only mechanism for telling "benign" drift from "malicious/abnormal" drift is a same-instant cross-device statistical-consensus vote (multiple same-type sensors agreeing) — it has no temporal/adversarial robustness check on its own online adaptation, it explicitly excludes gradual drift and treats single-sample anomalies as ignorable outliers, and it never discusses an attacker deliberately mimicking incremental/benign drift to poison the detector's adaptive windows over time. That is exactly the "boiling-frog" data-poisoning threat our project targets, and LE3D's cross-device voting defense would not transfer to our setting anyway, since our target deployment is ESP32-class and likely single-device or few-device (not the dense same-sensor-type mesh LE3D assumes), so the "ask your neighbours" trick is unavailable to us and we need an intra-device robustness mechanism instead (e.g., a slow/trusted reference window compared against a fast-adapting one, robust/trimmed-statistics window updates, or a rate-limited/gated adaptation step that only accepts drift consistent with historically-seen benign patterns). LE3D is also a sensor-integrity/data-drift framework, not a network-traffic intrusion detector, so our contribution requires transplanting its lightweight-ensemble-drift-detection recipe from raw sensor time-series onto IoT network-traffic feature streams (packet/flow statistics) for the IDS task, and layering on the explicit poisoning-resilience mechanism LE3D itself never attempts — combined with hardware-cost reporting in LE3D's own style but at true ESP32 scale (KB-level RAM, not a 1GB Pi), this gives us a defensible "novel combination + solution to a specific unaddressed IoT constraint" framing (adaptation-robustness under poisoning, on truly microcontroller-class hardware) rather than a wholly new algorithm, which fits the course's stated novelty bar.

deep.title: A Lightweight Concept Drift Detection and Adaptation Framework for IoT Data Streams
deep.authors: Li Yang and Abdallah Shami, Western University, London, Ontario, Canada (Optimized Computing and Communications Laboratory)
deep.venue_year: Accepted and to appear in IEEE Internet of Things Magazine; arXiv:2104.10529v1, submitted 21 Apr 2021 (cs.LG / cs.AI)
deep.fetch_status: Full success. Fetched the arXiv abstract page (title/authors/abstract confirmed) and the complete 8-page PDF full text (all sections: Introduction, Challenges/Solutions taxonomy, Proposed Framework, Algorithm 1 pseudocode, Performance Evaluation with all tables/figures, Conclusion, References). Nothing was inaccessible; no WebSearch relocation was needed since the given URL resolved directly to the correct paper. One caveat: this magazine-style article has no explicit "Limitations" or "Future Work" subsection (Section V is a short Conclusion that only restates contributions) — see stated_limitations_or_future_work for what is and isn't authors' own words.
deep.problem: IoT streaming-data analytics (using anomaly/intrusion detection as the running use case) faces two coupled challenges the authors frame as "high velocity/volume" and "high variability": (1) time & memory constraints of low-power, low-cost IoT devices that make batch retraining infeasible, and (2) concept drift — non-stationary, ever-changing statistical distributions of IoT data streams (caused by sensor aging, device replacement, system updates, seasonality, or abnormal events) that degrade a static model's detection accuracy over time. The goal is a lightweight method that detects drift and adapts the model automatically, without human intervention, under IoT devices' real time/memory constraints.
deep.method: A two-stage adaptive pipeline: (1) Offline stage — an initial LightGBM (gradient-boosted trees, chosen for its GOSS down-sampling and EFB feature-bundling, which cut training complexity from O(NF) to O(N'B)) is trained on a historical dataset, with 5 hyperparameters (n_estimators, max_depth, learning_rate, num_leaves, min_data_in_leaf) tuned via Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). (2) Online stage — the tuned model scores the incoming stream; a novel drift-adaptation algorithm, OASW (Optimized Adaptive and Sliding Windowing), watches for drift using a fixed-size sliding window (size t) that compares current-vs-previous-window prediction accuracy against two thresholds: α (warning level) and β (drift level). Once the warning threshold is crossed, a separate adaptive window (capped at t'_max) starts collecting incoming samples as "new-concept" data; if accuracy keeps falling to the β (drift) level, the model is retrained on those adaptive-window samples; collection/retraining continues until accuracy stabilizes (false alarm → window released, back to normal) or the window hits its cap (model retrained again for robustness). OASW's own 4 hyperparameters (α, β, t, t'_max) are likewise tuned by PSO. Training complexity is O(NM); runtime/space complexity is O(N). Code is public on GitHub (Western-OC2-Lab/OASW-Concept-Drift-Detection-and-Adaptation).
deep.dataset_used: Two public datasets, both reduced/subsampled and used as binary (attack vs. normal) classification: (1) IoTID20 (Ullah & Mahmoud, 2020) — a real, highly imbalanced IoT device traffic dataset (94% normal / 6% abnormal), subsampled by timestamp to 62,578 records. (2) NSL-KDD — the classic, balanced KDD-99-derived network-intrusion benchmark (not native IoT telemetry), reduced to 35,140 records (last 10% of train split + full test split), chosen specifically because it has a known sudden/severe concept drift between its train and test partitions.
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score (via hold-out and prequential/"test-then-train" online validation); average per-instance online prediction/test time in ms; total model memory usage in MB. No energy/power metric is reported anywhere in the paper.
deep.key_results: On IoTID20, the proposed OASW+LightGBM reached 99.92% accuracy / 99.93% precision / 99.98% recall / 99.96% F1 — beating the non-adaptive offline LightGBM (99.78%) and four state-of-the-art adaptive baselines (SAM-KNN 99.25%, HATT 99.01%, ARF 99.26%, SRP 99.27%), with the smallest memory footprint of the six methods (0.4MB) and 7.8ms average per-instance prediction time on a Raspberry Pi 3. On NSL-KDD, which has a severe drift at the test-set boundary, the proposed method held 98.31% accuracy / 98.57% P / 98.30% R / 98.43% F1, while the non-adaptive offline LightGBM collapsed to 84.25% accuracy without drift adaptation — the paper's central evidence for why drift adaptation matters. Baselines there ranged 94.11%-96.58%. Memory usage was again the smallest (1.8MB) and per-instance latency 9.1ms on the Pi 3 (compared to 43.4ms for SAM-KNN and 67.8ms for SRP; only ARF and HATT were faster but far less accurate). All experiments ran on a Raspberry Pi 3 (BCM2837B0, 1GB RAM) "representing a real IoT device," with additional latency numbers on a desktop i7-8700/16GB (1.3ms) and a Google Colab Xeon cloud instance (0.9ms).
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper has no dedicated "Limitations" or "Future Work" section — Section V (Conclusion) only restates the contributions and headline accuracy numbers. The closest thing to a self-identified limitation is a general statement made earlier about performance-based drift detection as a class of methods (Section II-B): "Performance-based methods can effectively detect the drifts that cause model degradation, but they require the availability of ground-truth labels" — which applies to OASW's own accuracy-based warning/drift comparison, though the authors never explicitly flag it as a limitation of their own method. Beyond that one sentence, everything below is my own inference from close reading, not the authors' words: (1) No adversarial or data-poisoning consideration anywhere — OASW's Algorithm 1 unconditionally trusts and retrains on whatever samples fall inside the adaptive window once an accuracy-based warning/drift trigger fires, with no sample vetting, provenance check, or robustness bound on the update; this is exactly the mechanism a slow "boiling-frog" poisoning attack would exploit. (2) Hardware realism gap: their "real IoT device" is a Raspberry Pi 3 — a quad-core Cortex-A53 @1.2GHz SBC with 1GB RAM running full embedded Linux — which is far more capable than an MCU-class ESP32 (dual-core Xtensa @240MHz, only 320-520KB RAM, no OS); no true MCU-class validation is attempted. (3) No energy/power measurement at all, only latency and RAM. (4) The drift evaluated is natural/benign dataset drift, not an adversarially engineered slow-poisoning scenario, and there is no attacker model in the evaluation. (5) Binary classification only (attack vs. normal), no multi-class attack typing.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This is genuinely the closest prior work to the project's core framing (lightweight, PSO/window-based adaptive anomaly detector for drifting IoT streams) and gives the project four concrete, citable gaps to position novelty against: (1) Poisoning-resilience — OASW's drift-adaptation loop (Algorithm 1) blindly accepts and retrains on any samples gathered in its adaptive window once accuracy crosses the α/β thresholds, with zero defense against a crafted slow/benign-looking shift; the project's core contribution (an adaptation mechanism that resists boiling-frog poisoning of its own drift-triggered retraining) directly targets this exact undefended surface — a mechanism-level vulnerability this paper does not even discuss, let alone mitigate. (2) Hardware realism — this paper's "real IoT device" validation is a Raspberry Pi 3 (1GB RAM, full Linux), which sits closer to an edge gateway than an MCU; the project's planned true ESP32-class (a few hundred KB RAM, no OS) on-device evaluation of RAM/latency/energy is a genuine step down in resource class that this closest paper never attempts, confirming the survey's note that real embedded-hardware validation combined with poisoning-resilience is an open combination. (3) Energy — this paper reports latency and memory but never power/energy draw; the project's energy evaluation is an added, currently-missing axis. (4) Label dependency — OASW's drift trigger is implicitly supervised (it compares online accuracy, which needs ground-truth labels arriving with the stream), which is impractical for a truly unsupervised on-device IDS; the project's explicitly unsupervised framing removes this dependency that OASW's own related-work discussion (Section II-B) flags as a general weakness of performance-based drift detection. Practically, this paper's OASW + LightGBM (or a distilled/quantized variant) is a strong, well-documented (public GitHub code) non-poisoning-resilient baseline the project can reimplement and directly compare against on both accuracy/drift-adaptation quality and, critically, on robustness under an injected slow-poisoning attack and on real ESP32 RAM/latency/energy — the two axes this paper's own evaluation leaves untested.

deep.title: Poisoning Attacks on Cyber Attack Detectors for Industrial Control Systems
deep.authors: Moshe Kravchik, Battista Biggio, Asaf Shabtai
deep.venue_year: 36th ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC '21), March 2021 (arXiv preprint posted Dec 2020, arXiv:2012.15740). Journal follow-up: "Practical Evaluation of Poisoning Attacks on Online Anomaly Detectors in Industrial Control Systems," Computers & Security, 2022 (DOI 10.1016/j.cose.2022.102901) — confirmed to exist via web search, matching the survey's claimed conference-to-journal trajectory.

deep.fetch_status: Successfully fetched and deep-read. Abstract confirmed directly from the arXiv abstract page. Full paper body (threat model, both attack algorithms, datasets, all tables/metrics, mitigation section, conclusion, and stated limitations/future work) was retrieved via the ar5iv HTML mirror of the same arXiv ID, since the native PDF fetch failed to decode. deep.problem: Neural-network-based (specifically autoencoder-based) cyber-attack detectors for Industrial Control Systems are typically retrained online using data collected during operation, so they can track natural concept drift in monitored sensor signals. The paper shows this retraining mechanism is itself an attack surface: an adversary who can falsify the readings of one or more sensors (but cannot penetrate the protected PLC/SCADA network) can gradually feed poisoned values into the retraining data stream so that the detector's decision boundary drifts to treat the attacker's eventual, larger malicious deviation as "normal." This is exactly the abstract "boiling-frog" pattern — slow, drift-camouflaged poisoning of an adaptive detector's own learning loop — applied to ICS sensor time series. The authors state they are "the first to demonstrate such poisoning attacks on ICS cyber attack online NN detectors."
deep.method: Threat model: white-box, single/few-sensor access, attacker knows historical sensor values, detector architecture, and retraining schedule; attacker must move the controlled sensor's data gradually toward the eventual attack point so each retraining step still looks like benign drift. Two poisoning algorithms are proposed: (1) Interpolation-based poisoning — a gradient-free method that iteratively interpolates between the current poisoned sample and the ultimate attack target, shrinking its step size whenever a candidate sample would trigger the detector's alarm, until it either succeeds or the step becomes negligible; cheap to compute. (2) Back-gradient optimization poisoning — a bilevel-optimization method that "unrolls" the detector's training process to compute second-order gradients of the attacker's objective with respect to the poisoning points, including a custom wrapper to handle the detector's sliding-window/sequence structure; more powerful but far more computationally expensive. Both are evaluated against autoencoder-based online detectors (only autoencoders were tested) on synthetic sine-wave signals and on real SWaT (Secure Water Treatment testbed) sensor/actuator data. The authors also test three candidate mitigations: lowering the detection threshold, lengthening the input sequence window, and running two detectors in parallel with different sequence lengths (dual-detector ensemble).
deep.dataset_used: (1) Synthetic dataset: linear-dependent sine waves (500-step period, amplitude range -0.5 to 0.5) with added Gaussian noise (mean 0, std 0.025), with injected attacks at two locations (SIN_TOP, SIN_BOTTOM). (2) SWaT (Secure Water Treatment) dataset — a real six-stage water-treatment ICS testbed from the Singapore University of Technology and Design, 51 sensor/actuator attributes, ~7 days of normal operation plus ~4 days containing attacks; the authors selected 7 of SWaT's attacks (attack IDs 3, 7, 16, 31, 32, 33, 36) that match their single-sensor manipulation threat model.
deep.metrics_reported: Attack magnitude (max deviation of spoofed vs. true sensor value achieved at test time); number of poisoning samples required to achieve successful evasion; detection performance as average F1 score across different input sequence lengths; execution/runtime of the poisoning algorithms (seconds); and, for the mitigation experiments, how detection F1 and required poisoning-sample counts change as the detection threshold, sequence length, or single- vs dual-detector configuration are varied.
deep.key_results: On synthetic data, back-gradient poisoning reached ~0.90 attack magnitude using 12-85 poisoning samples, versus ~0.80 magnitude for interpolation poisoning using 6-106 samples; interpolation ran in ~28-47s vs. ~53-84s for back-gradient. On SWaT, several real attacks (e.g., attack #3) could be poisoned into evading detection with as few as 1-2 poisoning samples at a threshold of 0.2, while others (e.g., attack #16) failed to be poisoned at longer sequence lengths / lower thresholds. Of the tested mitigations, lowering the detection threshold was the single most effective countermeasure (substantially raises the number of poisoning samples an attacker needs); lengthening the detector's input sequence window improved poisoning-resistance while costing only a 2-4% drop in baseline F1 (0.826 at length 10 vs 0.828 at length 30); and a dual-detector ensemble (short + long sequence length running in parallel) forced the attacker to need far more poisoning samples (12-62) than either single detector alone (3-8). Overall conclusion: NN/autoencoder ICS detectors are poisonable, but in most successful attacks the attacker needed long sequences of poisoning samples — often exceeding the size of normal training data — which the authors argue gives the detectors "a certain inherent robustness" in practice, since such prolonged tampering is itself hard to sustain undetected.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Authors explicitly flag, in their own words/paraphrase from the Limitations/Conclusion sections: (1) "this study only evaluated autoencoder-based detectors; studying the robustness of other NN architectures is a topic for future research" — no CNN/RNN/feedforward or non-autoencoder detector architectures were tested. (2) Evaluation was restricted to single-sensor attacks; extending the threat model to coordinated multi-sensor poisoning is left open. (3) Both poisoning algorithms require significant computational time, which the authors say makes them "inappropriate for real-time poisoning" — i.e., no real-time/on-the-fly attack variant was built or evaluated. (4) Validation was data-only (offline replay against the datasets); the authors state a "real-world [physical] testbed would be a natural next stage," meaning they did not validate the attack against a live running physical ICS. (5) The SWaT "attacks" used are simulated/injected, so ground-truth real attack values are not independently known. (6) The threat model itself is white-box (attacker has full knowledge of detector parameters/retraining schedule); black-box poisoning is not addressed and is left as a future direction. (7) Future work explicitly named: a hybrid/adaptive learning-rate scheduling algorithm combining interpolation and back-gradient strengths, deeper investigation of the dual-detector mitigation, and testing against additional ICS datasets beyond SWaT.
