deep.title: LE3D: A Lightweight Ensemble Framework of Data Drift Detectors for Resource-Constrained Devices
deep.authors: Ioannis Mavromatis, Adrian Sanchez-Mompo, Francesco Raimondo, James Pope, Marcello Bullo, Ingram Weeks, Vijay Kumar, Pietro Carnelli, George Oikonomou, Theodoros Spyridopoulos, Aftab Khan — Toshiba Bristol Research and Innovation Laboratory (BRIL), University of Bristol, and Cardiff University.
deep.venue_year: IEEE CCNC 2023 (Consumer Communications & Networking Conference), Las Vegas; arXiv:2211.01840, submitted 18 Nov 2022 (v2).
deep.fetch_status: Success — retrieved the complete paper (all 9 pages, through the References section) by downloading the PDF from arxiv.org/pdf/2211.01840 and reading it directly (image/OCR extraction of each page), after an initial WebFetch of the raw PDF text failed because arXiv PDFs are binary/compressed. Nothing below is inferred from a snippet alone; all figures and quotes are read from the actual paper.
deep.problem: IoT sensor data integrity is threatened by "data drift" — changes in a sensor stream's statistical distribution caused either by benign factors (faulty/aging sensors, natural environmental change) or by malicious action (unauthorized data tampering). Undetected drift disrupts downstream applications and biases their state. Existing ML-based drift detectors either need large labeled training sets and costly retraining (infeasible for resource-constrained IoT endpoints) or send raw data off-device to a more powerful node for retraining, which increases communication cost and creates new attack surface (data tampered/lost/leaked in transit). The paper's problem is therefore: build an unsupervised, lightweight, online drift-detection mechanism that (a) runs directly on a resource-constrained IoT device with minimal reconfiguration when new sensor types/streams appear, (b) needs only a handful of samples to initialize (not thousands), (c) never sends raw sensor data off-device, and (d) can additionally classify a detected drift as "natural" (benign) vs. "abnormal" (potentially malicious) by collaborating with neighboring devices.
deep.method: LE3D is a two-layer hierarchical ensemble framework. Layer 1 (per-device drift detection): each IoT device runs three lightweight, unsupervised, statistical streaming detectors in parallel on every sensor stream — ADWIN (Adaptive Windowing), PHT (Page-Hinkley Test, extended to be two-sided), and KSWIN (Kolmogorov-Smirnov Windowing). Hyperparameters for each detector/sensor-type pair are tuned via a two-step (coarse then fine) grid search, informed by a non-linear-regression model (built once from real data) relating the voting-window size to the magnitude of a mean-value shift. Only ~100 initialization samples are needed (justified via Central-Limit-Theorem reasoning), versus thousands for typical ML detectors. Per-sample, each of the three detectors casts a binary normal/abnormal vote; an adaptive voting window W_v (whose length is itself adjusted by the local trend/slope of the data, via linear regression over a separate window W_m) aggregates votes with 2-of-3 majority voting to decide whether the last L_v samples actually contain a drift — this reduces the false positives any single estimator would produce alone. Layer 2 (cross-device classification): once a device flags a local drift, it shares only its voting decision, a one-sample KS-test statistic (Z), sensor type, and metadata (not raw data) with neighboring devices monitoring similar sensor types. If the observed distributional distance is statistically insignificant across the neighborhood, the drift is classified "natural" (e.g., a room-wide temperature rise); if one device's drift is a statistical outlier relative to its peers, it is flagged "abnormal/malicious" and reported to a backend system. The system is implemented as a 3-tier (cloud/edge/endpoint) architecture over MQTT, in Python (River online-ML library, SciPy/NumPy, Flask, Eclipse Paho MQTT client), open-sourced at github.com/toshiba-bril/le3dDataDriftDetector.
deep.dataset_used: (1) A real-world dataset the authors collected themselves: 8 IoT endpoint devices (Nordic nRF52480 BLE SoC, USB-powered) equipped with a light sensor (ISL29125), accelerometer (MMA8452Q), and environmental sensor (BME680: temperature, humidity, pressure, VOC/CO2), deployed in an office/lab at the University of Bristol Communication Systems & Networks Laboratory, 15–22 Feb 2022 (ethics-approved), sampling every 10s over an IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH mesh network; publicly released at github.com/jpope8/synergia_datadrift_dataset. Used to fit the non-linear regression model and initialize estimator statistics. (2) For the quantitative F1-score evaluation, synthetic/emulated abrupt and incremental drift streams generated from the real sensor statistics for three sensor types (temperature, humidity, pressure) — 40 timeslots/stream, ~40k samples/experiment, averaged over 1000 experiments, sweeping drift magnitude q across 7 levels (σ²/3 up to 5σ²).
deep.metrics_reported: F1-score (chosen for class imbalance) vs. drift magnitude, per sensor type, compared against each individual estimator (ADWIN/PHT/KSWIN alone) and against the baseline PWPAE (Pooled Weighted Probability Averaging Ensemble — a 4-classifier supervised ensemble using SRP/ARF with ADWIN/DDM base estimators), evaluated both with and without continuous online retraining. Execution-time metrics: detector-initialization time (ms) and per-sample processing time (µs). Real-hardware resource metrics on a Raspberry Pi 3B+ Compute Module (BCM2837B0 Cortex-A53, 1.2GHz, 1GB RAM): CPU utilization (%), RAM utilization (%), and system load (via `uptime`), measured at incoming sample rates from 1Hz to 4000Hz, normalized to the RPi's 4 cores, over 20-minute runs. No energy/power (joule) measurements are reported anywhere in the paper.
deep.key_results: LE3D achieves up to 97% F1-score across sensor types and drift magnitudes, staying above 83% even at the smallest tested drift. It clearly outperforms any single estimator used alone, showing the voting ensemble is what drives accuracy. Against PWPAE: with continuous online retraining (label-fed every sample) PWPAE reaches F1≈99.8%, but this setup is explicitly noted as infeasible in real deployments since ground-truth labels are never available online; with retraining disabled (the realistic condition) PWPAE's F1 collapses to ≈32% (it degenerates to always predicting "normal"). On efficiency: LE3D initializes a detector in ~3ms vs. PWPAE's ~4.5ms, and processes a sample in only 150–600µs vs. PWPAE's 6500–8500µs (with training) / 2000–2800µs (without) — roughly 20x faster than PWPAE-with-training and >8x faster than PWPAE-without-training on average. PWPAE's realistic throughput is estimated at only ~150 samples/s; LE3D was evaluated up to 4000 samples/s. On the Raspberry Pi 3B+, LE3D keeps CPU utilization under 10% up to 2000Hz sampling (19.5% at 4000Hz) and RAM utilization always under 11.5% (rising only slightly with throughput, e.g., idle ensemble+MQTT = 7.8% RAM, climbing to 11.4% RAM at 4000Hz), with concrete per-rate numbers in the paper's Table V (1Hz: 0.45% CPU/7.8% RAM; 1000Hz: 7.6% CPU/8.7% RAM; 4000Hz: 19.5% CPU/11.4% RAM) — this table is exactly the format the survey flagged as a template for ESP32 hardware-cost reporting.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Explicitly stated by the authors as out of scope or left for future work: (1) Categorical data drift is unsupported — "Support for categorical data drift is considered a future extension to LE3D"; only raw continuous time-series data is handled. (2) Recurring drift and single-sample "blip" outlier events are excluded from the framework's scope entirely ("blip drift events are considered outliers and are ignored from our framework") — only abrupt and incremental drift are detected/evaluated. (3) Only three detection algorithms are used; the authors note "more estimators are required for different use-cases and can be easily integrated into LE3D" in future. (4) Cross-correlation of drift metadata between *different* sensor types (e.g., correlating a temperature drift with a humidity drift) is explicitly "outside of the scope of this work." (5) Neighbor discovery for the cross-device collaborative layer is unsolved by the framework itself — "The discovery of the neighbouring nodes is out of the scope of this work. Traditional routing protocols and DDS buses can provide such functionality" — i.e., LE3D assumes neighbors are already known. (6) Formal large-scale system scalability is explicitly not evaluated ("evaluating the scalability of our solution is out of scope of this work"); only qualitative design ideas are discussed, including a future "neighbour discovery mechanism" to optimize decision exchange at scale. (7) A concrete acknowledged bottleneck: the single-threaded Eclipse Paho MQTT client in Python caps achievable sample throughput; stated fixes for future work are "replacing the Paho MQTT library with another implementation, using a different messaging protocol, or subscribing to batches of data... and processing them asynchronously." (8) RAM slowly grows with throughput because historic samples are retained after processing; the authors note this "can be regulated by discarding historical data after expiration or when a pre-defined queue is full" — i.e., proposed but not yet implemented. (9) No adversarial or poisoning-robustness evaluation of any kind exists in the paper — the natural/abnormal classification relies purely on a single-shot cross-device KS-test comparison, with no threat model, no evaluation against an adaptive attacker, and no defense against an attacker who slowly shifts a device's own adaptive-window statistics over many cycles so that malicious drift is absorbed as "normal." (10) No energy/power measurements are reported at all — only CPU%, RAM%, load, and latency. (11) All hardware evaluation is on a Raspberry Pi 3B+ (quad-core Cortex-A53 @1.2GHz, 1GB RAM, running full Linux/Python/MQTT broker) — chosen by the authors merely as "a representative resource-constrained IoT device," not a true bare-metal microcontroller like an ESP32 (single/dual-core, hundreds of KB of RAM, no OS).
deep.relation_to_our_project: LE3D is highly relevant on three fronts. (1) Hardware-reporting template: Table IV (init time, per-sample latency in µs) and Table V (CPU%/RAM%/system-load vs. sampling rate 1Hz–4000Hz on real hardware) are exactly the reporting format the team should replicate for the ESP32 — but LE3D's own "resource-constrained" claim is comparatively soft (a Linux-capable RPi 3B+ with 1GB RAM and a Python/MQTT/River stack is orders of magnitude more capable than an ESP32's ~320–520KB SRAM, no-OS/RTOS environment). Reproducing this style of table on genuine MCU-class hardware, in C/C++ with no Python interpreter, and — critically — adding energy/power measurements (joules), which LE3D never reports at all, is itself a legitimate, defensible novelty/contribution angle ("closes a hardware-realism gap LE3D leaves open"). (2) Algorithmic base for the drift-adaptation half: LE3D's ADWIN+PHT+KSWIN ensemble with adaptive-window majority voting is a strong, citable, lightweight unsupervised building block the team can adopt or adapt as the "benign concept-drift adaptation" mechanism of their IDS, since it needs only ~100 samples to initialize and runs in microseconds per sample — well within ESP32 budgets. (3) The exact gap the project targets: LE3D's natural-vs-abnormal classifier is a single-shot, per-drift-event statistical comparison against neighbors' distributions; it has no defense whatsoever against a slow ("boiling-frog") adversary who nudges the device's own adaptive-window baseline (the very statistics ADWIN/PHT/KSWIN use to define "normal") gradually enough, over many adaptation cycles, that each individual step looks like ordinary benign drift and gets accepted, permanently corrupting what the detector treats as "normal." LE3D never poses or tests this threat model — no adversarial/poisoning evaluation, no bound on how much the adaptation mechanism itself may shift per unit time, no robustness metric. This is precisely the paper's own admitted scope boundary (it treats "is this drift natural or malicious" as answerable from a single snapshot comparison, never asking "has the adaptation process itself been gamed over time") and gives the team a concrete, well-evidenced gap to fill: a poison-resilient adaptation policy (e.g., rate-limiting/robust-statistics guards on how far the adaptive window's baseline may drift before requiring stronger corroboration, or a slow-drift-vs-attack discriminator) layered on top of an LE3D-style lightweight ensemble, evaluated with real ESP32 RAM/latency/energy numbers in the same style as LE3D's Tables IV–V. Additionally, LE3D's own finding that a supervised continuously-retrained baseline (PWPAE) collapses from F1 99.8% to ~32% the moment online labels are unavailable strengthens the case that naive continuous adaptation is fragile in realistic (label-free, and by extension poisoning-exposed) streaming settings — directly motivating why a smarter, protected adaptation policy is needed rather than naive online retraining.

deep.title: Can't Boil This Frog: Robustness of Online-Trained Autoencoder-Based Anomaly Detectors to Adversarial Poisoning Attacks
deep.authors: Moshe Kravchik and Asaf Shabtai, Dept. of Software and Information Systems Engineering, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva, Israel
deep.venue_year: arXiv:2002.02741 [cs.LG], submitted Feb 7, 2020 (v1). No separate conference/journal venue found via search — appears to remain an arXiv preprint.
deep.fetch_status: Full text obtained. arxiv.org/abs page gave the abstract; the PDF at arxiv.org/pdf/2002.02741 was fetched as raw bytes (WebFetch couldn't parse it as text) but was saved locally and read in full (all 13 pages, including figures/tables/algorithms and the Discussion & Conclusions section) with the Read tool's PDF extraction. All fields below are drawn from the actual paper text, not inferred.
deep.problem: Whether an online-trained (periodically retrained), semi-supervised, deep-NN regression-based anomaly detector in an Industrial Control System (ICS) can have its retraining process "poisoned" so that a specific target attack goes undetected, while the model keeps behaving normally on everything else (no false alarms). This exploits the fact that ICS detectors are periodically retrained on newly collected data to absorb legitimate concept drift ("online training"), which also hands an attacker a channel to gradually shift ("boil the frog") what the model considers normal. The paper frames this as the first study of poisoning attacks (as opposed to evasion attacks) against online-trained, semi-supervised, regression-based deep-NN detectors on multivariate physics-based time series — prior poisoning work targeted classification problems, not this regression/semi-supervised/online setting.
deep.method: Threat model: a white-box "malicious sensor" attacker who can spoof sensor values seen identically by both the PLC and the detector (cannot separately manipulate the two), with full knowledge of model architecture, weights, hyperparameters and the online retraining schedule (worst case). The attacker only injects poison points that do not themselves trigger alerts, mirroring the realistic assumption that only unflagged data is folded into retraining. Formalized as a bilevel optimization: outer objective finds a poisoning sequence D_p that makes the detector issue zero alerts on the target attack sequence and on clean validation data; inner objective is the detector's own training loss on D_tr ∪ D_p. Two poison-generation algorithms are proposed: (1) a back-gradient optimization algorithm (extending Muñoz-González et al.'s classification-domain method to this semi-supervised/regression/online setting), which rolls back the training optimizer's weight updates step by step using Hessian-vector products to compute the gradient of the attacker's objective w.r.t. the poisoning input; a novel "wrapper model" is built around the trained detector so this can be applied to the overlapping sliding-window subsequences typical of ICS detectors (a single manipulated timepoint affects multiple overlapping input sequences); (2) a simpler, much faster interpolative algorithm that iteratively interpolates between an initial poison point and the target attack, backing off the step size whenever an interpolated point triggers an alert. The target detector under test is an undercomplete autoencoder (UAE) with "inflating" encoder/decoder layers, implemented in TensorFlow, trained on reconstruction-error to a threshold. Effectiveness is measured via attack magnitude achievable, number of poisoning points required, number of optimization iterations, and iteration execution time.
deep.dataset_used: (1) Synthetic periodic signals — sine, double-sine, square (numpy.square), sawtooth (numpy.sawtooth) waveforms with Gaussian noise (mean 0, std 0.05), used to systematically vary attack location/magnitude/training-set size. (2) Real-world ICS data: the SWaT (Secure Water Treatment) dataset from the iTrust Centre / Singapore University of Technology and Design's scaled-down six-stage water treatment testbed — 51 sensor/actuator attributes at 1-second resolution, 7 days normal operation + 4 days of 36 labeled attacks. Ten sensor-value-spoofing attacks matching the paper's threat model were selected for the poisoning experiments (five other attacks were excluded because they didn't preserve feature statistics between train/test). This is physics-based ICS sensor/actuator telemetry, not IoT network traffic, and all experiments run on standard ML hardware (TensorFlow, Google Colab TPU) with no constrained-device evaluation.
deep.metrics_reported: Attack magnitude (max deviation between spoofed and original/target sensor value the attacker can force through undetected), number of poisoning points in the generated sequence, number of optimization iterations required to find a successful poisoning sequence, and per-iteration execution time (seconds, measured on TPU) for each algorithm/detector configuration. Success/failure is binary per attack: whether a poisoning sequence exists that raises zero alerts on both the target attack and clean validation data at a fixed anomaly threshold (0.2, with a 0.1 sensitivity check for one case).
deep.key_results: On synthetic data, both algorithms could poison the autoencoder, but the number of poisoning points needed grew roughly linearly with attack magnitude and with training-set size; back-gradient optimization reached larger attack magnitudes than interpolation (especially once overlapping-subsequence/multi-sequence modeling was used), at far greater computational cost (back-gradient: ~33-67 sec/iteration vs. interpolation: ~1.2-1.3 sec/iteration). Neither algorithm could poison attacks located at the signal's maximum ("SIN_TOP" location, i.e., pushing a sensor value above anything seen in training) at any meaningful magnitude. On the real SWaT dataset (10 attacks), poisoning succeeded for only 4 of 10 attacks, and only at attack magnitudes substantially clipped/reduced below the real attacks' actual magnitude; adding just 1-2 more correlated sensor features to the detector's input set fully closed the poisoning channel for 3 of those 4 (attacks #16, #33, #36); the remaining "success" (#31) turned out to already be below the detection threshold before poisoning even started, and disappeared entirely once the threshold was tightened from 0.2 to 0.1. Overall conclusion: physics-based, online-trained autoencoder ICS detectors are markedly more robust to poisoning than NN detectors in other domains such as image classification and malware detection — a long, white-box optimization procedure could not get the detector to accept a significant real anomaly as normal without also producing false positives on legitimate data.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: From the paper's own Discussion & Conclusions (Section VII), stated explicitly: (1) Only autoencoder-based detectors were evaluated; although the poisoning algorithms are architecture-agnostic in principle, robustness of other NN architectures (e.g., CNN/RNN-based ICS detectors) is left as future work. (2) The poisoning algorithms, in their current form, "require a very long time to calculate," making them "inappropriate for real-time poisoning" — improving their computational efficiency is flagged as an open problem. (3) The study only used standard gradient descent as the training optimizer; extending back-gradient poisoning to other popular optimizers (RMSProp, Adam) is noted as a promising future direction, since those can also be traced backward per prior work (Maclaurin et al.). (4) Future work will explore transferability of poisoning attacks between models trained with different optimizers. (5) The study used a purely data-driven / simulation-only verification approach with no access to a real ICS testbed; the authors explicitly name "validating the findings in a real-world testbed" as "a natural next stage of this research, possibly after finding a way to accelerate poisoning sequence generation" — i.e., they identify runtime cost as the blocker to real-world validation. (6) They suggest the algorithms/robustness question could be examined in other domains beyond ICS (signal processing, speech processing, medical diagnostics), implicitly flagging that their robustness finding is domain-specific to physics-bound ICS data and not established elsewhere (e.g., IoT network traffic is never mentioned or tested). No mention anywhere in the paper of resource-constrained/embedded hardware, RAM/latency/energy cost, or IoT network-traffic features — this is a hardware-agnostic, network-traffic-agnostic study entirely on physics-bound sensor telemetry.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is the direct origin of the "boiling frog" framing and attack model the project's title invokes — gradually poisoning the periodic/online retraining a detector uses to absorb legitimate drift — and it is exactly the paper to differentiate against, for several concrete reasons drawn straight from its own text: (1) Domain gap: it attacks physics-bound ICS sensor/actuator telemetry (SWaT water-treatment signals) with strong continuous, quasi-periodic internal structure — never IoT network traffic (packet/flow/protocol features), which is heterogeneous, bursty, and governed by device/protocol behavior rather than physical law. Their own conclusion — that ICS detectors resist poisoning because of "the physics-bound characteristics of a real-world process" and the models' small parameter counts — is explicitly a domain-conditioned finding; whether it holds for network-traffic-based IoT IDS is untested and is a legitimate, specific open question this project can answer empirically. (2) Hardware gap: everything here runs on TensorFlow/Colab TPU with no resource accounting; the authors themselves flag their poisoning algorithms as too slow "for real-time poisoning" and never touch RAM, latency, or energy — exactly the axis (ESP32-class on-device evaluation of poison-resilience vs. drift-adaptation vs. RAM/latency/energy) this project adds and that a reviewer/instructor focused on "edge intelligence for resource-constrained systems" would value. (3) Retraining-mechanism gap: their online training retrains a deep AE on rolling windows drawn from a near-million-row dataset via full TensorFlow gradient descent; an MCU-class detector instead needs a bounded-memory incremental/online learner (small buffer, lightweight update rule), which plausibly changes the poisoning dynamics — smaller models/buffers may be either easier or harder to "boil" than their large multi-feature AE, and that comparison is itself a contribution. (4) Reusable formal apparatus: their bilevel-optimization threat-model formalization (outer: attacker minimizes detector alerts over a poison sequence; inner: detector minimizes training loss including that poison; "only alert-free data re-enters training") gives a ready-made, citable formal frame for this project's own threat model section, and their evaluation axes (attack magnitude tolerated vs. number/duration of poisoning points needed, as a curve) map directly onto a poison-resilience metric for an IoT IDS. (5) Design cue: their finding that adding more correlated sensor features closed most successful poisoning channels suggests an analogous lightweight defense for constrained IoT devices — cross-feature/cross-flow consistency checks or a stricter/robust buffer-update rule — worth testing against MCU RAM budgets. (6) Positioning: this is a negative/robustness result (poisoning mostly failed) in ICS; the project's novelty claim is not "yet another poisoning attack" but testing whether that robustness generalizes to the IoT-network-traffic + severely resource-constrained + incremental-learning setting, and if it does not generalize (plausible given smaller buffers/models), proposing and evaluating a lightweight, ESP32-feasible defense — directly filling the gaps the authors themselves name (other architectures, other domains, real-world/constrained validation, faster/practical attack generation) rather than re-deriving them from scratch.

deep.title: Learn to Adapt: Robust Drift Detection in Security Domain
deep.authors: Aditya Kuppa and Nhien-An Le-Khac, School of Computer Science, University College Dublin, Ireland (corresponding: aditya.kuppa@ucdconnect.ie, an.lekhac@ucd.ie)
deep.venue_year: Computers and Electrical Engineering (Elsevier, SCI Q1, IF ≈3.81), Vol. 102 (2022), article 108239. Also posted as arXiv:2206.07581 [cs.CR] (June 2022) — the version actually read for this summary.
deep.verified_url: Full text read from: https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07581 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.07581). Official venue page (candidate URL given, returned HTTP 403 and was not accessible): https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S004579062200475X — also indexed at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.compeleceng.2022.108239
deep.fetch_status: Full text obtained and read cover-to-cover (all ~24 content pages, including all figures, tables, the Limitations section, and Conclusion) — not just the abstract. The ScienceDirect URL given in the task returned HTTP 403 Forbidden via WebFetch (typical bot-blocking on that platform). A web search located an open-access arXiv preprint of the same paper (arXiv:2206.07581), which was fetched as a PDF and read in full via the PDF reader. Content below is verified directly from that full text, not inferred from a snippet.
deep.problem: Deploying ML models in security domains (network intrusion detection, APT/C&C detection) must handle concept drift — data/feature distributions shifting from what the model was trained on — which is especially severe in security because of the ever-evolving threat landscape and scarce labeled data at deployment time. Existing drift-detection/retraining methods in the literature assume non-adversarial drift (clean incoming data, known drift characteristics, timely feedback) and are not robust when an attacker deliberately induces drift to evade the detector itself (as opposed to attacking the underlying classifier directly) — and they are also slow to discover genuinely new attack classes. The paper's stated goal is a drift detector that (1) accurately identifies drifted samples, (2) is robust/immune to attacker-induced ("adversarial") drift specifically targeting the drift detector, and (3) discovers new classes from drifted samples online, without needing all classes available at training time.
deep.method: A three-stage design: (1) An embedding network (encoder/decoder autoencoder) is trained with a combined loss — MSE reconstruction loss plus a supervised contrastive loss (temperature-scaled cosine similarity, τ=0.1) that pulls same-class embeddings together and pushes different-class embeddings apart — to map high-dimensional inputs into a compact 32-D latent space with tight class clusters. (2) A Nearest Class Mean (NCM) classifier operates on class prototypes (mean embeddings) in that latent space, using a distance function that combines an instance-level Euclidean distance with a group-level Riemannian/geometric divergence term (D = d_R + λ1·d_E, λ1=0.1) — this dual instance+group fidelity is the specific design choice meant to make the detector robust to adversarial (not just natural) drift. A sample is routed through a decision flow: drifted? → adversarial (reject/alert) or a plausible new concept? (3) New classes are discovered via a recursive update mechanism that accumulates drifted-sample embedding-vector deltas until they cross a preset threshold T (=3.5), forming a new class prototype and triggering encoder/NCM retraining — done without needing all classes at training time. To evaluate adversarial robustness, the authors devised two attack generators against their own detector: instance-based poisoning (bagging-based subsampling + PGD-based label-flip perturbations injected at ratios 5–25%) and concept-based poisoning (their prior "MAA" black-box-attack method used to inject 1–5 synthetic adversarial concepts/classes of 250 instances each).
deep.dataset_used: (1) A 2018-released network intrusion dataset (CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Sharafaldin et al., using a corrected/relabeled version per Engelen et al. 2021) — 7 attack categories (Brute-force, Heartbleed, Botnet, DoS, DDoS, Web attacks, Infiltration) captured from an infrastructure of 420 victim machines, 30 servers, 50 attacker machines; 72 bidirectional-flow statistical features extracted via a modified CICFlowMeter-v3. (2) An APT Command-and-Control dataset (Hawk-Eye: 3,894 FQDNs / 1,894 domains with campaign metadata) combined with a web-page categorization dataset (100,000 sampled URLs, 134 lexical/host-based features), forming a deliberately imbalanced combined dataset. 75/25 train-test split; PyTorch, Adam optimizer, lr=0.0001, 300 epochs, batch size 128 (URL) / 256 (Network).
deep.metrics_reported: Precision, Recall, F1-score of the drift detector as n=1..4 classes are dropped from training and treated as drifted; AUROC for new/unknown-class (OOD-style) detection versus One-Class SVM, OpenMax, and a Euclidean-distance baseline; average incremental accuracy under a class-incremental learning protocol as new classes are exposed over time; accuracy-degradation curves versus percentage of poisoned/adversarial instances injected (5–25%) and versus number of injected adversarial concepts (1–5), benchmarked against 4 baselines (plain Autoencoder, ADCA+MMD via Alibi-Detect, INSOMNIA, CADE); and standard precision/recall/F1 in a non-drift, non-adversarial binary control setting (Benign vs. Infiltration) against a plain MLP classifier.
deep.key_results: Drift detection: proposed method beats all 4 baselines at both n=2 and n=4 dropped classes on both datasets, e.g. Network-data F1 0.942→0.813 as dropped classes go 2→4 (vs. CADE 0.897→0.704, INSOMNIA 0.849→0.659, ADCA 0.798→0.671, plain AE 0.777→0.630); URL-data F1 0.906→0.842 (vs. ADCA 0.878→0.674, AE 0.721→0.606) — and its degradation with more dropped/unseen classes is markedly smaller than the baselines'. New-class detection AUROC: ~85–93% for the proposed method vs. 53–80% for One-Class SVM/OpenMax/Euclidean-distance baselines. Adversarial robustness: under 5–25% poisoned instances or 1–5 injected adversarial concepts, baselines that matched the proposed method's accuracy in the non-adversarial setting (e.g. CADE, which shares the contrastive-loss idea) collapse steeply, while the proposed method degrades much more gracefully — attributed to the combined Euclidean+geometric NCM distance. Non-adversarial control: on Benign-vs-Infiltration classification the proposed method (P=0.996, R=0.999, F1=0.997) performs on par with a standard MLP (P=0.998, R=1.0, F1=0.998), i.e. the robustness gains don't cost baseline accuracy.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: From the paper's own Section 8 "Limitations" (paraphrased close to verbatim): (1) "we have not thoroughly studied the time and space complexity of the algorithm," despite acknowledging that "inference times and response times are critical for any production grade system" running a drift detector in-line with a deployed classifier — explicitly left to future work, and never addressed anywhere else in the paper (no runtime/memory numbers, no embedded/IoT hardware discussion at all — everything is PyTorch on standard infrastructure). (2) Many detector misses were traced to labeling errors or large feature-set overlap between classes in the training data; the authors note real-world training sets are "prone to labeling errors" that "may lead to a false sense of drifts," and say they "plan to tackle this problem in future." (3) They note that "threat models and attacks on drift detectors are rare" in the literature (since a drift detector is an auxiliary sub-module the adversary has limited visibility into), that they devised only "two novel attacks" themselves for testing, and that studying these attacks "in depth... under different threat models" is future work — i.e., their own poisoning attacks are static/one-shot severity sweeps (fixed instance ratio or fixed count of injected concepts per experiment), not a sustained multi-round campaign against their own online recursive-update mechanism. (4) The system "does not provide an explanation interface" for analysts; they envision (but defer) using k-nearest-neighbor queries in latent space to support one.
deep.relation_to_our_project:
This is a strong, directly relevant methodological neighbor for the drift-adaptation half of the project, and the survey's characterization holds up: it is one of few papers putting adversary-vs-drift-detector robustness squarely in network-security data (network intrusion + APT), evaluated with a serious protocol (precision/recall/F1 vs. unseen classes, AUROC vs. OOD baselines, degradation curves vs. poison severity) against real competing baselines (CADE, INSOMNIA, ADCA+MMD).

Three concrete links to our project:
1. Reusable design + evaluation template: the contrastive-embedding + NCM classifier with a combined instance-level (Euclidean) and group-level (geometric/Riemannian) distance is a validated pattern for separating "benign drift" from "adversarial/poisoned drift" — exactly our project's core algorithmic problem. Their evaluation protocol (precision/recall/F1 sweeps over unseen classes, AUROC vs. OOD baselines, accuracy-degradation-vs-poison-severity curves) is a template our mid-review/final evaluation can mirror and extend, which strengthens the "proper evaluation" criterion for an A/A* framing.
2. A near-direct invitation for our novelty: the authors explicitly flag, as unstudied, exactly the axis our project is built around — time/space complexity of the drift detector — with no mention anywhere of embedded/IoT hardware, RAM, latency, or energy. We can frame part of our contribution as taking this class of security-domain, poison-resilient drift detector to the on-device (ESP32-class) regime the authors themselves said was left open: quantifying real hardware cost, and where the full architecture doesn't fit in a few hundred KB of RAM, engineering a compressed/quantized variant that preserves the poison-resilience property.
3. A genuine threat-model gap for our "boiling-frog" framing: their own poisoning attacks (bagging+PGD instance poisoning at fixed 5–25% ratios; MAA-based injection of 1–5 synthetic concepts) are single-shot severity sweeps on a static train/test split, not a sustained, low-rate, incremental poisoning campaign carried out across many successive online adaptation/retraining rounds where each round's poison budget is small enough to mimic ordinary benign drift. The authors' own Limitations section admits they only tested "two novel attacks" and left deeper study "under different threat models" to future work — this is precisely the sequential/slow-poisoning threat model our project targets, and stress-testing (and hardening) a contrastive/NCM-style detector — or an on-device descendant of it — against that specific temporal attack is a legitimate "new combination / unaddressed IoT constraint" novelty angle.

One caveat: their datasets (CSE-CIC-IDS2018 enterprise traffic; APT C&C + web categorization) are security-relevant but not IoT-device traffic, so this paper alone doesn't establish IoT applicability — our project should still validate on an IoT-flavored intrusion dataset (e.g., BoT-IoT, TON_IoT, or a CICIoT variant) alongside adopting this paper's detector/evaluation ideas. The baselines it benchmarks against (CADE, INSOMNIA, ADCA) are also worth citing directly in our related-work section as the competitive set in this specific niche.

deep.title: Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing
deep.authors: Albert Bifet and Ricard Gavaldà, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (LSI dept.), {abifet,gavalda}@lsi.upc.edu
deep.venue_year: Proceedings of the 2007 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining (SDM 2007), Minneapolis, MN, pp. 443-448. Preprint dated 17 October 2006. (DOI: 10.1137/1.9781611972771.42)
deep.verified_url: https://www.cs.upc.edu/~Gavalda/papers/adwin06.pdf (author's own open-access mirror of the full SDM'07 paper; the DOI itself resolves to the paywalled SIAM epubs page, https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611972771.42, which was not accessible)
deep.fetch_status: FULL TEXT OBTAINED. The DOI (https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611972771.42) redirects to the paywalled SIAM epubs page and was not directly readable. However, WebSearch located the authors' own open-access PDF mirror of the identical paper (https://www.cs.upc.edu/~Gavalda/papers/adwin06.pdf, 17 pages incl. appendix + references), which I fetched and read page-by-page (all 17 pages, including figures and tables) to verify title, authors, abstract, full method, all experiments/tables, and the conclusions/future-work section verbatim. Nothing below is inferred from an abstract alone; all of it is drawn from the full text.
deep.problem: The paper addresses the general problem of learning/mining from a data stream whose generating distribution D_t changes over time ("concept drift" / "distribution change"), where a client algorithm needs to: (1) detect when change occurs, (2) decide which examples to keep vs. forget (i.e., maintain updated sufficient statistics), and (3) revise its model when significant change is detected. Existing approaches were unsatisfactory: fixed-size sliding windows force the user to guess a time-scale of change a priori (small windows = reactive but noisy; large windows = accurate but stale during drift); decay-function weighting has the same tradeoff hidden in a decay constant; heuristic variable-size-window methods (Widmer & Kubat 1996; Klinkenberg & Joachims 2000) have no rigorous performance guarantees and are computationally expensive; and prior theoretical work with rigorous guarantees (e.g. Bartlett et al., Helmbold & Long) had never been tested in real learning/mining contexts and typically assumed a known bound on the rate of change. The paper's stated goal is a window-management algorithm that adapts its own size online from the data, with NO user-specified time-scale parameter, and with provable bounds on false-positive and false-negative change-detection rates.
deep.method: Two algorithms, both called "ADWIN" (ADaptive WINdowing), operating on a stream of reals/bits x_1,...,x_t drawn independently from possibly-changing distributions D_t with unknown mean mu_t: (1) ADWIN (basic): keeps ALL raw values in a variable-length window W; at every new arrival it exhaustively tests every possible split W = W0·W1 (older·newer) and, if the observed sub-window averages differ by more than a Hoeffding-bound-derived cut threshold epsilon_cut(δ) [refined in practice via a normal-approximation variant using the observed variance, Eq. 3.1], it drops W0 (declares change, shrinks the window). Theorem 3.1 proves: (a) if mu_t is truly constant within W, P(ADWIN shrinks W at this step) ≤ δ (false-positive bound); (b) if some split has true means differing by >2·epsilon_cut, ADWIN shrinks with probability ≥ 1-δ (false-negative bound). This version is memory- and time-inefficient because it stores the whole window explicitly and checks all O(n) cut points. (2) ADWIN2: a memory/time-efficient re-implementation using a variant of "exponential histograms" (data-stream summarization structures) that keeps O(log W) buckets (more precisely O(M·log(W/M)) memory words for a tunable parameter M), checks only O(log W) candidate cut points instead of all of them, and processes each new element in O(1) amortized / O(log W) worst-case time (O(log²W) worst-case per element including the cut search). ADWIN2 preserves essentially the same statistical guarantees as ADWIN (Theorem 3.2) and is used as the algorithm in all experiments. The paper also shows analytically that for a step change of size epsilon, ADWIN shrinks after O(mu·ln(1/δ)/epsilon²) steps, and for a gradual (linear-slope alpha) change it starts shrinking after O(mu·ln(1/δ)/alpha²)^(1/3) steps -- i.e., detection is provably slower/delayed the more gradual the drift is. ADWIN2 is then plugged into two learning algorithms to demonstrate the "internal" (embedded) use pattern: (i) an incremental Naïve Bayes predictor, where one ADWIN2 instance is created per (attribute-value, class) count so each conditional-probability count adapts at its own rate; (ii) an incremental k-means clusterer, where one ADWIN2 instance tracks each centroid coordinate to detect when a centroid has moved.
deep.dataset_used: Synthetic: (1) random Bernoulli bit streams with a hidden, occasionally-changing probability p, used to measure false-positive/false-negative rates of ADWIN2 as a bare estimator (Table 1); (2) triangular-wave, square-wave, and staircase synthetic streams of various periods, up to 10^6 points, used to compare ADWIN2 against fixed-size and fixed-size-with-flushing windows via L1/L2 distance to the true generating probability (Tables 2-5) and via relative error for rare/small-probability events (Table 6); (3) Bernoulli streams of length 2×10^3 to 10^6 with a stationary phase followed by a linear-slope phase of varying steepness, used to compare ADWIN2 as a change detector against Gama et al.'s (2004) drift-detection method (Table 7); (4) a rotating-hyperplane concept (from Hulten, Spencer & Domingos 2001), 8 discrete attributes/2 classes in 2 values, weights varying over time, used with the incremental Naïve Bayes predictor (Table 8); (5) k-Gaussian synthetic clustering data, 10^6 points, k=5 moving centroids at different velocities/variances, used with the incremental k-means clusterer (Tables 11-12). Real-world: the Electricity Market Dataset (ELEC2), collected by M. Harries (1999) from the Australian New South Wales Electricity Market and previously used by Gama et al. -- 45,312 instances (7 May 1996 - 5 Dec 1998), 48 instances/day, 5 input fields (day of week, timestamp, NSW demand, Vic demand, scheduled inter-state transfer) plus a binary class label for whether the 24h moving-average price went up or down; used only with the Naïve Bayes predictor (Tables 9-10). No network-traffic, IoT, or intrusion-detection dataset of any kind is used anywhere in the paper.
deep.metrics_reported: Rate of false positives / false negatives in change declaration (checked against the theoretical δ bound); L1 and L2 distance between the tracked estimate and the true generating probability; average maintained window width; relative estimation error |true - estimated|/true for rare-event probabilities; for the change-detector comparison: % of trial runs in which change was detected within the last 1,000 samples, and mean ± standard deviation of detection time; for Naïve Bayes and k-means: predictive accuracy (%) / sum-of-distances-to-centroids of a "dynamic" model built with each windowing strategy versus a periodically-rebuilt "static" baseline model, plus the ratio %Dynamic/%Static; rough wall-clock processing time and average number of buckets used (as a proxy for memory), explicitly NOT rigorously optimized or benchmarked (see limitations below).
deep.key_results: (1) Measured false-positive rates are always below the specified δ, often far below it for small μ (Table 1; e.g. μ=0.01 gives ~0 false positives at all δ tested). (2) As an estimator on periodic synthetic streams, ADWIN2 tracks the true probability about as well as, or only slightly worse than, the single BEST fixed-size window (whose size happens to match the true period), and far better than any fixed window whose size is badly mismatched to the unknown period -- i.e. ADWIN2 gets fixed-window-optimal performance without knowing the period. (3) For tracking small/rare probabilities, ADWIN2 clearly beats fixed windows of any size (Table 6; e.g. at true probability 1/8192, ADWIN2's relative error is ~0.10 vs. 1.31-1.93 for fixed windows). (4) As a change detector versus Gama et al.'s method, ADWIN2's detection rate stays roughly constant as stream length L grows, whereas Gama's detection rate degrades sharply with L (e.g. at L=10^6 and slope 4×10^-4, Gama detects change in only 5% of runs vs. 83% for ADWIN2), though ADWIN2's mean detection latency is sometimes larger than Gama's, especially in the no-change/false-alarm condition. (5) Embedded in Naïve Bayes, the "ADWIN2 per count" incremental scheme is the best or near-best dynamic model on both the synthetic hyperplane data (99.36% of the static-model accuracy ceiling) and the real ELEC2 dataset (77-84% of the static ceiling depending on evaluation protocol), consistently outperforming fixed and fixed-flushing windows in most settings (one exception on ELEC2 attributed to the dataset's short, ~10-20-sample runs of identical values, which favor very short/myopic windows). (6) Embedded in k-means, ADWIN2-tracked centroids stay closer to the true moving centroids than any fixed-size or fixed-flushing window across nearly all tested variances and velocities (Tables 11-12). (7) Rough resource figures (Java, 3.0GHz Pentium, 1GB RAM, Windows XP, non-optimized code): ADWIN2 used on average ~45 buckets and ~23 seconds to process 10^6 samples per estimator instance in the comparative experiments; ~1060 seconds / ~34 estimators (<32s, <60 buckets each) in the Naïve Bayes benchmark; a boolean sliding window of 60 buckets (representing windows up to length 2^12=4096 with M=5) needs roughly 300 bytes, and a real-valued one about 540 bytes.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper contains several explicit self-acknowledged limitations, quoted/paraphrased directly from the text: (a) On resource cost (Section 7, most directly relevant to an ESP32 RAM/latency baseline): "In the experiments above we have only discussed the performance in terms of error rate, and not time or memory usage. Certainly, this was not our main goal in this paper, and we have in no way tried to optimize our implementations in either time or memory (as is clearly indicated by the choice of Java as programming language)." -- i.e., the authors explicitly did NOT produce an optimized, resource-benchmarked implementation; all reported time/memory numbers are "rough figures" meant only to "suggest that our approach can be fairly competitive after some optimization work," measured on a desktop-class machine (3.0GHz Pentium, 1GB RAM), nowhere near embedded/ESP32-class constraints. (b) Formal Conclusions/future-work (Section 8): "Future work must include more thorough experimentation, both with more real-world datasets and in combination with other learning algorithms. As mentioned before, we are currently working in the integration of ADWIN2 in decision-tree induction methods." (c) End of Section 7: "we are investigating the possibility of making better predictions from the contents of the window. Right now, the prediction at every time step is simply the average of the elements in the window. But if change is occurring, it may be better to give more weight to most recent examples -- the question is then how much more weight? We have recently reported on using Kalman filters together with an earlier (less sensitive) version of ADWIN2..." (d) A theoretical caveat stated early on (Section 3.1): "Since the values of mu_t can oscillate wildly, there is no guarantee that mu_W or mu_hat_W will be anywhere close to the instantaneous value mu_t, even for long W" -- the guarantees are about the windowed average tracking the windowed expectation, not the instantaneous true mean. (e) An empirically-shown (not just stated) limitation: gradual/slow drift is detected much later than abrupt drift of comparable eventual magnitude (Figures 2 vs. 3/5, and the O(...)^{1/3} delay bound for linear-slope changes) -- the algorithm is provably slower to react to slow drift, by design of its statistical test. Nowhere does the paper discuss or test adversarial manipulation of the input stream; the framing throughout assumes D_t changes "naturally," not that an adversary is deliberately crafting the sequence to game the epsilon_cut threshold.
deep.relation_to_our_project: ADWIN/ADWIN2 is the direct, citable theoretical and empirical baseline for the "drift-adaptation module" piece of the project, and its own stated gaps map almost exactly onto the project's novelty claims: (1) RAM baseline: ADWIN2's O(log W) [precisely O(M log(W/M))] memory-word bound and its concrete bucket counts (~45-60 buckets, ~300-540 bytes for W up to ~4096) give a hard, well-documented number to benchmark any ESP32-class drift-tracking structure against -- "our on-device module uses X bytes vs. ADWIN2's theoretical/measured ~300-540 bytes for a comparable window." (2) The paper's own admitted limitation -- "this was not our main goal... we have in no way tried to optimize our implementations in either time or memory" and all measurements were on a 3GHz desktop with 1GB RAM in Java -- is exactly the gap the project exploits: nobody has evaluated ADWIN-style adaptive windowing under real ESP32-class RAM/latency/energy constraints, and this is squarely within the instructor's listed interest in "edge intelligence for resource-constrained systems." (3) Poisoning-resilience novelty: ADWIN's guarantees (Theorem 3.1) assume D_t changes according to some natural process, not an adversary; and the paper's own results show that gradual/slow drift is inherently harder and slower for the Hoeffding-based test to catch than abrupt drift (Figs. 2/3/5, and the derived O(...)^{1/3} detection-delay formula for linear slopes). This is precisely the mechanism a "boiling-frog" data-poisoning attacker would exploit: by shifting the traffic statistics by less than epsilon_cut per adaptation step, an attacker can walk ADWIN's window (and hence the "normal" model it feeds) toward including attack traffic while staying, by the algorithm's own design, within its accepted false-negative slack. The paper never considers or defends against this -- it is an unaddressed gap in the foundational drift-detection literature, giving the project a well-grounded technical target: build a drift-adaptation mechanism (ADWIN-based or otherwise) augmented with poisoning-resistance (e.g., bounding cumulative unverified drift, requiring cross-feature corroboration, or rate-limiting adaptation) before committing shrink/model-update decisions. (4) Design-pattern reuse: the paper's "one ADWIN2 instance per statistic" pattern (used for each Naïve Bayes count and each k-means centroid coordinate) is a directly reusable template for an ESP32 IDS -- maintain one lightweight adaptive-window tracker per traffic feature (packet rate, flow duration, byte counts, etc.), each independently adaptive, which the project can extend with a poisoning-aware gating layer. (5) Dataset gap: ADWIN was validated only on one low-dimensional real dataset (ELEC2, electricity price time series) plus synthetic streams -- never on network/IoT traffic or an intrusion-detection setting -- so there is no prior empirical evidence either way for how ADWIN-style adaptive windowing behaves on IoT network-flow features, reinforcing that the project's evaluation (unsupervised, on-device, drifting IoT traffic, under poisoning) fills a genuinely open, citable gap rather than duplicating existing work.

deep.title: Learning with Drift Detection
deep.authors: João Gama, Pedro Medas, Gladys Castillo, Pedro Rodrigues — LIACC & Fac. of Economics, University of Porto; University of Aveiro (Portugal)
deep.venue_year: Advances in Artificial Intelligence – SBIA 2004 (17th Brazilian Symposium on AI), Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNAI) vol. 3171, Springer, 2004. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-540-28645-5_29
deep.problem: Standard ML assumes training examples are i.i.d. draws from a stationary distribution. This paper addresses learning when that distribution changes over time ("concept drift"), defining a "context" as a maximal stretch of examples generated by a stationary distribution. The goal is to directly detect the moment(s) a context changes (abrupt or gradual) so a model can be re-trained using only the examples that belong to the new context, instead of relying on ad hoc fixed/adaptive time windows or example-weighting heuristics (the two prior-art families the paper reviews: FLORA/Widmer-Kubat, and Klinkenberg's/Klinkenberg-Joachims' monitoring/SVM-window approaches).
deep.method: The Drift Detection Method (DDM), used online with any classifier (tested as a wrapper, so it is learner-agnostic). For each incoming labeled example i, the current model predicts and the outcome is a Bernoulli trial (correct/incorrect). The running error rate p_i and its standard deviation s_i = sqrt(p_i(1-p_i)/i) are computed. Under the PAC-learning premise, p_i should keep decreasing while the distribution is stationary (Binomial ≈ Normal for n>30), so a statistically significant rise signals drift. DDM keeps two running registers, p_min and s_min, updated whenever p_i+s_i is lower than the current p_min+s_min (i.e., tracking the historical best point). Two thresholds relative to that minimum trigger state changes: a WARNING level at p_i+s_i ≥ p_min + 2·s_min (~95% confidence, marks the start index k_w of a candidate new context) and a DRIFT level at p_i+s_i ≥ p_min + 3·s_min (~99% confidence, index k_d). If drift is confirmed, a new model is retrained using only examples from k_w to k_d; if the error instead falls back below warning before reaching drift, it is treated as a false alarm and discarded. Memory/compute cost is O(1) per example (just p_min, s_min, and running p_i/s_i) — this is exactly what makes it the classic "cheapest" drift detector cited in the survey. The authors note the method generalizes to other loss functions (e.g., MSE for regression) by choosing appropriate α values.
deep.dataset_used: (1) 8 synthetic concept-drift streams from Kubat & Widmer's suite, each 1000 examples/context, 2 classes, 50/50 balanced: SINE1, SINE2 (abrupt, noise-free, 2 relevant attrs), SINIRREL1, SINIRREL2 (same as SINE1/2 plus 2 irrelevant attrs), CIRCLES (gradual drift, 4 contexts defined by 4 growing circles — the paper's only gradual-drift dataset), GAUSS (abrupt, noisy, Gaussian-distributed classes), STAGGER (abrupt, symbolic attributes: size/color/shape), MIXED (abrupt, 2 boolean + 2 numeric attributes). (2) One real-world dataset: ELEC2, the Australian New South Wales electricity market dataset (Harries 1999) — 45,312 instances, 7 May 1996–5 Dec 1998, 5 fields (day, time, NSW demand, Vic demand, scheduled inter-state transfer), label = price direction vs. a 24h moving average; used for two prediction tasks (last-day, last-week horizon) with CART (via R) as the base learner. (3) UCI ADULT census dataset, used only as a stability/false-alarm control (concept assumed stationary).
deep.metrics_reported: Final 0/1 error rate of the trained model, compared with vs. without drift detection, broken out per synthetic dataset × per base learner (Perceptron, neural network, decision tree) — Table 1. For ELEC2: test-set error rate compared against a "lower bound" (an infeasible oracle that exhaustively searches training-window cuts against the true test labels) and two "upper bound" ad hoc heuristics (train on all data; train on last year only) — Table 2. Also qualitative online error-rate traces (error vs. number of examples processed) with warning/drift markers — Figures 1–3.
deep.key_results: On the synthetic streams, DDM-triggered retraining reduced final error for nearly every algorithm/dataset pair, with the largest gains for the higher-capacity learners — e.g. STAGGER: neural net 0.351→0.002, decision tree 0.265→0.016; SINE1: NN 0.489→0.019, DT 0.490→0.081. The one gradual-drift dataset, CIRCLES, showed markedly smaller and less consistent gains: Perceptron slightly worsened (0.410→0.413), NN improved only 0.233→0.225, and even the best case (DT: 0.205→0.109) was proportionally smaller than the abrupt-drift datasets' improvements. On ELEC2, the DDM-wrapped decision tree matched the (label-peeking) lower-bound error on the 1-day-ahead task (0.104 vs. 0.104) and came close on the 1-week task (0.199 vs. lower bound 0.190), beating both ad hoc heuristics (train-on-all-data: 0.187/0.235; train-on-last-year: 0.125/0.247). On the assumed-stationary ADULT dataset, DDM never fired a drift signal, offered as evidence against false alarms on stable data.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper has no separate "Limitations" section — everything is folded into a short Conclusions paragraph. Verbatim future-work statements: "We intend to proceed with this research line with other learning algorithms and real world problems. We already started working to include the drift detection method in an incremental decision tree. Preliminary results are very promising. The algorithm could be applied with any loss-function given appropriate values for α. Preliminary results in regression domain using mean-squared error loss function confirm the results presented here." Important caveat for your use: the paper never explicitly names a weakness on slow/gradual drift, nor discusses adversarial manipulation, poisoning, or robustness of its own p_min/s_min running statistics — that gap is not stated by the authors, only inferable empirically from the comparatively weak/inconsistent CIRCLES (gradual-drift) numbers in Table 1 versus the strong abrupt-drift results elsewhere. The paper's only "attack surface" test is a benign stability check (ADULT), not an adversarial one.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This is the right anchor paper for the "drift-adaptive" half of your ESP32-class IDS. (1) Mechanism fit: DDM needs only two running scalars (p_min, s_min) plus the current p_i/s_i, giving true O(1) memory and O(1) per-packet compute with no matrix ops — the cheapest possible retraining trigger for MCU RAM/latency/energy budgets, and it is explicitly a model-agnostic wrapper (tested over Perceptron/NN/decision tree), so it can sit on top of whichever lightweight anomaly detector (autoencoder, one-class classifier, etc.) you choose for the IDS core without redesign. (2) Supervision gap: DDM's error signal requires a ground-truth label per example (p_i is literally the observed error rate against y_i). Your project is framed as unsupervised/on-device intrusion detection, so DDM as published cannot be dropped in unmodified — you need a proxy error signal (e.g., reconstruction-error threshold crossings, self-consistency/pseudo-label agreement, or a semi-supervised trickle of labels) to feed the same p_i/s_i machinery; making this substitution rigorous is itself a piece of novelty. (3) Boiling-frog fit: DDM's drift trigger only fires when p_i+s_i exceeds p_min+3·s_min — a threshold measured relative to a historical minimum that itself keeps sliding down as i grows (s_i shrinks with more samples). A slow, small-per-cycle distributional creep (exactly your poisoning threat model) can raise error just gradually enough to never cross 3σ, letting p_min/s_min drift along with the attack instead of flagging it — mechanically consistent with the paper's own weakest empirical results being on its one gradual-drift dataset (CIRCLES), even though the authors never frame this as a limitation themselves. (4) Novelty angle for your project: the paper predates any adversarial framing entirely (its only "attack" test is a benign no-false-alarm check on stationary ADULT data). That leaves an explicit gap — a poisoning-resilient variant of a DDM-style O(1) detector (e.g., rate-limiting how far p_min/s_min can be walked per adaptation cycle, requiring corroborating slow-timescale evidence before committing a context switch, or bounding retraining-window contamination) evaluated for real hardware cost on ESP32 — which maps directly onto your stated novelty axis ("a solution to a specific IoT constraint not adequately addressed").
