deep.problem: Concept drift detectors for streaming data all implicitly assume that any detected change in the stream comes from a legitimate, non-malicious source. The paper's problem statement (quoted/paraphrased from the intro and "Limitations of existing drift detectors" section): existing drift detectors "are not capable of differentiating between real and adversarial concept drift" -- they are simple thresholding modules that just measure statistical difference between two windows of data, with no ability to learn or adapt themselves, and are "very sensitive to any perturbations in data," offering "no robustness to poisoning attacks." The paper asks: what happens if a malicious party injects false data into the stream specifically crafted to simulate concept drift (a poisoning attack), in order to force the underlying classifier to adapt to fake changes, damage it, or paralyze its adaptation? The stated "Goal of the paper": "To develop concept drift detector capable of efficient change detection, while being robust to adversarial and poisoning attacks that inject fake concept drifts."
deep.method: Two main contributions form the method: (1) A taxonomy of adversarial concept drift with two attack types: (a) Instance-based poisoning attacks -- the attacker injects singular corrupted instances (label flips or feature corruption) scattered through the stream; individually low-rate and sometimes noise-like, but crafted with malicious intent and more frequent than natural anomalies; these don't cause false drift detection but impair adaptation to real drift. (b) Concept-based poisoning attacks -- the attacker crafts a coherent block/cluster of poisoned instances that itself satisfies the cluster/smoothness assumptions of a real concept, evading outlier/novelty detectors; these can both trigger false drift alarms and critically misguide or completely nullify adaptation to real drift, and are described as far more damaging than instance-based attacks. (2) A new drift detector, RRBM-DD (Robust Restricted Boltzmann Machine Drift Detector): a trainable 3-layer RBM (visible/feature layer, hidden layer, class layer) that tracks reconstruction-error trends (via linear regression over mini-batches, validated with Granger causality) as the drift signal, made robust via (i) a robust online gradient-descent procedure that downweights/truncates the influence of likely-adversarial instances during weight updates, and (ii) an augmented energy function with an embedded noise/gating model that can filter out entire poisoned sub-distributions (concept-based attacks) rather than just single instances. (3) A new evaluation metric, Relative Loss of Robustness (RLR): for a given poisoning level l, RLR_l = (M0 - Ml)/M0, i.e., the fractional performance drop of an algorithm from its clean-stream performance M0 to its performance Ml under poisoning level l; an aggregated RLR = (Σ ω_l · RLR_l)/#L averages this (with user-settable weights ω_l) across all tested poisoning intensities to give one robustness score.
deep.dataset_used: 12 benchmark data streams total. 6 artificial streams generated with the MOA framework: Hyperplane (incremental drift), LED (sudden drift), RBF-gradual, RBF-sudden, SEA (gradual drift), RandomTree (sudden drift) -- 1-3 million instances each. 6 real-world streams: ecbdl14 (Protein Structure Prediction, 9.6M instances, 631 features, 2 classes), higgs (High-energy Physics Classification, 4.95M instances, 28 features), IntelLab (Intel Lab Sensors, 2.3M instances, 6 features, 58 classes), "iot" = IoT Botnet Attacks dataset (7.06M instances, 115 features, 11 classes -- an N-BaIoT-style statistical-feature botnet-traffic dataset), kddcup = KDD Intrusion Detection (3.1M instances, 41 features, 24 classes -- the classic KDD Cup network-intrusion benchmark), susy (Supersymmetric Particle Detection, 2.3M instances, 18 features, 2 classes). All streams have real or unknown drift type per Table 1. Poisoning attacks were synthetically injected into these streams (there being no real-world benchmark for adversarial concept drift): instance-based poisoning at label-flip ratios {0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25}; concept-based poisoning by injecting {10, 30, 50, 70, 100} artificial 250-instance adversarial concepts generated via MOA. A separate experiment also varied label sparsity at {5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%} labeled instances.
deep.metrics_reported: Prequential accuracy of the base classifier (Adaptive Hoeffding Decision Tree, used identically across all compared detectors for fairness); the proposed Relative Loss of Robustness (RLR), both per-level and aggregated; average Friedman rank across benchmarks, with Bonferroni-Dunn post-hoc statistical testing at significance level alpha = 0.05.
deep.key_results: RRBM-DD was compared against 5 reference drift detectors (EDDM, ECDD, FHDDM, RDDM, WSTD). Across both the instance-based-poisoning experiment and the concept-based-poisoning experiment, RRBM-DD obtained the best (rank ~1.00) average Friedman rank on both prequential accuracy and RLR, statistically outperforming all reference detectors (e.g., in the instance-based experiment, competitor average ranks ranged roughly 3.05-5.88, versus RRBM-DD's ~1.00). RRBM-DD's own RLR values (higher = a smaller relative loss, i.e. more robust, in this write-up's convention) stayed high (roughly 0.69-0.95 across the 12 streams) under instance-based attacks and similarly strong (~0.60-0.90) under concept-based attacks, versus much larger relative performance drops for the reference detectors. This robustness held up under sparse labeling (5-30% labeled instances) as well. An ablation study (RRBM-DD vs. a plain RBM-DD, a gradient-only variant, and an energy-function-only variant) showed the plain RBM-DD ranked worst (~4.00), the robust-gradient-only variant helped most against instance-based attacks, the robust-energy-function-only variant helped most against concept-based attacks (because its embedded noise model can down-weight whole poisoned sub-distributions, not just single instances), and the full combined RRBM-DD (rank ~1.00) benefited from both components being complementary.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Directly quoted from Section 6, "Conclusions and future works," "Future works" paragraph: "RRBM-DD opens several directions for future research. We plan to modify its cost functions in order to tackle the issue of simultaneous adversarial concept drift and dynamic class imbalance, as well as develop deep architectures based on RRBM-DD." Two additional implicit limitations, stated earlier in the paper, matter for our project: (1) the authors explicitly note "there are no real-world benchmarks for adversarial concept drift," so all poisoning attacks in their evaluation are synthetically injected label-flips or synthetic MOA-generated concepts rather than attacks captured from a real adversary or a real deployed system; (2) the entire evaluation, including on their own "iot" botnet and "kddcup" intrusion-detection streams, is run as an offline/desktop-scale streaming benchmark using a full RBM classifier -- there is no discussion anywhere in the paper of memory footprint, inference latency, energy consumption, or any embedded/resource-constrained deployment; RRBM-DD's hardware cost and applicability to constrained IoT/edge devices is never addressed or mentioned as a consideration.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is exactly what the survey note flagged it as: the vocabulary and evaluation backbone for our core novelty claim, currently unapplied to IoT/embedded settings. Concretely: (1) Vocabulary/taxonomy reuse -- their instance-based vs. concept-based adversarial-drift taxonomy is a ready-made, citable framework for formalizing our "boiling-frog" poisoning threat model: a slow, low-rate label/feature-level poisoning campaign against our on-device detector's evolving "benign traffic" baseline is best described in their terms as a slow-drip instance-based attack that can gradually shade into a concept-based attack once enough poisoned points form a coherent adversarial cluster the detector's adaptation mechanism accepts as "the new normal." We can cite their finding that concept-based attacks are categorically more dangerous (can both trigger false drift AND corrupt adaptation) to justify why "boiling frog" poisoning of an unsupervised IDS's drift-adaptation loop is a serious, non-trivial threat, not just noise. (2) Metric reuse -- Relative Loss of Robustness (RLR) is directly reusable as one of our core evaluation axes: run our on-device detector's adaptation on a clean drifting-benign stream vs. the same stream with graded "boiling-frog" poisoning injected, and report RLR (or an IDS-appropriate variant using detection F1/AUC/TPR-at-fixed-FPR instead of prequential accuracy) as our robustness metric, aggregated across poisoning intensities exactly as they do. (3) Precise gap to fill -- the authors' own stated future work ("develop deep architectures based on RRBM-DD") and their explicit absence of any hardware-cost or embedded-deployment discussion is precisely the gap our project's grading rubric wants filled: a "new combination" / "solution to a specific IoT constraint not adequately addressed." Our contribution can be framed as taking their instance-based/concept-based taxonomy and RLR metric -- validated by them on a full, non-lightweight RBM run on desktop-scale streams that already include an IoT botnet dataset and a KDD-style intrusion dataset -- and re-deriving a lightweight, ESP32-RAM/latency/energy-budgeted unsupervised drift-adaptive detector (e.g., a small autoencoder, streaming-sketch, or other TinyML-friendly architecture in place of their full RBM) that is evaluated with the same RLR-style poisoning-robustness metric AND real hardware cost numbers they never report. (4) Dataset overlap as a validation bridge -- their benchmark suite already contains an "IoT Botnet Attacks" stream (115 features, N-BaIoT-style) and a "KDD Intrusion Detection" stream, so we have a directly comparable, previously-poisoning-tested dataset family to build our on-device evaluation around, letting us position results against this paper's numbers rather than starting from scratch. In short: this paper supplies the formal poisoning-vs-drift vocabulary and the robustness metric; our project supplies the missing on-device/IoT-constrained instantiation and hardware-grounded evaluation that the authors never attempted and explicitly left as future work.

deep.title: Poisoning Attacks on Federated Learning-based IoT Intrusion Detection System
deep.authors: Thien Duc Nguyen, Phillip Rieger, Markus Miettinen, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi (Technical University of Darmstadt, Germany)
deep.venue_year: Workshop on Decentralized IoT Systems and Security (DISS) 2020, co-located with NDSS Symposium, 23-26 Feb 2020, San Diego, CA. DOI: 10.14722/diss.2020.23003
deep.fetch_status: success_full_text — WebFetch downloaded the PDF (383KB, 7 pages) and it was read in full via the Read tool's native PDF extraction. All sections (abstract, system/threat model, attack, evaluation, defenses, related work, conclusion, references) were verified directly from the source text; nothing below is inferred from a snippet or secondary source.
deep.problem: The paper shows that FL-based IoT network intrusion detection systems (specifically the DIoT system of Nguyen et al., ICDCS 2019) are vulnerable to backdoor/poisoning attacks. In DIoT-style FL, per-household "Security Gateways" (SGWs, e.g. home routers) passively collect device traffic, train local GRU-based anomaly-detection models per IoT device type, and send them to a central Aggregator that runs FedAvg to produce a global model redistributed to all SGWs. The paper's goal: show an adversary can implant a backdoor into this global model so that malicious traffic (e.g. Mirai malware) is misclassified as benign, i.e. the detector stops raising alarms on that attack pattern — and do so WITHOUT compromising any SGW/client, only compromising ordinary IoT end devices.
deep.method: Instead of modifying malware traffic itself to evade detection at inference time, the attack targets the DATA-COLLECTION stage: the attacker uses compromised IoT devices (not the SGW/client itself) to inject a small, controlled amount of malicious traffic into the stream that the SGW passively records as "benign" training data. Over repeated FL training rounds this poisoned data is folded into the local model and then, via FedAvg, into the global model, gradually teaching it that the malicious pattern is normal (this is exactly a "boiling-frog" gradual/stealthy poisoning of an online-adapting detector). The key control knob is Poisoned Data Rate (PDR) = |D_A|/|D_ik| (poisoned traffic injected vs. benign traffic the compromised device generates) — the attacker tunes PDR to balance backdoor effectiveness against staying under two detection layers: (1) the SGW's own traffic-level anomaly detector, and (2) any model-level anomaly detection run by the Aggregator across client model updates. Poisoned Model Rate (PMR) = m/n is the fraction of SGWs with at least one compromised device; the threat model assumes m < n/2. Attacker has full white-box knowledge of the DIoT system but no control beyond the compromised IoT devices, and does not need to compromise clients/gateways (unlike prior FL-poisoning attacks such as Bagdasaryan et al.'s constrain-and-scale, which assume full client compromise) — a strictly weaker, more practical attacker capability. The paper also evaluates two categories of existing FL-poisoning defenses against this attack: (a) a generalized clustering-based defense (k-means on pairwise L2-norm distances between client model updates into 2 groups, generalizing Auror/Krum-style approaches), and (b) a differential-privacy-style defense (update clipping + Gaussian noise, per McMahan et al.).
deep.dataset_used: Three real-world datasets from 46 commodity IoT devices plus real Mirai malware traffic, split into 24 device-type-specific datasets (each client holds ~3000 packets; a "window" = 250 samples): (1) DIoT-Benign — benign traffic from 18 IoT devices in a real smart home (from the original DIoT paper); (2) UNSW-Benign — benign traffic from 28 IoT devices in an office over 20 days (Sivanathan et al., IEEE TMC 2018); (3) DIoT-Attack — attack traffic from 5 IoT devices infected with real Mirai malware, covering 13 attack types (infection, scanning, SYN flood, HTTP flood, etc.).
deep.metrics_reported: Backdoor Accuracy (BA) — fraction of malicious samples the poisoned model falsely classifies as normal (attack success rate); Main Task Accuracy (MA) — fraction of normal/benign samples still correctly classified as normal (collateral damage to legitimate detection); Poisoned Data Rate (PDR) — |D_A|/|D_ik|, the attacker's injected-vs-benign traffic ratio; Poisoned Model Rate (PMR) — m/n, fraction of Security Gateways with compromised devices.
deep.key_results: (1) Stealth threshold at the traffic-detection layer: across 7,688 windows (250 samples each) from 5 device types (AmazonEcho, DlinkCam, DLinkType05, EdimaxPlug, NetatmoWeather), the attacker needed to inject PDR = 36.7% ± 6.5% malicious data on average before the SGW's own traffic anomaly detector flagged the window. (2) Attack accuracy (Netatmo data, 100 simulated clients): BA = 100% for essentially all PMR values except PMR ≤ 5%; e.g. with PDR = 35%, BA = 100% is achieved with only PMR = 20% (just 20% of gateways need a compromised device). MA stayed at 100% for all attacks — the attack is invisible from benign-accuracy monitoring alone. (3) Against the generalized clustering defense (100 clients, 75 benign/25 malicious, PMR = 25%): the attack's L2-norm distribution imitates benign clients well up to PDR ≤ 20% (BA reaches 100% after 3 training rounds and evades clustering); PDR = 30% is too high and gets filtered out by clustering. So the attacker's safe operating zone is 10% < PDR ≤ 20%. (4) Against the differential-privacy defense (clipping boundary = 2, Gaussian noise std swept 0.0001–0.0075): the attack still succeeds, reaching BA = 100% after 4 rounds at PDR ≥ 20% even at the highest noise level tested — but that highest noise level also drops MA to 94.2%, so the authors conclude DP is "not practical" as a defense (it damages legitimate detection without stopping the attack).
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper explicitly states both evaluated defense families (clustering-based cross-client comparison, and DP clipping+noise) are ineffective or impractical against their attack, and closes with a "Possible Mitigation Approaches" section proposing three directions they explicitly leave as future work (none implemented/evaluated in this paper): (a) new server-side FL poisoning defenses at the Aggregator — better features/clustering algorithms to flag poisoned model updates, without touching the IoT detection component; (b) filtering or tolerating poisoned data on the CLIENT side — since Security Gateways have full control of their own training data, applying existing centralized-learning defenses such as noisy-data tolerance or outlier-data mitigation locally; (c) identifying malicious traffic injection — improving detection sensitivity so even small amounts of injected malicious traffic are caught at the injection stage rather than only at the model-aggregation stage. The conclusion states plainly: "This raises the need for new defense mechanisms against our attacks on FL-based IoT intrusion detection system." Additional (unstated-but-evident) scope limits: evaluation runs on a server (20-core Xeon, 64GB RAM, 4x GPUs) with no consideration of resource-constrained/embedded hardware cost (RAM, latency, energy); the attack-accuracy sweep was run primarily on one device type (Netatmo) with simulated clients; and the threat model/evaluation treats "normal" traffic as a static target to be corrupted rather than a legitimately drifting distribution — there is no benign concept-drift baseline against which the poisoning is disentangled.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is confirmed as the closest existing precedent for the project's exact core attack intuition: gradual, stealthy, below-threshold data poisoning (their PDR knob) that backdoors an anomaly detector which is continuously retrained/adapted on live traffic — precisely the "boiling-frog" mechanism the project targets. However, the paper's setting and its own defenses are fundamentally MULTI-CLIENT/FEDERATED: the SGW-Aggregator-FedAvg architecture, and both defenses it tests (k-means clustering of model updates, and DP clipping/noise) are cross-client comparison mechanisms — they only exist because there are many peer models to compare against each other, and the paper shows they already fail or cost accuracy in that setting. The project's single-device, on-device (ESP32-class) setting removes this cross-client backstop entirely: there is no Aggregator, no fleet of peer gateway models, and no FedAvg to average out or cluster-detect a poisoned update against. This is a clean, well-supported differentiator: the project must find a different signal (e.g., using a single device's own temporal/statistical history to distinguish legitimate concept drift from adversarial "boiling-frog" drift) since the paper's mitigations are structurally inapplicable. Additionally, the paper never evaluates hardware cost (it runs entirely on a Xeon/GPU server), leaving RAM/latency/energy evaluation on real constrained hardware as untouched territory the project directly claims. Finally, the paper's own stated future-work directions — especially (b) client-side poisoned-data filtering/tolerance and (c) improving injection-time detection sensitivity — describe almost exactly the technical gap the project's single-device, drift-aware, poison-resilient detector would need to fill; the paper names this gap but does not build a solution, giving the project a citable, explicit "gap in the literature" to build against.

deep.title: Data Poisoning Attack against Neural Network-Based On-Device Learning Anomaly Detector by Physical Attacks on Sensors
deep.authors: Takahito Ino, Kota Yoshida, Hiroki Matsutani, Takeshi Fujino (Ritsumeikan University; Keio University)
deep.venue_year: Sensors (MDPI, Basel), Vol. 24, Issue 19, Article 6416, published 3 Oct 2024. DOI: 10.3390/s24196416
deep.verified_url: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11479347/ (open-access mirror; canonical: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/24/19/6416, DOI 10.3390/s24196416) — full text fetched and confirmed via WebFetch, metadata cross-checked via WebSearch against the MDPI and NCBI/PMC listings.
deep.fetch_status: Full text successfully fetched via WebFetch (PMC open-access page). Content cross-verified against a second WebSearch pass, which independently confirmed title, all four author names, both affiliations, journal, volume/issue, and article number. No paywall or extraction failure encountered — extraction below is drawn from the actual paper, not an abstract-only snippet.
deep.problem: Security of on-device learning (ODL) Edge AI anomaly detectors deployed on factory machinery. On-device learning lets an edge device retrain itself in the field to adapt to legitimate environment/concept changes, but this also opens an attack surface: an adversary with physical proximity to the sensor (not the network or the chip) can tamper with what the device believes is "normal" training data, without any digital access to the device. The paper specifically targets systems that combine (a) a multi-instance on-device anomaly detector and (b) an automatic concept-drift detector that spawns a new "normal" instance when drift is detected — asking whether an attacker can physically fool the drift-triggered self-adaptation into learning attacker-chosen data as normal.
deep.method: Threat model: attacker has physical (not network/firmware) access near the sensor during the device's training/adaptation phase and wants to make a real abnormal machine state go undetected in the future. Attack mechanism: acoustic/ultrasonic wave injection at a tuned frequency and sound-pressure level (tested 2700-3200 Hz audible and 25,300-25,800 Hz ultrasonic bands) aimed at a MEMS accelerometer (ADXL345, 100 Hz sampling, x-axis) to induce a synthetic vibration peak in the sensor's frequency spectrum that closely mimics the real abnormal signature (e.g., they reproduce a ~2.88 Hz imbalance peak by injecting ~2806.6 Hz acoustic energy at ~9.91 V). Victim system architecture: ONLAD (ON-device sequential Learning semi-supervised Anomaly Detector), an OS-ELM (Online Sequential Extreme Learning Machine) autoencoder trained incrementally without batches; a multi-instance scheme where separate small ELM "instances" each learn one normal operating pattern, with the lowest-reconstruction-error instance used at inference; and a lightweight centroid-based concept-drift detector (tracks running training/test centroids, computes a normalized-distance drift rate θ, and spawns a new instance when θ exceeds θdrift=2.0). Setup: two glued cooling fans (one deliberately imbalanced) generate real "normal" vs "abnormal" vibration; 1000 samples/condition; 800-point FFT windows (800 input/output nodes, 10 hidden nodes, sigmoid activation); implemented on Raspberry Pi Pico and Raspberry Pi 4. During attack, the acoustically-poisoned "normal" data is engineered to cross the drift threshold, causing the device to spawn and learn a new, poisoned "normal" instance on its own — a legitimate self-adaptation mechanism weaponized against itself.
deep.dataset_used: No public/named dataset — a self-collected lab dataset. Vibration data from two mechanically coupled CFZ-120F cooling fans (Ainex), one intentionally unbalanced, recorded via an ADXL345 accelerometer under three conditions (normal/balanced, real abnormal/unbalanced, and acoustically poisoned-normal), 1000 samples per condition, converted to 800-feature frequency spectra via 800-point FFT windows.
deep.metrics_reported: RMSE-based anomaly error against a fixed threshold θerror=4.25×10⁻¹⁰; drift-rate θ against threshold θdrift=2.0; binary normal/abnormal classification outcome; accelerometer peak amplitude as a function of injected acoustic frequency and sound-pressure level (with baseline noise floor ≤0.015 with no attack); attack success measured as whether real abnormal vibration is (mis)classified as normal post-poisoning.
deep.key_results: No-attack baseline: the detector correctly flags real abnormal vibration as "abnormal" (below-threshold error for normal, above-threshold for abnormal) — system works as designed. Under attack: the crafted acoustic injection pushes the drift statistic past θdrift, causing the device to autonomously create a second, poisoned "normal" instance; afterward, real abnormal vibration is fully absorbed by that poisoned instance and misclassified as "normal" — i.e., the paper reports a 100% attack success rate (complete evasion of the real abnormal condition) versus 100% correct detection with no attack, achieved via a single physical acoustic injection episode with no logical/network access to the device.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper explicitly does not propose any defense: "Since users and developers cannot always control the training data in on-device learning Edge AIs, developing effective countermeasures against such attacks is required" — flagged as necessary but out of scope, i.e., no countermeasure is designed or evaluated. Scope limitations they name directly: they demonstrate the attack "with one of the typical cases of abnormal data" and evaluate only "one normal state" scenario (though they argue the attack should generalize across the number of normal states); they state as explicit future work: "we plan to demonstrate this attack on other abnormal detection setups... to show this threat applies in various cases," and they note the physical/acoustic-injection threat "is not limited to accelerometers... expected to apply to all systems that use sensors" but do not test other sensor modalities themselves. The attack as demonstrated is a single, deliberately-tuned injection engineered to cross the drift threshold in one shot — the paper does not consider or test a slow, incremental/sub-threshold poisoning process across many adaptation cycles.
deep.relation_to_our_project:
This is indeed the closest existing precedent to the team's project, and it maps almost point-for-point onto the "Poison-Resilient On-Device Intrusion Detection for Drifting IoT" concept — while leaving exactly the gaps the team's proposal targets:

1. Same vulnerable primitive, different domain. The paper attacks a lightweight, edge-deployable "centroid-distance vs. threshold" concept-drift detector that auto-spawns a new learned "normal" instance once drift crosses θdrift — structurally identical in spirit to any drift-adaptive on-device IDS that must decide when observed traffic has legitimately shifted vs. when it's being attacked. The team's ESP32-class IDS will face the same core design tension (adapt to benign drift vs. resist adversarial drift) but in the network-traffic-feature domain instead of accelerometer/vibration data, and on genuinely more resource-constrained hardware (Pi Pico/Pi4 in this paper vs. ESP32, which has tighter RAM/energy/latency budgets — directly relevant to the instructor's edge-intelligence and resource-constrained-systems research interests).

2. Broadens the threat model beyond digital poisoning. Most on-device-learning poisoning work assumes an attacker who edits feature vectors or labels directly; this paper is rare in demonstrating a real, physical-channel attack (acoustic injection on a real MEMS sensor, real hardware) that requires no logical access. This validates that "physical/analog channel poisoning of an on-device learner's own adaptation loop" is a credible, hardware-realistic threat class worth building on, and gives the team a concrete precedent to cite for why physical- or sensor-adjacent poisoning of IoT devices is not just a theoretical concern.

3. The explicit, named gap is the team's core novelty. The authors state outright that they did not propose or evaluate any defense ("developing effective countermeasures... is required" — future work), and they only tested a single-shot, deliberately threshold-crossing injection rather than a slow, sub-threshold "boiling-frog" style attack spread across many adaptation cycles. This is precisely the two-part gap the team's project fills: (a) a genuinely different/harder threat model — a gradual poisoning strategy that nudges the drift statistic just under θdrift on each adaptation cycle so no single step triggers rejection, cumulatively corrupting the "normal" model over time (something this paper's one-shot injection does not test or defend against), and (b) an actual resilience/defense mechanism plus a real-hardware (ESP32-class) cost evaluation (RAM, latency, energy), which this paper never attempts. Framed this way, the team's contribution is a direct, well-motivated extension of a peer-reviewed Q1-adjacent (MDPI Sensors) paper's own stated future-work call — strong material for the "novelty = gap-filling extension" framing the grading rubric rewards.

4. Reusable technical reference points. The paper's centroid-based drift-rate formula, multi-instance/lowest-error-instance inference scheme, and OS-ELM-based lightweight online learner are good candidate baseline mechanisms (or points of comparison/contrast) for the team's own drift-adaptation design and for constructing the "boiling frog" attack formally (e.g., bounding each step's centroid shift below θdrift while accumulating drift over N cycles).
