deep.problem: Traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) are trained offline and statically, so they cannot keep pace with IoT environments where normal system behavior and attacker strategies evolve over time (concept drift), and they require continuous manual labeling of streaming traffic to stay current, which is labor-intensive and impractical at scale. The paper's stated goal is a dynamic, "labor-free" IDS that both detects intrusions (including zero-day/unseen attack types) and keeps adapting itself online without human-provided labels.
deep.method: Two coupled pieces: (1) an Anomaly Detection Module (ADM) — an autoencoder trained with a novel "Cluster Repelling Contrastive" (CRC) loss (applied to both encoder and decoder outputs, temperature τ=0.02, cosine similarity) that pulls normal samples' representations together and repels abnormal ones; classification is done by fitting the resulting cosine-similarity scores to two Gaussian distributions (normal/abnormal) via MLE and assigning each new sample to whichever Gaussian gives higher likelihood — so no manual anomaly threshold is chosen. (2) An online/self-updating framework: incoming unlabeled traffic is pseudo-labeled by the current ADM (an anomaly label triggers an immediate alarm); after every m new samples (2000 for NSL-KDD, 2784 for UNSW-NB15) the model is fine-tuned on the expanded pseudo-labeled dataset. Two specific safeguards are used to limit pseudo-label error accumulation: the Gaussian parameters used to decide "normal" are re-estimated only from the original trusted initial data X0 (not from pseudo-labeled data), and a fixed-rate random label-flip (λ=20% for NSL-KDD, 5% for UNSW-NB15) is injected during fine-tuning "to diversify wrong judgments from a singular direction" and reduce overfitting to incorrect pseudo-labels; an encoder/decoder voting step also picks the higher-confidence of the two sub-model predictions.
deep.dataset_used: NSL-KDD (125,973 train / 22,544 test rows; 24 attack types in train vs 38 in test, i.e. includes zero-day attacks; 4 attack categories DoS/U2R/R2L/Probing; preprocessed to 121 dims) and UNSW-NB15 (175,341 train / 82,332 test rows; 9 attack types; all 42 attributes retained, preprocessed to 196 dims). Both are general network-intrusion benchmark datasets, not IoT-device-specific traffic captures.
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score (overall and per-attack-category, especially for zero-day/unseen attack detection), and an online-vs-offline training accuracy comparison. No latency, memory, energy, or throughput metrics are reported anywhere in the paper.
deep.key_results: On NSL-KDD: AOC-IDS reaches 88.90% accuracy / 85.99% precision / 96.21% recall / 90.81% F1, beating baselines FeCo (81.10% acc / 81.72% F1) and CIDS (82.29% acc / 80.65% F1). On UNSW-NB15: 89.19% accuracy / 90.65% precision / 89.70% recall / 90.14% F1. On zero-day/unseen-attack categories, AOC-IDS detects >91% across categories, far above supervised baselines like RF/XGBoost (<50% on some unseen categories). Comparing the paper's own online setting to a fully-offline (fully labeled) version of the same model: NSL-KDD online 88.90% vs offline 91.02% (−2.12 pts), UNSW-NB15 online 89.19% vs offline 89.67% (−0.48 pts) — i.e. the self-labeling online loop costs only a small accuracy gap versus full supervision.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper has no dedicated "Limitations" or "Future Work" section. The closest the authors come to naming a gap is describing their decision rule as being "more resistant to false label information" because it relies on distribution shape (Gaussian fit to trusted initial data) rather than raw class labels — but this claim is asserted, not evaluated against any adversary. Nothing in the paper models or tests: (a) adversarially crafted/attacker-controlled pseudo-labels or a deliberate slow (non-i.i.d., temporally correlated) drift in the input stream designed to poison the periodic fine-tuning step — only i.i.d. random label-flipping noise is considered, and only as a regularizer chosen by the defenders, not as an attack; (b) any computational-cost, latency, memory footprint, energy, or embedded/edge-hardware deployment feasibility, despite motivating the work with IoT streaming data.
deep.relation_to_our_project: AOC-IDS is an excellent, concrete "victim mechanism" for the project for two independent reasons that line up with the two headline contributions of "Poison-Resilient On-Device Intrusion Detection for Drifting IoT": (1) Poisoning angle — its online framework is a fully specified, open-source (GitHub), unsupervised, self-labeling adaptation loop: pseudo-label → periodic autoencoder fine-tune every m samples, with two named but adversarially-untested safeguards (Gaussian-from-trusted-data-only, fixed-rate random label flip, encoder/decoder voting). Because these safeguards only counter i.i.d. random pseudo-label noise, a "boiling-frog" attacker who nudges the traffic distribution slowly across many successive m-sample update windows (each shift small enough to look like benign drift) could gradually drag the trusted Gaussian decision boundary and the CRC-learned representation toward attacker-defined "normal," entirely within what AOC-IDS's own defenses were designed to tolerate. This is precisely the concrete, named, unprotected mechanism the project proposed to target — the paper's authors state no adversarial analysis was done, and none appears to exist in the paper's discussion or results, confirming this as a legitimate, citable gap. (2) On-device angle — the paper never measures latency, RAM/memory, energy, or evaluates on embedded/resource-constrained hardware; it is validated purely as a simulated online learner on general network-IDS benchmarks (NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15), with models up to a [196,128,64,128,196]-dimension autoencoder retrained via SGD every 2000–2784 samples. Reporting real ESP32-class RAM/latency/energy costs for (a) inference and (b) periodic online fine-tuning of an AOC-IDS-style or a deliberately shrunk variant is a second, independent, and unaddressed gap the project can fill. Practically, the team can use AOC-IDS's CRC-loss autoencoder + dual-Gaussian decision rule + pseudo-label update loop as (i) a strong, reproducible baseline to benchmark novelty/poison-resilience against, (ii) the concrete attack surface for the "boiling frog" red-team study, and (iii) a starting architecture to compress for ESP32 deployment. One caveat for the project's IoT framing: NSL-KDD/UNSW-NB15 are general network-intrusion datasets, not literally IoT-device traffic, so the team should also plan to validate against (or additionally use) an IoT-specific dataset (e.g., CICIoT2023, TON_IoT, BoT-IoT) alongside or instead of AOC-IDS's original datasets when writing up novelty/evaluation claims.

deep.title: CND-IDS: Continual Novelty Detection for Intrusion Detection Systems
deep.authors: Sean Fuhrman (ECE, UC San Diego), Onat Gungor (CSE, UC San Diego), Tajana Rosing (CSE, UC San Diego)
deep.venue_year: 62nd Design Automation Conference (DAC 2025); arXiv:2502.14094v1 [cs.CR], submitted 19 Feb 2025
deep.fetch_status: Success — full paper text retrieved and read directly (all 7 pages incl. algorithm, equations, tables, references), not just the abstract. No details invented.
deep.problem: ML-based IDS solutions overlook two things: (1) continually changing/evolving data streams — attacks and traffic distributions shift over time and degrade static, offline-trained models; (2) lack of labeled attack data, since labeling zero-day attacks in real deployments is often infeasible, so supervised or even labeled-continual-learning approaches don't transfer to practice. Existing continual-learning IDS work (Kozik et al., Amalapuram et al., etc.) all still require labeled attack data, and existing novelty-detection (ND) methods (Isolation Forest, LOF, OC-SVM) degrade under continually shifting data ("catastrophic forgetting" in the ND model itself). CND-IDS is positioned as the first continual novelty-detection approach for IDS, requiring zero attack labels.
deep.method: Two-part pipeline, trained only on data assumed normal (no attack labels at all): (1) Continual Feature Extractor (CFE) — an MLP autoencoder trained with a novel loss L_CND = L_CS + λR·L_R + λCL·L_CL, where L_CS is a cluster-separation loss (K-Means pseudo-labels + triplet-margin loss pushing apart points near vs. far from a held-out "clean normal" subset), L_R is autoencoder reconstruction MSE, and L_CL is a latent-regularization continual-learning loss (MSE between current and past-model embeddings of the same input, preventing catastrophic forgetting without storing old data — only a saved past model state). (2) PCA-based novelty detector — PCA is fit on the CFE-encoded "clean normal" subset (10% of normal data held out); anomaly score = feature reconstruction error (FRE) after inverse PCA transform; a threshold τ (via the Best-F method) turns FRE into attack/normal predictions. Data is split into "experiences" (the dataset used m=2), each introducing some new attack types, simulating an evolving attack landscape; the model is retrained/updated at each experience and evaluated on all experiences' test sets (past = backward transfer/forgetting, future = forward transfer/zero-day detection).
deep.dataset_used: Four "realistic" IDS datasets: X-IIoTID (820,502 samples, 18 attack types, IIoT), WUSTL-IIoT-2021 (1,194,464 samples, 4 attack types, IIoT), CICIDS2017 (2,830,743 samples, 15 attack types, general network), UNSW-NB15 (257,673 samples, 10 attack types, general network).
deep.metrics_reported: F1 score; continual-learning metrics derived from the F1 result matrix — AVG (average F1 on current/seen-attack experience), FwdTrans (forward transfer, i.e. performance on future/zero-day experiences), BwdTrans (backward transfer, i.e. forgetting, negative = catastrophic forgetting); PR-AUC (threshold-free evaluation, chosen over ROC-AUC due to class imbalance); average per-sample inference time (ms).
deep.key_results: CND-IDS beats two unsupervised continual-learning (UCL) baselines (ADCN, LwF-style autoencoder+K-Means) on every dataset: up to 4.50x AVG improvement over ADCN and 6.1x over LwF; up to 6.47x FwdTrans improvement over ADCN and 3.47x over LwF (averaged across datasets: 1.88x/1.78x AVG and 2.63x/1.60x FwdTrans improvement over ADCN/LwF respectively). Average BwdTrans: CND-IDS +0.87% (positive on 3/4 datasets, meaning past performance sometimes improves) vs. ADCN -0.06% (net forgetting) vs. LwF +0.09%. Against SOTA novelty detectors (LOF, OC-SVM, PCA, Deep Isolation Forest), CND-IDS wins on every dataset: 1.16x average-F1 improvement over DIF and 1.08x over plain PCA; also best on threshold-free PR-AUC. Ablations confirm both L_CS and L_R are needed (removing either hurts all metrics); removing L_R+L_CL raises AVG but causes strongly negative BwdTrans (-11.26%), i.e., forgetting. Inference overhead: 0.0019 ms/sample on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU + AMD EPYC 7343 16-core CPU — fastest among CL methods (ADCN 0.406ms, LwF 0.068ms), essentially tied with plain PCA (0.0018ms), and called "negligible" relative to the ~27.77ms average median flow duration across datasets. This timing was measured only on server-class hardware, not embedded hardware.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper has no explicit "Limitations" or "Future Work" section — the Conclusion just restates the contributions. The only self-flagged caveat is a one-line note that "Our code will be released upon acceptance," indicating the implementation was not public at submission. Beyond that, the gaps relevant to our project are gaps of omission rather than authors' stated admissions: (1) Zero adversarial or data-poisoning analysis anywhere in the paper — the entire continual-adaptation loop (per-experience PCA refit on a "clean normal" subset, CFE updates via L_CND) implicitly trusts that the unlabeled "normal" stream it is fit to is genuinely benign; nothing in the method, ablations, or evaluation considers an adversary contaminating that stream. (2) All experiments and the inference-time/overhead claim run on a desktop-class NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU + 16-core server CPU — there is no embedded/edge deployment, no RAM/memory-footprint analysis, no energy measurement, and no model-size/quantization discussion for constrained devices like an ESP32. (3) The number of experiences (m=2) was chosen "after careful experimentation" without an explicit sensitivity/drift-rate study. (4) Their notion of "continual adaptation" is about newly appearing ATTACK classes across experiences, not about drift in the definition of "normal" traffic itself — the normal-data distribution used for Nc/PCA fitting is treated as consistently trustworthy and stationary in composition, never as something that itself needs to adapt while resisting manipulation.
deep.relation_to_our_project:
CND-IDS is an excellent, precisely-specified related-work anchor and non-adversarial baseline for our project, exactly as characterized in the survey note. Fit and gaps:

1. Methodological overlap (why it's a strong baseline): CND-IDS is unsupervised (zero attack labels, only assumes access to normal data), continually adapting (per-experience CFE + PCA refit), and novelty-detection-based (reconstruction-error anomaly scoring with thresholding) — structurally the same paradigm our project needs for the "unsupervised, drift-adaptive" half of our problem. Its loss decomposition (L_CS cluster-separation + L_R reconstruction + L_CL continual-learning regularizer) and its per-experience data-preparation protocol (holding out a "clean normal" subset Nc, refitting PCA on CFE-encoded Nc at every experience) are concrete, reusable design starting points we can cite, adapt, or directly benchmark against, since CND-IDS reports numbers on exactly the datasets (CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15, and, notably, the IIoT-specific X-IIoTID and WUSTL-IIoT) that would let us do like-for-like comparison.

2. The core poisoning gap we target: CND-IDS's adaptation mechanism (refit PCA on Nc, update CFE via L_CND) trusts every experience's "normal"-labeled data as ground truth with no contamination check. A slow ("boiling-frog") poisoning attacker who gradually shifts what looks like normal traffic across experiences would directly exploit this: the CFE's embedding space and PCA's fitted manifold would drift to absorb the attacker's traffic as benign, and nothing in CND-IDS's loss terms (L_CS separates clusters within the *current* trusted data; L_CL only fights catastrophic forgetting, not contamination) would detect or resist this. This is precisely the vulnerability our project's threat model addresses, and it lets us frame our contribution cleanly: use CND-IDS's own per-experience refit procedure as the unprotected baseline to demonstrate the poisoning attack works, then propose a poisoning-resilient variant of the adaptation rule (e.g., trust-scoring or robust statistics before admitting samples into the "normal" set/PCA fit, bounding the rate of manifold drift per experience, or a discriminator distinguishing gradual poisoning from genuine benign drift).

3. The second gap — genuinely benign drift vs. new-attack drift: CND-IDS's continual learning setting is about newly appearing attack CLASSES across experiences, not about drift in the normal-traffic distribution itself; the normal class is implicitly treated as compositionally stable across experiences. Our project's "adapts to benign concept drift in normal traffic" framing is a different (and underexplored) axis CND-IDS doesn't test — a legitimate, citable novelty gap.

4. The on-device gap: CND-IDS's "negligible overhead" claim (0.0019ms/sample) is measured on an RTX 3090 GPU + 16-core EPYC server CPU, not on any resource-constrained device. It reports no RAM footprint, no model size/quantization, no energy numbers. Its architecture (4-layer, 256-hidden-neuron MLP autoencoder + arbitrary-dimension PCA) is very unlikely to be ESP32-deployable as specified. This directly matches the second pillar of our project (real hardware cost — RAM, latency, energy on ESP32-class hardware), letting us position our contribution as validating (or refuting) whether a CND-IDS-style continual novelty-detection pipeline can actually run on-device once compressed/adapted, with real measured numbers where CND-IDS has none.

Overall: CND-IDS gives us a credible, DAC-2025-caliber SOTA unsupervised continual-novelty-IDS baseline to cite and benchmark against on shared datasets, while cleanly vacating exactly the two axes (poisoning-resilience of the adaptation loop, and on-device ESP32-class resource validation) our project's novelty claim rests on — supporting the "solution to a specific IoT constraint not adequately addressed" bar for an A/A*-level contribution without requiring us to invent a wholly new technique from scratch.

deep.title: PACOL: Poisoning Attacks Against Continual Learners
deep.authors: Huayu Li (University of Arizona, Tucson) and Gregory Ditzler (EpiSys Science, Philadelphia; affiliated with University of Arizona and Rowan University when the work was performed).
deep.venue_year: arXiv:2311.10919 [cs.LG], submitted 18 Nov 2023. Also listed on SSRN. No evidence found (checked via WebSearch) of publication in a peer-reviewed conference/journal — treat as an arXiv preprint, not a confirmed A/A* venue paper.
deep.fetch_status: Full success. WebFetch retrieved the abstract page directly. The PDF (arxiv.org/pdf/2311.10919) could not be parsed by WebFetch's text pipeline (raw binary), but it was auto-saved locally, and I read it in full via the Read tool (rendered as page images, pages 1-20 of 20): Abstract, Introduction, Related Work (2.1 Continual Learning, 2.2 Adversarial ML), Method (Sec 3: regularization/replay preliminaries, label-flipping attack, PACOL derivation, PGD optimization, white/gray/black-box threat models), Experiments (Sec 4: datasets, attacks on regularization-based methods with Table 1 and Figure 1, attacks on DGR with Table 2 and Figure 2, defenses with Tables 3-4 and Figure 3), Conclusion (Sec 5, including explicit limitations/future-work/ethics paragraphs), Acknowledgements, and the start of the References list. No details below were invented; anything not directly read is flagged as such.
deep.problem: Continual learning (CL) systems trained sequentially on streaming tasks are known to suffer catastrophic forgetting, but the paper's problem is adversarial: can an attacker who injects a small fraction of poisoned samples into future, "non-targeted" tasks deliberately force a CL model to forget a specific, already-learned "targeted" task, while leaving performance on other tasks roughly unaffected? Prior CL-poisoning work ("false memory formation") relied on mislabeled backdoor-trigger samples. PACOL's problem is to do this (a) without changing any labels (clean-label attack) and (b) without needing access to the original historical data of the targeted task, i.e., a stealthier, harder-to-detect route to targeted catastrophic forgetting in continual learners.
deep.method: Two attacks are compared. (1) Label-flipping (baseline): inject samples drawn from the targeted task into later non-targeted tasks and flip their labels to a wrong class — optimization-free but easy to detect. (2) PACOL (main contribution): a clean-label, l-infinity-norm epsilon-bounded adversarial perturbation attack. Starting from a single gradient-descent step under label-flipping, the authors show the poisoning effect is driven by a "malicious gradient" term; PACOL crafts perturbed inputs X_adv (with their true, unchanged labels) whose gradient matches that malicious gradient, formalized as minimizing a distance between two gradients — either l2 (Euclidean, used for the MNIST variants) or negative cosine similarity (used for SVHN/CIFAR). Perturbations are optimized via Projected Gradient Descent, looped K times across different training/parameter states (so the poison stays effective throughout training) and clipped to a valid pixel range; the model is updated with Adam. Three adversary-knowledge levels are defined: white-box (full model/parameter access, but explicitly NOT the regularization importance matrix or the replay generator, "to keep the approach generalizable"), gray-box (same architecture, no parameters — attack crafted via a surrogate model of identical architecture), and black-box (different, unknown architecture — surrogate model of a different type, e.g., different MLP size, or VGGNet surrogate vs. ResNet20 target). PACOL is evaluated against three regularization-based CL algorithms (EWC, Online EWC, Synaptic Intelligence) and one generative-replay method (Deep Generative Replay using a WGAN-GP), and against four generic outlier/anomaly-detection defenses (l2-norm outlier removal, One-Class SVM, Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor) applied on raw pixels, deep-feature embeddings, and t-SNE embeddings.
deep.dataset_used: Four image-classification continual-learning benchmarks, all built from standard vision datasets, each split into 5 sequential tasks: Rotation-MNIST (R-MNIST, domain-incremental, each task a different rotation of the 10-digit classification), Split-MNIST (S-MNIST, task-incremental, 5 binary digit-pair tasks), Split-SVHN (S-SVHN, 5 binary tasks on Street View House Numbers — more challenging natural images), and Split-CIFAR-10 (S-CIFAR, 5 binary tasks over 10 object classes). Task 1 is always designated the "targeted task"; poison (1%, 3%, or 5% of training data) is injected into tasks 4 and 5 ("non-targeted tasks"). Backbones: MLP (400 units, 2 hidden layers) for R-MNIST; vanilla CNN for other MNIST variants; ResNet20 for S-SVHN/S-CIFAR with VGGNet as the black-box surrogate. No network-traffic, time-series, or IoT/tabular datasets are used anywhere in the paper — it is entirely an image-classification study.
deep.metrics_reported: Primary metric: classification accuracy / test error (%) on the targeted task's held-out validation set after the model has trained through the full 5-task poisoned stream, reported as mean ± 95% confidence interval over 10 runs, at poison ratios of 0% (clean), 1%, 3%, 5%, separately for white-box/gray-box/black-box PACOL and for label-flipping (Tables 1-2, Figures 1-2). Secondary metric: defense "success rate" (%) — the fraction of poisoned samples correctly filtered out by each of the four anomaly-detection defenses, at filtering "budgets" of 1-5% of the dataset, across three embedding spaces (raw data, deep features, t-SNE) (Tables 3-4). A qualitative check (Figure 3) visually compares poisoned vs. benign images to argue PACOL's perturbations are imperceptible to human inspection.
deep.key_results: (1) Both attacks degrade targeted-task accuracy as poison ratio rises from 1% to 5%, across all four CL algorithms (EWC, Online EWC, SI, DGR) and all four datasets — demonstrating the vulnerability is general, not specific to one algorithm type. (2) White-box PACOL causes the largest accuracy drop among the three PACOL knowledge levels, but gray-box and black-box PACOL (using surrogate models) remain effective, showing the attack transfers without full model access. (3) Label-flipping typically causes even larger raw performance degradation than PACOL, but at the direct cost of being far easier to detect. (4) Counter-intuitively, the generative-replay method (DGR) was found to be MORE vulnerable to poisoning than the regularization-based methods — the authors state "only 1% label-flipped data can significantly degrade the accuracy on the targeted task" under DGR, despite replay buffers intuitively being expected to counteract the "false memory" poison. (5) On stealthiness/detectability: label-flipped samples are readily caught by standard defenses (e.g., l2-norm outlier defense removes nearly all label-flipped samples on the R-MNIST 0-1 subset, and roughly half on the harder S-CIFAR subset, at a 5% budget), whereas most defenses largely fail against PACOL's imperceptible perturbations (success rates frequently near 0% for Isolation Forest/Local Outlier Factor against PACOL). One-Class SVM on deep-feature embeddings was the single defense that filtered a meaningful fraction (~half) of PACOL's poisoned samples on S-CIFAR, but no defense reliably caught PACOL across all settings — confirming the paper's central stealthiness claim.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Quoting the Conclusion directly: "the primary purpose of this work is to raise the community's awareness to focus on robust learning algorithms against adversarial threats in continual learning settings... the experiments in this work are limited to specific types of concept forgetting." On future work, verbatim: "Our future work includes developing data-, algorithmic- and architecture-level strategies to ensure adversarial robustness for continual machine learning models. Another area of critical investigation is a formal benchmark or adversaries in continual and lifelong learning environments." The authors also flag an ethical limitation: "the proposed approach has ethical implications because adversarial data can be used to target forgetting in a way that violates fairness in machine learning... we urge that care be taken when these models and techniques are used in practice." Additional explicit scoping choices stated in the method section (not framed as "limitations" but are effectively acknowledged constraints): the white-box adversary is deliberately NOT given access to the regularization importance matrix or the replay generator ("to keep our approach generalizable"), and the authors note white-box attacks are "challenging to implement in a real-world setting because accessing the model and its parameters can be difficult," which motivated the gray-/black-box variants. Beyond these author-stated points: the paper itself proposes no new defense (it only benchmarks existing generic outlier detectors, which it shows largely fail), and never evaluates on network/time-series/IoT data or on resource-constrained/embedded hardware (all experiments are image classification on MLP/CNN/ResNet20 backbones) — this scope gap is evident from what the paper does NOT cover, though the authors do not phrase it in exactly these words.
deep.relation_to_our_project: PACOL strengthens and broadens the project's threat model exactly as the survey note anticipated. Currently the working title frames poisoning as a single "boiling-frog" boundary-shift attack on drift adaptation. PACOL supplies a second, formally distinct attack goal that maps directly onto the on-device IDS: instead of (or in addition to) slowly shifting what counts as "normal," an attacker can target the device's continual/drift-adaptation mechanism to induce catastrophic forgetting of a specific previously-learned attack signature — i.e., make the ESP32-class detector selectively "unlearn" how to catch one known intrusion class while its behavior on other traffic looks unchanged, which is arguably a more dangerous and more covert goal for a network IDS than gradual boundary drift alone. Two aspects transfer especially cleanly: (1) PACOL's clean-label constraint (the attacker perturbs feature values within an l-infinity bound but cannot alter labels) is a much closer match to realistic on-device/unsupervised IoT settings than label-flipping, since an attacker sending network packets has no way to rewrite the ground-truth labels an unsupervised/self-labeling on-device learner assigns during its own adaptation — this gives a citable, formalized justification for treating "clean-label, gradient-aligned" poisoning as the realistic threat class for the project's own attacker model. (2) PACOL's gradient-matching/PGD attack construction is computationally nontrivial (multi-loop PGD across parameter snapshots, needing a surrogate model for gray/black-box), which supports an asymmetry argument useful for the project's contribution framing: attack generation is expensive and must happen off-device (on attacker compute), while the project's defense must run within an ESP32's tight RAM/latency/energy budget — a specific IoT constraint PACOL never addresses since it evaluates only image-classification benchmarks (MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR) on MLP/ResNet20/WGAN-GP backbones, with zero network-traffic data and zero hardware-cost evaluation. That gap — no clean-label, catastrophic-forgetting-style poisoning attack (or defense) has been studied on network/IoT data, under resource constraints, on-device — is precisely the novelty slot the project can occupy: a poison-resilient, resource-aware, on-device drift-adaptation mechanism for IoT intrusion detection, evaluated against both PACOL-style clean-label forgetting attacks and boiling-frog boundary drift, with real ESP32-class RAM/latency/energy numbers. This also lines up with the instructor's stated research areas (edge intelligence for resource-constrained systems; IoT network security/attack detection), and PACOL's own stated future work ("developing data-, algorithmic- and architecture-level strategies... robustness for continual machine learning models," "a formal benchmark... for adversaries in continual and lifelong learning") is effectively an open invitation for exactly this kind of applied, hardware-grounded follow-on contribution. One caveat worth noting to the team: PACOL is an arXiv preprint with no confirmed peer-reviewed venue found, so it should be cited as a preprint, not as an established A/A*-venue result, when building the literature narrative.

deep.title: Machine Learning with Adversaries: Byzantine Tolerant Gradient Descent
deep.authors: Peva Blanchard, El Mahdi El Mhamdi, Rachid Guerraoui, Julien Stainer (all EPFL, Switzerland; El Mahdi El Mhamdi marked as contact author). Acknowledgments credit Georgios Damaskinos and Rhicheek Patra (EPFL Distributed Computing group) for the framework used to test Krum.
deep.venue_year: NeurIPS (NIPS) 2017 — 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Long Beach, CA, USA. A brief-announcement preliminary version appeared at ACM PODC (Principles of Distributed Computing) 2017. Funded in part by ERC grant 339539 (AOC) and Swiss NSF grant 200021_169588 (TARBDA).
deep.fetch_status: SUCCESS — full text obtained. The candidate URL resolved directly; no relocation via WebSearch was needed. The NIPS landing page was fetched first (abstract + metadata), then the linked full PDF (9 pages, main body — the paper defers some proofs and a ConvNet/Medoid experiment to a separate supplemental .zip that was not opened) was downloaded and read directly page-by-page as images (not just an auto-summary), so all details below are read from the primary source text, figures and equations rather than inferred.
deep.problem: Distributed SGD is normally implemented as one parameter server broadcasting a parameter vector x_t to n worker processes each round; each worker returns a gradient estimate, and the server aggregates them (classically by averaging) to update x_t. The paper asks: how can this aggregation be made resilient when up to f of the n workers are Byzantine, i.e., can send arbitrary vectors for any reason (bugs, network asynchrony, biased local data, or an actual attacker), without restricting the dimension d of the parameter space or the cost function's convexity? They first prove (Lemma 1) that ANY aggregation rule that is a linear combination of the workers' vectors (e.g. plain averaging, or even a "closest to the barycenter" squared-distance rule) can be forced by a single Byzantine worker to output an arbitrary vector, preventing convergence — so linear/near-linear aggregation is fundamentally not Byzantine-tolerant, even against one adversarial worker.
deep.method: They formalize an (α,f)-Byzantine-resilience property (Definition 1): an aggregation rule F is resilient if, even with f of its n inputs adversarial, (i) the expected output vector stays within an angle-bounded cone around the true gradient g, and (ii) F's higher statistical moments stay bounded relative to the correct gradient estimator's moments. They then propose Krum, a nonlinear SELECTION (not averaging) rule: for each proposed vector V_i, compute a score s(i) = sum of squared Euclidean distances from V_i to its (n-f-2) closest neighbors among all n proposed vectors; Krum outputs the single V_i with the smallest score (ties broken by smallest worker id). Intuition: it blends "majority-based" robustness (looking at the densest local neighborhood) with "closest-to-barycenter" ideas, while staying cheap — expected time complexity O(n²·d) (Lemma 2), linear in dimension d, versus the exponential cost of naive majority-subset search. Proposition 1 proves Krum is (α,f)-Byzantine resilient whenever 2f+2 < n (i.e., f < (n-2)/2, tolerating up to just under n/2 Byzantine workers, the theoretically optimal breakdown point known for the geometric median) and the correct gradient estimator's standard deviation is small enough relative to ||g|| (a condition improvable by using larger mini-batches, since averaging over a mini-batch divides σ by sqrt(batch size)). Proposition 2 then proves that SGD driven by Krum's output converges almost surely to a "flat" region of a (possibly non-convex) cost function under standard SGD step-size/moment conditions plus this resilience property. They also introduce Multi-Krum: instead of keeping only the single best-scoring vector, keep the m best-scoring vectors and average them; m=1 recovers Krum, m=n recovers plain averaging, letting a practitioner trade off resilience against convergence speed.
deep.dataset_used: Spambase (UCI binary spam-classification dataset) with a two-hidden-layer MLP, and MNIST (image classification) with the same MLP architecture (a ConvNet variant for MNIST is reported only in the supplemental material, not fetched here). n = 20 simulated worker processes in all experiments; each correct worker estimates its gradient on a mini-batch (batch size varied, e.g. size 3 in the main convergence plots).
deep.metrics_reported: Cross-validation error plotted against SGD round number (up to 500 rounds), and cross-validation error measured at round 500 as a function of mini-batch size. No wall-clock/compute-cost numbers, no accuracy-vs-communication tradeoffs, and no hardware resource metrics (RAM, latency, energy) are reported.
deep.key_results: (1) With 0% Byzantine workers, plain averaging converges faster than Krum — Krum has a real "cost of resilience" when there is no attack. (2) With 33% Gaussian-noise Byzantine workers (vectors drawn N(0, isotropic cov, std=200)), averaging fails to converge at all, while Krum converges essentially as if 0% of workers were Byzantine. (3) Under a stronger "omniscient" attack (a Byzantine worker computes the true gradient over the whole dataset, then sends the exact opposite vector scaled to large magnitude), increasing the mini-batch size sharply shrinks Krum's accuracy gap versus clean averaging: with mini-batch ≈10 (MNIST) or ≈30 (Spambase), Krum under 45% omniscient Byzantine workers matches averaging under 0% Byzantine workers. (4) Multi-Krum (with m = n−f) under 33% Gaussian Byzantine workers converges just as fast as plain averaging with 0% Byzantine workers — i.e. it recovers both resilience and speed simultaneously, outperforming both Krum and a "Medoid" baseline (median-inspired, reported in supplemental material). (5) Theoretically, Krum's tolerable Byzantine fraction (n-2)/(2n) approaches the optimal breakdown point of 1/2 as n grows, matching the geometric median's known-optimal (but not exactly/efficiently computable) breakdown point.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper has no dedicated "Limitations" section, but Section 7 ("Concluding Remarks") states several explicit boundaries/open problems in its own words: (1) On the geometric median (which achieves the theoretically optimal 1/2 breakdown point): "no closed form nor an exact algorithm to compute the geometric median is known (only approximations are available) and their Byzantine resilience is an open problem" — stated as an explicit open problem. (2) The Medoid variant (minimizes sum of distances to ALL other vectors, not just the m nearest) "is outperformed by multi-Krum" per their own supplementary experiments. (3) Most importantly for scope: the authors explicitly distinguish their contribution as addressing robustness at a COARSE-GRAINED level only — "the unit of failure is a worker" behaving arbitrarily during TRAINING (adversarial gradients) — and explicitly flag as a separate, unaddressed "natural question" the FINE-GRAINED view of whether the model itself (individual neurons/synapses) is robust to internal perturbations, pointing to a different paper of theirs for that. They further state explicitly: "being robust... as a model, either to adversarial examples or to internal perturbations, does not necessarily imply robustness to adversarial gradients during training. Similarly, being distributively trained with a robust aggregation scheme such as Krum does not necessarily imply robustness to internal errors of the model or adversarial input perturbations that would occur later during INFERENCE." I.e., they explicitly state Krum protects only the training-time gradient-aggregation step, not inference-time robustness. (4) The Multi-Krum trade-off parameter m is presented as something "the practitioner" manually sets for a "specific trade-off between convergence speed and resilience" — no adaptive/automatic method to choose m or f is given. Beyond what is explicitly stated, note two gaps I infer rather than the authors stating outright (flagged here as inferred, not verified author claims): the model formalizes only a SINGLE synchronous round at a time, comparing n SIMULTANEOUS peer workers' vectors to each other — there is no treatment of an adversary that moves gradually across many rounds while staying inside each round's accepted neighborhood (a slow/"boiling-frog" style drift), nor any notion of legitimate concept drift to distinguish from attack-induced drift; and no experiments report memory, latency, or energy cost on resource-constrained hardware — all evaluation is accuracy/round-count only, on standard ML frameworks with a 20-worker federated-style setup.
deep.relation_to_our_project: Krum is the direct conceptual ancestor of the project's proposed "anomaly-gated update" rule, and the mapping is fairly literal. Krum's core mechanic is: given n simultaneous candidate vectors (one per worker, in one synchronous round), score each by the sum of squared distances to its m=n-f-2 nearest NEIGHBORS among the others, and accept only the vector(s) that sit in the densest local neighborhood — implicitly assuming that honest/correct vectors cluster together and a bounded number of Byzantine vectors are geometric outliers relative to that cluster. The project's adaptation replaces the axis of comparison: instead of comparing n vectors submitted by n different WORKERS at the SAME time step (cross-worker), it would compare a device's own recent statistics/candidate-update vectors across a rolling window of past TIME STEPS (cross-time-window) on a single ESP32-class sensor with no peers to aggregate against. Concretely, a "temporal Krum" gate would maintain a small buffer of the last n feature-summary or gradient-like update vectors from the on-device unsupervised drift-adaptation process, score each new candidate update by its distance to its m nearest neighbors within that recent-history buffer, and only admit it into the running "normal" model if it looks geometrically consistent with the recent trusted trend — otherwise treat it as a suspected poisoning step and reject/down-weight it. This directly targets the explicit gap the paper leaves open: Krum's own model treats each round independently across simultaneous peers and has no concept of legitimate drift versus attack drift, so a slow "boiling-frog" attacker who nudges the device's own adaptation gradually, always staying within one round's accepted neighborhood, is not modeled or defended against by Krum as written — that is exactly the novelty gap our project's title targets. Cost-wise, Krum's own overhead is O(n²·d) per round (n = number of workers, d = gradient dimension, potentially huge in federated deep learning, which the paper itself flags as a real concern at "hundreds of billions" of parameters); the project's reformulation shrinks both axes drastically — n becomes a small rolling window (e.g., 5-20 recent windows, not tens of simultaneous machines) and d becomes a compact per-window feature/statistic vector (not a full model gradient), which is exactly the "drastically reduced cost" the survey note anticipated and is concretely checkable in the ESP32 RAM/latency/energy evaluation the project already plans — an evaluation axis this seminal paper never performs (it reports only accuracy vs. round count on standard ML frameworks, no hardware cost numbers at all). Two more paper-level findings are directly reusable in the project's experiment design: (a) Blanchard et al. show that increasing mini-batch size sharply cuts Krum's "cost of resilience" (accuracy loss vs. plain averaging) — by analogy, the project should test whether increasing the temporal aggregation window analogously trades off poison-resilience against on-device latency/energy; (b) their (α,f)-Byzantine-resilience definition, bounding the angle between the accepted update and the true direction, is a template the project could adapt into a "resilience-to-slow-poisoning" definition bounding how far the on-device decision boundary can be dragged per unit of injected malicious traffic over a drift window. Overall, this paper supplies the exact "new combination applied to a specific IoT constraint" the course's novelty bar asks for: Krum is proven, well-cited, and explicitly leaves both the temporal/gradual-adversary case and constrained-hardware deployment unaddressed, and it is a legitimate, well-scoped ancestor to cite and adapt from rather than compete directly against.

deep.title: Byzantine-Robust Distributed Learning: Towards Optimal Statistical Rates
deep.authors: Dong Yin, Yudong Chen, Kannan Ramchandran, Peter Bartlett (UC Berkeley EECS/Statistics; Yudong Chen at Cornell School of ORIE)
deep.venue_year: ICML 2018 — Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), vol. 80, pp. 5650-5659. Also arXiv:1803.01498 (posted March 2018, revised v2 Feb 2021).
deep.fetch_status: Full success. Fetched the arXiv abstract page and downloaded/read the full PDF (16 of ~30+ pages, covering Abstract, Intro, Problem Setup, both robust-GD algorithms, all six theorems, the lower bound, the full Experiments section, and the Conclusions section) via WebFetch + direct PDF page extraction. Venue/publication venue (ICML 2018) confirmed independently via WebSearch against dblp and the PMLR proceedings page. No details below were invented; anything not visible in the read pages is flagged as such.
deep.problem: In a standard master/worker distributed-learning setup (empirical risk minimization), nm data points are drawn i.i.d. and split evenly across m worker machines (n points each); an unknown α fraction of the m workers are "Byzantine" — they can send the master arbitrary, adversarial (not just noisy) messages instead of correct gradients/updates, and may collude with full knowledge of the data and algorithm. Prior robust-distributed-learning work either gave unclear/sub-optimal statistical guarantees or required communicating full datasets (too costly). The paper asks two linked questions: (1) what is the best possible statistical estimation error any algorithm can achieve under an α-fraction Byzantine threat (a minimax lower bound), and (2) what communication-efficient (O(d) per round) algorithm actually attains it.
deep.method: Two families of algorithms, both replacing naive averaging of worker messages with a robust coordinate-wise aggregator: (1) Robust Distributed Gradient Descent (Algorithm 1) — each round the master broadcasts the current parameter, normal workers send local gradients, and the master aggregates with either Option I: coordinate-wise median, or Option II: coordinate-wise β-trimmed mean (per dimension k, drop the largest/smallest β-fraction of the m values, average the rest; β must be chosen ≥ the true Byzantine fraction α). (2) A Robust One-Round Algorithm (Algorithm 2) — each worker instead sends its own local ERM solution once, and the master takes the coordinate-wise median of these m solutions, cutting communication to a single round. The paper proves non-asymptotic statistical error bounds for all three algorithm/loss-class combinations (strongly convex, convex-non-strongly-convex, smooth non-convex population loss) under stated moment assumptions (bounded gradient variance+skewness for median; sub-exponential gradients for trimmed mean), and separately proves a matching minimax lower bound (Section 6) showing the achieved rate cannot be improved. Coordinate-wise median/trimmed mean are computed independently per dimension via a sort/selection over the m received values — i.e., no matrix operations, straightforward O(m) to O(m log m) work per coordinate (O(dm log m) total per round), which is why the project's source survey flagged them as the cheapest near-minimax-optimal robust aggregators.
deep.dataset_used: Two settings: (a) A synthetic linear-regression example (Gaussian noise, quadratic loss) used only to instantiate and verify the theoretical variance/skewness/sub-exponential assumptions (Propositions 1-2), not a benchmark dataset. (b) MNIST (60,000 training images) for the empirical experiments (Section 7), randomly partitioned into m simulated worker-machine subsamples: m=40 for the logistic-regression gradient-descent experiment, m=10 for the CNN gradient-descent experiment and for the one-round-algorithm experiment. Byzantine workers were simulated with a label-flipping attack (label y replaced by 9−y) using otherwise moderate-valued (non-extreme) gradients, chosen specifically to be hard to detect. Experiments were run in TensorFlow on Microsoft Azure — no IoT, embedded, or resource-constrained hardware was used anywhere in the paper.
deep.metrics_reported: Theoretical: ℓ2 parameter-estimation error ||ŵ − w*||2 (strongly convex case), excess population risk F(w) − F(w*) (convex case), and gradient-norm-to-a-critical-point min ||∇F(w^t)||2 (non-convex case), all as high-probability non-asymptotic bounds in terms of α, n (per-worker samples), m (number of workers), and d (dimension). Empirical: test classification accuracy (%) and test error vs. number of parallel iterations (convergence curves).
deep.key_results: Theory: trimmed-mean GD achieves error rate Õ(α/√n + 1/√(nm)), proven order-optimal for strongly convex losses (requires knowing/upper-bounding α via β≥α, and sub-exponential gradient tails). Median-based GD achieves Õ(α/√n + 1/√(nm) + 1/n) — order-optimal only when n≳m, but needs no knowledge of α and only a weaker bounded-skewness assumption. The one-round median algorithm matches the median-GD rate using just one communication round, but the formal guarantee is proved only for strongly-convex quadratic losses. A matching lower bound Ω(α/√n + 1/√(nm)) shows these rates are minimax-optimal (cannot be improved by any algorithm). Empirical (MNIST, label-flip attack): logistic regression, α=0.05, m=40 — plain mean-aggregation accuracy collapses from 88.0% (no attack) to 76.8%, while median recovers 87.2% and trimmed mean 86.9%. CNN, α=0.1, m=10 — mean drops from 94.3% to 77.3%, median recovers 87.4%, trimmed mean 90.7% (best here). One-round algorithm, logistic regression, α=0.1, m=10 — mean drops from 91.8% to 83.7%, median-based one-round recovers 89.0%, despite the loss being non-quadratic (outside the proven regime), showing practical robustness beyond the theory's formal scope.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: Directly from the paper's own text (Introduction §1.1, Related Work §2, and algorithm-specific caveats), not inferred: (1) Dimension dependence is left open — the authors state the rates may not have optimal dependence on parameter dimension d, and call developing algorithms with optimal high-dimensional scaling "an interesting and important future direction." (2) Communication efficiency beyond one round is unaddressed — they explicitly note that Byzantine-robust versions of more sophisticated communication-efficient schemes (DANE, Disco, distributed SVRG, which beat one-round accuracy at low cost in the non-Byzantine literature) do not yet exist and call this "an interesting future direction." (3) Connection to modern high-dimensional robust/list-decodable estimation (which tolerates >50% corruption) is flagged as not directly applicable to their general-loss distributed setting, again named as "an interesting future problem" to investigate an extension. (4) All three main theorems require an explicit upper-bound condition on the Byzantine fraction α (roughly α below ~1/2 minus terms in n, m, d, gradient skewness/tail) — the methods are not robust to a majority-adversarial (α≥1/2) population. (5) Trimmed mean specifically requires the practitioner to set β ≥ true α in advance (an operational limitation — the true corruption fraction must be known or over-estimated, and over-estimating β degrades statistical efficiency); median avoids this but pays an extra O(1/n) term and needs n≳m to be optimal. (6) The one-round algorithm's proof only covers quadratic losses over W=R^d; general-loss guarantees are explicitly left unproven (only empirically tested). (7) Implicit but structurally fundamental limitation (not phrased as "future work" but load-bearing for our project): the whole statistical model assumes nm data points "sampled independently... and distributed evenly" and fixed once at the start, with Byzantine machine membership fixed throughout — i.e., a static, i.i.d., one-shot batch setting. There is no treatment anywhere in the paper of a non-stationary/drifting true distribution, nor of a slow/adaptive/time-varying attacker (their label-flip attack is constant from round one). No hardware-resource evaluation (RAM, latency, energy) is attempted; experiments run on Azure servers via TensorFlow.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is the direct theoretical anchor for the robust-aggregation piece of your project, and its own scope gaps map almost exactly onto your intended contribution. Structural fit: its "master aggregates gradients/updates from m workers, α fraction of which are adversarial" setup is mathematically the same shape as your problem of "aggregate per-window drift statistics computed over sub-windows/segments of one ESP32's traffic stream, some fraction of which the attacker has slowly poisoned" — workers-in-space become windows-in-time. That reframing lets you reuse coordinate-wise median and trimmed mean directly as the robust core of your drift-adaptation update rule (e.g., robustly aggregating per-feature mean/variance deltas or lightweight model-update statistics across recent sub-windows before applying them to the on-device model), which is exactly why your survey flagged them as the most MCU-feasible candidates: the paper confirms they need only a per-coordinate sort/selection over the window (no matrix inversion or iterative optimization), giving cheap, well-characterized O(m) to O(m log m)-per-coordinate cost. Theoretical reuse: the paper's proven, minimax-optimal error rates (Õ(α/√n + 1/√(nm)) for trimmed mean, plus its matching lower bound) give you a citable, rigorous baseline to adapt into your own theoretical-guarantee section — you can frame your contribution as deriving an analogous bound for the online/windowed/single-device case, explicitly building on this static-batch result. Practical design fork it surfaces for you: median needs no knowledge of the corruption fraction α but is only rate-optimal when n≳m and pays an extra 1/n term, while trimmed mean is fully optimal but requires you to pre-set β≥α — i.e., to know or upper-bound how much of your traffic window is poisoned. Since your "boiling-frog" attacker's effective corruption level is exactly the thing your system doesn't know and that grows slowly over time, this is a concrete methodological choice your project must make (e.g., default to median for its no-knowledge property, or add an online estimator of the effective poisoned-fraction to safely set β for trimmed mean) — and citing this paper is how you justify that design decision. The precise gap that motivates your novelty claim: the paper explicitly restricts itself to a static, i.i.d., one-shot batch of data with a fixed-membership, worst-case-but-constant adversary, and its own future-work notes (dimension-dependence, Byzantine-robust communication-efficient variants, extension to majority-corruption/high-dimensional robust estimation) never touch non-stationarity or a slow/adaptive attacker at all — it has no notion of legitimate concept drift to preserve while rejecting malicious drift. Your project's core contribution — telling apart benign concept drift (which the detector should adapt to) from adversarial "boiling-frog" drift (which it should reject), using these same cheap aggregators repurposed for temporal windows, and then reporting the RAM/latency/energy cost on real ESP32-class hardware — is precisely the combination of gaps (non-stationarity + adaptive slow poisoning + on-device resource accounting) this ICML 2018 paper neither claims nor evaluates, which is exactly the kind of "solution to a specific IoT constraint not adequately addressed" novelty your grading rubric asks for, grounded in a legitimate, rigorous prior-art baseline rather than an unsupported claim.

deep.authors: Euclides Carlos Pinto Neto, Sajjad Dadkhah (corresponding), Raphael Ferreira, Alireza Zohourian, Rongxing Lu, Ali A. Ghorbani — Faculty of Computer Science, University of New Brunswick (UNB), Fredericton, Canada. Editor: Antonio Puliafito.
deep.venue_year: Sensors (MDPI, Basel), Vol. 23, Issue 13, Article 5941, published 26 June 2023. DOI: 10.3390/s23135941. PMID 37447792 / PMCID PMC10346235.
deep.verified_url: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10346235/ (open-access full text, identical to https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/23/13/5941 which returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch)

The paper's stated goal: "propose a novel and extensive IoT attack dataset to foster the development of security analytics applications in real IoT operations," where all attacks are executed by malicious IoT devices (not just against them).
deep.method: Built a real physical testbed (CIC IoT Lab) with 105 real IoT devices (67 directly participating in attacks/traffic, 38 connected via 5 Zigbee/Z-Wave hubs) across categories: smart speakers (Alexa/Google Nest/Sonos), IP cameras, smart bulbs/plugs, sensors (door/window/motion/flood), hubs (SmartThings, Philips Hue Bridge, AeoTec, Ring, Fibaro), and 7 Raspberry Pi 4 units used as the attacking IoT nodes. A Gigamon network tap gave passive full-duplex capture of all traffic via dual Wireshark monitors; pcaps were merged (mergecap) and totaled ~548 GB. 33 distinct attacks across 7 categories were executed device-to-device: DDoS (12: ACK/UDP/ICMP/PSHACK/RSTFIN/HTTP/SYN floods, fragmentation variants, SynonymousIP), DoS (5: TCP/HTTP/SYN/UDP flood variants), Reconnaissance (5: ping sweep, OS scan, vuln scan, port scan, host discovery), Web-based (6: SQLi, command injection, backdoor malware, upload attack, XSS, browser hijacking), Brute Force (1: dictionary), Spoofing (2: ARP, DNS), Mirai (3: GREIP flood, Greeth flood, UDPPlain). Traffic was split into 10 MB chunks and processed with DPKT to extract 47 flow/packet-level features (flow duration, header length, protocol/TTL, TCP flag counts, app-layer protocol flags, packet-size statistics, IAT, and higher-order stats — magnitude, radius, covariance, variance, weight). Features were aggregated over sliding windows (10 packets for smaller/low-volume attack classes, 100 packets for high-volume classes like DDoS/DoS/Mirai) using Pandas/NumPy, then combined into a final labeled CSV. Benchmarking: 5 ML/DL models (Logistic Regression, Perceptron, AdaBoost, Random Forest, DNN) trained with an 80/20 split and StandardScaler normalization, evaluated on 3 task framings — binary (benign vs malicious), 8-class (grouped by attack category), and 34-class (benign + each individual attack).
deep.dataset_used: CICIoT2023 itself — ~48.3 million labeled flow records total. Class distribution: DDoS 33,984,560; DoS 8,090,738; Benign 1,098,195; Mirai 2,634,124; Spoofing 486,504; Recon 354,565; Web 24,829; Brute Force 13,064 rows. Heavily imbalanced (largest single attack: DDoS-ICMP Flood at 7.2M rows; smallest: Uploading Attack at 1,252 rows; benign traffic is only ~2.3% of the total). Publicly hosted by UNB's Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity: https://www.unb.ca/cic/datasets/iotdataset-2023.html, released under CC BY 4.0.
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy, Recall, Precision, and F1-score, reported per model per task (binary / 8-class grouped / 34-class multiclass), plus confusion-matrix-level qualitative analysis of which classes get confused.
deep.key_results: Binary classification: all 5 models exceed 98% accuracy; Random Forest best overall (Acc 0.997, F1 0.965), AdaBoost close behind (F1 0.956), DNN F1 0.940, while simple linear models (LogReg, Perceptron) trail on F1 (~0.81-0.88) despite high accuracy — a sign of class-imbalance masking. 8-class grouped classification: Random Forest (Acc 0.994, F1 0.719) and DNN (Acc 0.991, F1 0.697) clearly outperform LogReg/Perceptron/AdaBoost, whose F1 collapses below 0.56 (AdaBoost actually drops to 0.351 accuracy here). 34-class multiclass: Random Forest again best (Acc 0.992, F1 0.714), DNN second (Acc 0.986, F1 0.672); linear/boosting baselines fall further behind (F1 ~0.45-0.49). deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The paper has no separate "Limitations" section, but acknowledges specific weaknesses in its discussion: minority/low-volume attack classes (Web-based, Brute Force) are poorly separated from Benign/Recon/Spoofing traffic because "the underlying traffic for those scenarios can be similar," which the authors say they "intend to explore ... further in future works." (e.g., attacks using future protocols)." Notably, the paper does NOT discuss concept drift or adversarial/poisoning robustness at all — those are gaps entirely unaddressed by the original authors, later picked up by follow-on work (see below), which is exactly the opening for this project.
deep.relation_to_our_project: CICIoT2023 is the correct anchor dataset for this project for several concrete reasons: (1) Scale/realism — 105 real devices, 33 attacks, IoT-to-IoT attack traffic (including a genuine Mirai botnet-style scenario) makes it the most representative available benchmark for an ESP32-class on-device IDS, far more realistic than older single-attacker datasets. (2) Explicit gap = your novelty. The original paper neither studies concept drift nor adversarial/poisoning robustness — it evaluates static, IID 80/20 splits only. That is precisely the "stated limitation" the brief was looking for: a clean, citable gap to fill. (3) Class imbalance and per-class confusion (Web/Brute-Force being conflated with Benign/Recon/Spoofing) is itself a useful stress-test surface: a slow "boiling-frog" poisoning attack would plausibly try to exploit exactly this ambiguous decision boundary to relabel poison traffic as benign over time. Practical implication for your team: plan to construct your drift and poisoning scenarios on top of CICIoT2023 rather than assume the raw captures already contain exploitable natural drift — e.g., chronologically/device-subset resample to simulate benign concept drift (new device types, firmware-like behavior shifts) and inject a controlled slow label-flip/boiling-frog poisoning attack against your model's online adaptation loop, using CICIoT2023's 47-feature flow representation (which is already lightweight enough to be extracted or approximated on an ESP32-class device) as your feature space. This directly supports the RAM/latency/energy hardware-cost evaluation axis of your working title, since the paper's own feature set and per-flow footprint are documented in enough detail (Table 4, 47 features) to scope an on-device feature extractor.

deep.title: Hybrid Intrusion Detection System with Real-Time Concept Drift Detection for Enhanced IoT Security
deep.authors: Muath A. Obaidat, Meryem Abouali, Aneeza Shakeel
deep.venue_year: Sensors (Basel, Switzerland), MDPI — published 12 August 2026. DOI: 10.3390/s26165117
deep.fetch_status: Successfully fetched via WebFetch — full text (not just abstract) was accessible through the PMC page, including methods, numeric results tables, confusion-matrix values, and discussion/limitations text. Cross-checked with an independent WebSearch query, which returned matching authors, journal, DOI, framework description, and identical leave-one-family-out numbers (85.26% / 85.18% / 7.05%), so the extraction is corroborated, not a single-source hallucination.
deep.problem: IoT devices are deployed at scale (smart cities, healthcare, industrial automation, transportation, smart grids, cyber-physical infrastructure) under tight resource constraints (processing, memory, battery, bandwidth), which makes conventional heavyweight security mechanisms hard to deploy consistently. Most ML-based IDSs are built under a static-distribution assumption, so their accuracy degrades as traffic evolves over time due to firmware changes, device onboarding, protocol updates, user-behavior variation, or adaptive attackers. The paper's problem is therefore twofold: (1) build an IDS that detects intrusions in IoT network traffic with high accuracy, and (2) give that IDS real-time awareness of concept drift in the traffic distribution, so degradation can be detected/flagged rather than silently occurring.
deep.method: A hybrid architecture with three components fused by a union rule: (1) a supervised Random Forest classifier trained on labeled benign/malicious traffic for primary intrusion classification; (2) an unsupervised Isolation Forest anomaly monitor trained ONLY on benign samples (a deliberate correction of prior work that trained Isolation Forest on attack-dominated data), intended to catch anomalies the supervised model misses; (3) a Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) two-sample statistical test applied per-feature across chronological time windows to detect concept drift in the incoming traffic distribution. The final intrusion decision is a hybrid/union fusion of the Random Forest and Isolation Forest outputs. Drift detection is monitoring-only in this paper — the system flags drift via the KS test but does not perform automated retraining; any model update in response to detected drift is described as a human-supervised/scheduled process, not an automated closed loop. All experiments ran on a shared HPC server (PSC Bridges-2: 5 CPU cores, ~22.75 GB allocated RAM, an allocated-but-unused NVIDIA V100-32 GPU) — i.e., CPU-based models, no embedded/edge hardware involved.
deep.dataset_used: CICIoT2023, used chronologically (not shuffled/randomized), which is exactly the same core dataset and ordering the user's project targets. From the full 46,686,579-record dataset, the authors took a chronologically-ordered systematic sample (every 12th row across 169 time-ordered files, with an 80/20 train/test split performed at the file level before sampling to avoid leakage), yielding 3,890,621 records total: 3,144,527 for training and 746,094 for test. Class balance was heavily skewed: 2.35% benign (91,595 records) vs 97.65% attack traffic (3,799,026 records). All 46 original numerical features were retained; features were Z-score standardized using statistics fit only on the training split.
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, False Positive Rate (FPR), Specificity, Balanced Accuracy, and full confusion-matrix components (TP/TN/FP/FN). For the drift-detection component: per-feature KS-test statistics and p-values across chronological windows (46 features tested).
