deep.title: Exploiting Machine Learning to Subvert Your Spam Filter
deep.authors: Blaine Nelson, Marco Barreno, Fuching Jack Chi, Anthony D. Joseph, Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein, Udam Saini, Charles Sutton, J. D. Tygar, Kai Xia (University of California, Berkeley)
deep.venue_year: First USENIX Workshop on Large-Scale Exploits and Emergent Threats (LEET), April 2008
deep.fetch_status: success — full 9-page PDF retrieved and its text independently verified with pdftotext (not just the auto-summarized WebFetch pass, which I cross-checked and caught inventing a nonexistent "Usenet Proxy-Gambit" attack name; the real paper has no such attack, only a "Usenet dictionary attack" that uses word frequencies from a Usenet corpus).
deep.problem: The paper studies how an adversary who can inject a small fraction of the training data used by a statistical spam filter (they target SpamBayes, a pure Bayesian/Fisher-combination learner) can corrupt that data to make the filter misclassify legitimate ("ham") email. This is a "Causative" attack (the attacker influences training, not just crafts evasive test-time spam) with an "Availability" goal (drive up false positives / unsure classifications on ham rather than just sneak spam through). They study two variants: an Indiscriminate "dictionary attack" that tries to disable the filter for everyone, and a Targeted "focused attack" that tries to silently block one specific future email or class of email the victim would otherwise receive.
deep.method: They formalize an attacker taxonomy along three axes (Causative/Exploratory, Integrity/Availability, Targeted/Indiscriminate) inherited from their own earlier work. Attack 1, the dictionary attack: send attack emails (always labeled spam) containing large numbers of words likely to appear in legitimate mail, so that after retraining those words carry a high spam score and future ham gets misclassified; word lists come from the GNU Aspell English dictionary (98,568 words) or from the most frequent ~90,000 words in a Usenet corpus. Attack 2, the focused attack: if the attacker knows (or can guess, with probability p) the words in a specific target ham email, craft attack spam containing those words so that particular future email gets pushed into the spam/unsure bucket. They also derive, analytically, the "optimal" attack as a function of the attacker's knowledge distribution over the victim's vocabulary, showing the dictionary and focused attacks are the optimal strategies at the two extremes (no knowledge vs. full knowledge). They evaluate with K-fold cross-validation (10-fold for the dictionary attack, 5 repetitions for the focused attack). Two defenses are proposed: (a) RONI (Reject On Negative Impact) — for each candidate training email, retrain a small classifier with and without it and measure its incremental effect on misclassifications over a held-out validation set, rejecting emails whose negative impact is statistically distinguishable from benign impact; (b) a dynamic threshold defense that recomputes SpamBayes' spam/ham decision thresholds from a validation split instead of using static defaults, so attacks that uniformly shift scores are less effective.
deep.dataset_used: Main corpus: the TREC 2005 spam corpus (built from the Enron email corpus), 92,189 emails — 52,790 spam and 39,399 ham. Word sources for building attack payloads: the GNU Aspell English dictionary v6.0 (98,568 words) and a Usenet postings corpus (Shaoul and Westbury, 2005–2007), from which the top ~90,000 frequent words were used.
deep.metrics_reported: Percent of ham misclassified as spam, and as spam-or-unsure (since SpamBayes has a three-way ham/unsure/spam output, plain false-positive rate is not enough). For the focused attack: percent of target emails whose classification flips, as a function of the fraction of target tokens the attacker guesses correctly and of the number of attack emails injected. For RONI: the average marginal change in correctly-classified ham ("ham-as-ham") count on a held-out validation set when a candidate email is added to training, compared between confirmed attack emails and ordinary non-attack spam emails.
deep.key_results: Controlling just 1% of the training messages (101 of 10,000) with the Usenet-word dictionary attack was enough to misclassify 36% of ham messages, rendering the filter effectively unusable; an idealized "optimal" attack drove ham misclassification toward 100% even faster. The focused attack changed a targeted email's classification 60% of the time when the attacker correctly guessed only 30% of that email's tokens, and misclassified the target as spam 32% of the time using 100 attack emails against a 5,000-message inbox. RONI, in a small preliminary experiment (20-message training / 50-message validation splits, 5 repetitions), caught 100% of dictionary-attack emails with zero false flags on benign email — each dictionary attack email caused an average drop of at least 6.8 correctly-classified ham messages, versus at most 4.4 for ordinary spam, giving a clean separating threshold. However, RONI completely failed to distinguish focused-attack emails from benign email. The dynamic threshold defense reduced ham misclassification under the dictionary attack but pushed nearly all spam into the "unsure" bucket instead, i.e., it traded one error type for another rather than truly neutralizing the attack.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The authors explicitly state RONI's central blind spot: it "fails to differentiate focused attack emails from non-attack emails" because a dictionary attack broadly and measurably degrades the small validation sample RONI checks against, while a focused/targeted attack's effect is concentrated on a specific future email not represented in that sample, so it produces no detectable per-email impact signal. They call the resulting problem important and unsolved, writing that "developing effective defenses is an important open problem." They also flag that their RONI results come from a small, preliminary setup and say they plan to extend it "with larger test sets along with a larger variation in the number of attack emails." Separately, they note the dynamic-threshold defense's spam-as-unsure failure mode is unresolved and that they are "exploring this defense under other choices of the thresholds." They explicitly leave derivation of an attacker's optimal strategy under partial (non-extreme) knowledge of the victim's vocabulary to future work, and they explicitly decline to model a defender who inspects training data or an attacker who adapts to evade such inspection, calling that an "arms race" they avoid pursuing. Finally, in their conclusion they speculate — without testing — that "similar techniques may also be effective against other learning systems, such as worm or intrusion detection," an explicitly untested extrapolation from 2008.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is the literal origin of RONI, the foundational "does this sample hurt validation performance" defense against training-time (Causative) poisoning, and its own reported failure mode maps almost exactly onto the threat model the project needs to defend against. RONI only works when each poisoned sample's marginal impact is large enough to statistically separate from benign impact on a small validation sample (dictionary attack: -6.8 vs -4.4 ham-as-ham per email). Against the focused attack — whose per-sample effect on that validation sample is small/invisible because the damage is concentrated elsewhere (a future target email) — RONI is blind. A slow "boiling-frog" poisoning campaign against a drift-adapting on-device IDS is structurally the same failure mode generalized: instead of concentrating low visibility on one target message, the attacker spreads low-impact-per-sample contamination across many adaptation rounds so no single update crosses a RONI-style significance threshold, while the cumulative effect still relocates the decision boundary. This gives the project a directly citable, 2008-vintage precedent that (a) names and formally demonstrates this exact class of blind spot in impact-based poisoning defenses, and (b) never resolves it — the authors call defending against low-visibility/targeted poisoning "an important open problem" and never test it against IDS at all, only speculating IDS could be a future application. Practically, classical RONI is also computationally unusable on an ESP32: it requires repeated retrain-and-compare cycles per candidate sample against a held-out labeled validation set, which the project's resource budget (RAM, latency, energy) and unsupervised/streaming setting cannot support. That gap is exactly what motivates the project's proposed contribution flagged in the task: a cheap, streaming, O(1)-per-sample proxy statistic (e.g., an incremental measure of how much a candidate sample shifts the on-device model's internal decision statistics, mirroring RONI's negative-impact test without full retraining) that must be explicitly evaluated — and likely hardened, e.g., via aggregation over sliding windows or slow-drift-vs-attack discrimination — against the same low-impact-per-sample / distributed poisoning scenario RONI could never catch. Framing the project's novelty this way (closing an 18-year-old, explicitly acknowledged gap between impact-based poisoning defenses and low-visibility/distributed attacks, under new ESP32-class resource constraints and legitimate concept drift) gives a clean, defensible "gap in prior work" story for the mid-review and final paper.

deep.title: Robustness Analysis of Machine Learning Models for IoT Intrusion Detection Under Data Poisoning Attacks
deep.venue_year: arXiv preprint, posted 15 April 2026 (arXiv:2604.14444). No peer-reviewed venue/journal was found in the fetched content — treat as an unreviewed preprint, not a confirmed A/A* or Q1 publication.
deep.authors: Fortunatus Aabangbio Wulnye, Justice Owusu Agyemang, Kwame Opuni-Boachie Obour Agyekum, Kwame Agyeman-Prempeh Agyekum, Kingsford Sarkodie Obeng Kwakye, Francisca Adomaa Acheampong
deep.verified_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14444 (abstract); full text rendered at https://arxiv.org/html/2604.14444 ; PDF at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.14444
deep.problem: How data poisoning attacks compromise the reliability of ML-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) in IoT environments. Specifically: how different poisoning strategies affect model performance, and whether there is a "comparative fragility across model families" — i.e., which classifier types hold up and which collapse under poisoned training data — to inform which ML approaches are safe to deploy in adversarial IoT settings.
deep.method: Trains four classifiers — Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and a Deep Neural Network (DNN) — on each of three IoT/IIoT network-traffic datasets, first on clean data (baseline) and then on data poisoned by four static attack techniques applied once to the training set: (1) Label Flipping — reassigning ground-truth labels to incorrect classes to corrupt decision boundaries; (2) Outlier Injection — injecting extreme/noisy feature values to distort the feature distribution; (3) Feature Impersonation — altering selected feature values so malicious samples mimic benign traffic, aimed at evasion; (4) Generic Synthetic Outliers — fabricated, statistically abnormal samples to reduce reliability. Preprocessing was normalization, feature scaling, and categorical encoding (datasets reported as having no missing values). Poisoning contamination rates/parameterization are not explicitly specified in the extracted text. Robustness is assessed purely as a one-shot train-on-poisoned/test comparison — there is no online, incremental, or continually-adapting model in the study; each poisoning condition is a separate static retraining, not a gradual attack unfolding over time against a live-updating detector.
deep.dataset_used: Three real-world IoT/IIoT network-traffic datasets: CICIoT2023 (~1,048,575 instances, 47 features, 105 devices, 33 attack types), Edge-IIoTset (~2,219,201 instances, 63 variables/1176 network+system-level features, 14 IIoT attack types), and N-BaIoT (~1,018,298 instances, 116 features, Mirai/Bashlite botnet infections).
deep.metrics_reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score, computed on clean vs. poisoned test conditions. "Robustness" is operationalized as relative percentage performance degradation between the clean baseline and each poisoned condition (no adversarial-training-specific or drift-specific metrics; no resource metrics such as RAM, latency, or energy).
deep.key_results: On the clean CICIoT2023 baseline: RF 99.29% accuracy / 74.24% F1; GBM 99.06% accuracy / 71.06% F1; LR 83.88% accuracy / 53.89% F1. Under poisoning, label flipping was the most damaging attack, cutting accuracy by up to ~40% in severe cases, with LR and DNN showing the largest declines while RF and GBM stayed comparatively stable ("ensemble-based models exhibit comparatively stable performance"). Outlier-based attacks had dataset-dependent (mixed) effects; generic synthetic outliers had milder effects than the structured attacks (label flipping, feature impersonation). Overall conclusion: tree-ensemble methods (RF, GBM) are notably more robust to these poisoning strategies than linear/deep models (LR, DNN), whose decision boundaries are more easily distorted.
deep.stated_limitations_or_future_work: The authors call for: (1) "real-time adversarial detection mechanisms, adaptive learning strategies" for IoT NIDS; (2) "hybrid approaches combining ensemble learning with federated learning"; (3) "realistic, large-scale attack simulations on live IoT environments to validate model robustness outside controlled settings" (i.e., they acknowledge their evaluation was in a controlled, offline, non-live setting); and (4) "differential privacy and blockchain-based validation" for data-integrity assurance. Notably, the paper does NOT explicitly discuss: poisoning-rate/contamination-level sensitivity, cross-dataset/cross-environment generalization of the attacks, or deployment feasibility on resource-constrained IoT/edge devices (no RAM/latency/energy analysis at all) — these read as implicit, unacknowledged gaps rather than stated limitations, since the paper's own framing is purely accuracy/robustness of classification.
deep.relation_to_our_project: This paper is a strong, directly adaptable source for the project's threat model and evaluation methodology, and it also cleanly demarcates the exact gap the project should fill. Reusable parts: (a) it supplies a validated, ready-made four-technique poisoning taxonomy — label flipping, outlier injection, feature impersonation, and synthetic-outlier injection — that can be reimplemented and, critically, converted from the paper's one-shot/static poisoning of a fixed training set into a slow, "boiling-frog" variant injected incrementally into the stream an online-adapting detector uses to update itself; (b) it uses the same three IoT/IIoT benchmark datasets (CICIoT2023, Edge-IIoTset, N-BaIoT) the project can draw on to construct a benign-traffic stream with realistic concept drift plus a controllable poisoning injection schedule; (c) its finding that ensemble/tree-based models are more robust than LR/DNN under static poisoning is a useful baseline to contrast against — the project's unsupervised, adaptive, on-device detector should be benchmarked against both a static classifier (replicating this paper's setup) and against itself with adaptation disabled, to isolate how much of the vulnerability comes specifically from online adaptation. The key gap this paper leaves open — and which the project should target as its novelty — is threefold and matches the paper's own future-work language almost exactly: (1) it never tests an online/continually-adapting model, only static one-shot retraining on a corrupted dataset, so it cannot show how a slow, gradual poisoning attack degrades a model's ongoing self-updates over time (the project's core "boiling-frog" attack on an online-adapting detector is exactly the "adaptive learning strategy" + "real-time adversarial detection mechanism" the authors say is needed but do not build); (2) it never addresses benign concept drift at all — poisoning here is a corruption of a fixed dataset, not an attack that must be distinguished from legitimate, gradual shifts in normal traffic, which is the central discrimination problem the project is solving; and (3) it performs no resource-constrained/on-device evaluation whatsoever (no RAM, latency, or energy figures, and the models — especially DNN/GBM — are not shown to be ESP32-feasible), whereas hardware-cost evaluation on real ESP32-class hardware is a required, differentiating contribution of the project. In short, this paper establishes that poisoning static IoT-IDS classifiers is a real, measurable problem and gives a borrowable attack toolkit and datasets, but it explicitly stops short of the online-adaptation, drift-awareness, and edge-deployment dimensions — which is precisely the novelty claim the project should build its A/A*-level contribution around.

Practically: we can use the per-device TON_IoT telemetry CSVs (e.g., Weather, Thermostat, Fridge -- closest in spirit to ESP32 + sensor setups) as the benign-traffic baseline source, engineer our own synthetic drift and poisoning injections on top of it (since neither exists in the original data), and report our own on-device resource measurements that this paper never attempted.

lens.lens: Methods/algorithms audit: for every paper in the corpus, classify (a) what mechanism it uses to adapt a detector to a changing "normal," and (b) what mechanism, if any, it uses to keep that adaptation from being manipulated by an adversary — then look for a combination of an adaptation-mechanism family and a defense-mechanism family that no paper in the corpus actually builds or evaluates together, especially under real MCU-class resource constraints.
lens.whats_been_done: Drift-adaptation mechanisms present in the corpus fall into a few families: (1) frozen/no-adaptation baselines — Kitsune (KitNET freezes after train-mode), N-BaIoT, the ESP32/ESP32-S3 decision-tree/NN papers (Manocchio et al., "Empowering IoT Security"), ArrythML, and the hardware-aware ML/DL IDS paper — none adapt post-deployment at all; (2) statistical streaming drift DETECTORS — ADWIN/ADWIN2 (Bifet & Gavaldà, exponential-histogram windowing, Hoeffding-bound cut test), DDM (Gama et al., p_min/s_min running-error thresholds, supervised), KSWIN/PHT as used inside LE3D, and the KS-test used (monitoring-only, no retrain) in the 2026 Hybrid IDS paper; (3) threshold-triggered RETRAIN/adaptation loops built on top of such detectors — OASW (accuracy-threshold-gated adaptive window + retrain, PSO-tuned), LE3D (3-detector majority vote + cross-device natural-vs-malicious corroboration), ONLAD (centroid-distance θdrift trigger that spawns a new learned-normal instance), AOC-IDS (periodic pseudo-label fine-tune every m samples with a Gaussian anchored to fixed initial trusted data X0 and random label-flip regularization), CND-IDS (per-"experience" CFE+PCA refit against a held-out clean-normal subset with a continual-learning regularizer against forgetting), and the tinyFL loop in the 2026 TinyML survey (distribute→on-device fine-tune→FedAvg aggregate). Poisoning-defense mechanisms present are essentially all CROSS-WORKER/CROSS-CLIENT: Krum/Multi-Krum and coordinate-wise median/trimmed-mean (Blanchard et al.; Yin et al.) score or aggregate several SIMULTANEOUS peer updates against each other; clustering-based FL defenses and differential-privacy clipping+noise (both shown to fail or cost accuracy in "Poisoning Attacks on FL-based IoT IDS"); RRBM-DD's robust gradient truncation + noise-gated energy function (single-model, but still evaluated only on a full desktop RBM with no adaptation-commit gating); RONI (Nelson et al., retrain-with/without-sample impact test — explicitly shown blind to low-per-sample-impact/distributed poisoning); and the "Learn to Adapt" contrastive+NCM combined Euclidean/geometric distance. Attack-methodology papers (the two ICS "boiling frog" papers, "Adversarial Concept Drift Detection," "Poisoning FL-based IoT IDS," PACOL, and the physical-sensor-acoustic-injection paper) establish gradual/incremental, alarm-avoiding, bilevel-optimization-style poisoning of an online-retrained detector as a real, demonstrated attack pattern, but do so on ICS regression autoencoders, FL aggregation, or image classifiers — never on an IoT-network-traffic anomaly detector's own threshold-gated adaptation loop, and (with the partial exception of the physical-sensor paper, which is single-shot) never incrementally across many adaptation cycles.
lens.whats_missing: No paper combines a genuine temporal drift-ADAPTATION mechanism (ADWIN/DDM/KSWIN-style detector plus a commit/retrain step, as in OASW/LE3D/ONLAD/AOC-IDS/CND-IDS) with a poisoning defense that actually works in a SINGLE-DEVICE, no-peers setting. Every robustness mechanism that has been evaluated against gradual/incremental poisoning (Krum, Multi-Krum, coordinate-wise median/trimmed mean, FL clustering defenses, differential privacy) is structurally cross-client: it needs multiple simultaneous peer model-updates to compare against each other, and the one FL-IoT-IDS paper that tests this in an IoT context shows even those defenses fail or cost accuracy under a slow "boiling-frog" attacker (PDR-tuned). None of those aggregators has been re-purposed along the TIME axis (comparing a single device's own recent history of window-statistics/updates to itself) instead of the WORKER axis. Conversely, every mechanism that DOES operate on a single device's own temporal stream (ADWIN, DDM, OASW, LE3D's per-device layer, ONLAD's centroid trigger, AOC-IDS's periodic fine-tune, CND-IDS's per-experience refit) has no adversarial defense at all — LE3D explicitly scopes out sustained/incremental attacks (only single-shot natural-vs-malicious classification via neighbor comparison, and admits neighbor discovery itself is unsolved); OASW blindly retrains on anything inside its adaptive window; AOC-IDS's and CND-IDS's "trusted anchor" (fixed X0 Gaussian / held-out clean Nc) is never stress-tested against gradual contamination, only against i.i.d. label noise or new benign attack classes; ONLAD's physical-poisoning paper demonstrates exactly this class of attack succeeding (100% success) against a centroid-drift trigger but proposes zero defense and tests only a single deliberately-tuned injection, not a slow multi-cycle campaign. The two papers that DO formalize slow/incremental/bilevel-optimization poisoning of an online-retrained detector ("Can't Boil This Frog," "Poisoning Attacks on Cyber Attack Detectors for ICS") do so only on ICS physics-bound sensor autoencoders, on unconstrained desktop/TPU hardware, with zero RAM/latency/energy accounting — never on IoT network-traffic features, never on genuinely MCU-class hardware. RONI's own failure mode (blind to distributed, low-per-sample-impact poisoning) has never been re-derived as a cheap streaming/incremental statistic (existing RONI needs a full retrain-compare per candidate sample, which nothing in this corpus shows as MCU-feasible). Finally, PACOL's clean-label, catastrophic-forgetting attack goal (as opposed to boundary-shift/false-normal poisoning) has been tested only on image-classification continual learners (MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR) — never on a network-traffic anomaly detector, and never combined with any of the above adaptation or defense mechanisms.

candidate_directions.name: Temporal Robust Aggregation for On-Device Drift Adaptation
candidate_directions.description: Replace the unconditional 'trust everything inside the adaptive window' commit step used in OASW/LE3D/ONLAD/AOC-IDS with a Krum-style or coordinate-wise-trimmed-mean/median-style robust aggregator (Blanchard et al.; Yin et al.), but re-derive its comparison axis from CROSS-WORKER (many simultaneous peer devices, as in the FL-IoT-IDS poisoning paper and Krum's own setting) to CROSS-TIME (a single ESP32's own rolling buffer of the last n window-statistics or candidate update vectors produced by a lightweight streaming drift detector, e.g. an ADWIN/DDM/KSWIN-style trigger as used in LE3D). Each new candidate update is only committed if it is geometrically/statistically consistent with its k nearest neighbors in that recent-history buffer (Krum-style score) or survives per-coordinate trimming (Yin et al.-style), rather than being trusted just because a threshold was crossed. Evaluate against a genuine incremental/bilevel-optimization 'boiling frog' attacker (methodology ported from the two ICS poisoning papers and the FL-IoT-IDS paper's PDR-tuning idea) applied to IoT network-traffic features (CICIoT2023/TON_IoT/N-BaIoT), across many adaptation cycles, with real ESP32 RAM/latency/energy measured using the hardware-cost protocols already validated in this corpus (Manocchio et al.'s nested-if codegen + micros() harness; the hardware-aware ML/DL IDS paper's inline power-meter methodology; LE3D's CPU%/RAM% vs. throughput tables).
candidate_directions.why_novel: No paper in the corpus applies a cross-worker Byzantine-robust aggregator along the time axis of a single device's own adaptation history. The corpus's own FL-IoT-IDS poisoning paper and the Krum paper both implicitly require multiple simultaneous peers, which a single ESP32 does not have; every single-device drift-adaptation paper (OASW, LE3D, ONLAD, AOC-IDS, CND-IDS) commits updates without any robust-statistics gate at all. This is a genuinely new combination, not an incremental tweak on any one paper.
candidate_directions.risk: Needs enough temporal samples in the rolling buffer to make neighbor-distance/trimming statistically meaningful without blowing the RAM budget; may require careful tuning of buffer size k versus detection latency, and the theoretical (α,f)-resilience guarantees from Krum/Yin et al. do not automatically transfer from an i.i.d.-worker assumption to a temporally correlated single stream, so new guarantees (or an empirical-only claim) would need to be derived.

candidate_directions.name: Rate-Limited Trust-Region Adaptation Anchored to a Slowly-Refreshing Clean Baseline
candidate_directions.description: Generalize the static 'trusted anchor' pattern already present piecemeal in AOC-IDS (fixed Gaussian fit only to initial data X0) and CND-IDS (held-out clean-normal subset Nc, refit per experience) into an explicit, provably-bounded control mechanism: the anchor is allowed to update over long timescales (so the detector doesn't go stale across a real deployment lifetime, unlike AOC-IDS's permanently frozen X0), but each adaptation cycle's movement of the decision boundary is capped by an explicit rate limit / cumulative drift budget, derived from ADWIN's own theoretical detection-delay bound for gradual drift (its derived O(...)^{1/3} slower-detection result for linear-slope changes) as the justification for why unbounded per-cycle commitment is unsafe. Directly targets the exact failure the physical-sensor-poisoning paper demonstrated (single deliberately-tuned injection crosses θdrift once, spawns a poisoned 'normal' instance, 100% attack success) but never defended, and closes OASW's and DDM's identical blind spot (unconditional retrain/threshold-cross triggers commitment with no bound on cumulative drift).
candidate_directions.why_novel: Every paper that uses a trusted-anchor idea (AOC-IDS, CND-IDS) keeps that anchor permanently static, so it is not really solving benign long-term drift, only tolerating short-term i.i.d. label noise. No paper couples a refreshing anchor with an explicit cumulative-drift rate limit derived from drift-detection theory (ADWIN's own delay bound), and no paper defends the exact single-shot poisoning mechanism the physical-sensor-attack paper demonstrated succeeds 100% of the time against an undefended centroid-drift trigger — extending that same undefended mechanism to a sustained multi-cycle attack and then rate-limiting it is untried.
candidate_directions.risk: A rate limit that's too tight will reproduce the same 'never really adapts' problem the project is trying to fix (i.e., it degenerates back toward a frozen baseline under genuine fast benign drift, like a new device type joining the network); the right budget-setting policy (fixed vs. adaptive to observed benign-drift variance) is itself open and would need empirical tuning per traffic feature.

candidate_directions.name: Streaming, O(1)-per-sample RONI Analog via Accumulated-Impact Sequential Testing
candidate_directions.description: RONI (Nelson et al., the origin of impact-based poisoning defense) needs a full retrain-and-compare per candidate training sample and is explicitly shown blind to low-per-sample-impact/distributed poisoning — both properties make it unusable as-is on an ESP32 and irrelevant to a boiling-frog attacker by the authors' own admission. Build a cheap streaming proxy: instead of a per-sample retrain-compare, accumulate a lightweight 'impact' statistic per admitted sample (e.g., the shift it induces in the on-device model's internal decision statistic — reconstruction error distribution, centroid position, or gradient-alignment norm) using a Page-Hinkley/CUSUM-style running accumulator (borrowing the accumulation MACHINERY of DDM/PHT, but accumulating IMPACT rather than error), so that many small, individually-invisible poisoned samples are caught cumulatively even though no single one crosses a per-sample threshold.
candidate_directions.why_novel: RONI's own paper (2008) names low-visibility/distributed poisoning detection as an 'important open problem' and never solves it; nothing in the corpus revisits RONI's blind spot with a streaming, resource-bounded reformulation, and nothing combines PHT/DDM-style sequential-accumulation machinery with an IMPACT signal (as opposed to an ERROR signal, which is what DDM/PHT use and which requires labels) for a genuinely unsupervised, MCU-feasible setting.
candidate_directions.risk: Defining an unsupervised 'impact' proxy that reliably separates gradual-poisoning impact from ordinary benign-drift impact is the hard, unresolved part of this direction — it may reduce to a variant of Direction 1 or 2 unless a genuinely distinct signal (e.g., gradient-alignment rather than distributional distance) is used, so this is the most exploratory of the three and would benefit from being framed as a component/ablation inside Direction 1 rather than a fully separate project.

candidates.name: TimeKrum — Cross-Time Robust-Aggregation Gate for On-Device Drift Adaptation
candidates.problem_statement: Single-device, unsupervised drift-adaptation loops for IoT NIDS (OASW's accuracy-threshold retrain, LE3D's ADWIN/PHT/KSWIN majority vote, ONLAD's centroid-distance trigger, AOC-IDS's periodic pseudo-label fine-tune, CND-IDS's per-experience PCA refit) all commit whatever data falls inside their trigger window with zero adversarial vetting. Meanwhile every existing Byzantine-robust aggregator that actually defends an update step (Krum/Multi-Krum, coordinate-wise median/trimmed-mean) is structurally cross-worker: it scores several simultaneous peer model updates against each other, which a lone ESP32 does not have, and the one paper that tests these defenses in an IoT setting (the FL-IoT-IDS poisoning workshop paper) shows they already fail or cost accuracy against a slow, PDR-tuned 'boiling-frog' attacker even WITH multiple peers. No paper re-derives Krum/trimmed-mean along the time axis of a single device's own adaptation history.
candidates.proposed_method_sketch: Build a lightweight ESP32-class feature extractor (subset of the 47-115 incremental statistical features used in N-BaIoT/CICIoT2023/Kitsune) feeding a small one-class detector (autoencoder or centroid), with an ADWIN- or DDM-style drift trigger deciding when to propose an adaptation step (à la LE3D/OASW). Instead of committing the proposed update unconditionally, maintain a small rolling buffer (k=5-20) of the device's own last accepted window-statistic/update vectors and score the new candidate via a Krum-style k-nearest-neighbor distance (or per-coordinate trimmed mean/median, Yin et al.-style) against that buffer; commit only if the candidate is geometrically consistent with recent trusted history, otherwise reject/down-weight it. Attack it with a genuine incremental bilevel-optimization or interpolation-based 'boiling-frog' poisoner (ported from the two ICS online-poisoning papers and the FL-IoT-IDS PDR-tuning idea) applied to IoT network-traffic features (CICIoT2023 and/or N-BaIoT) across many adaptation cycles, not a single-shot injection. Report detection F1/TPR-at-fixed-FPR under clean benign drift vs. poisoned drift (an RLR-style aggregate robustness metric), plus RAM, per-adaptation-cycle latency, and energy on real ESP32 hardware, benchmarked against the Manocchio et al. nested-if/micros() harness and the hardware-aware ML/DL IDS paper's inline power-meter protocol.
candidates.why_novel: This is a genuinely new combination confirmed absent from the corpus: cross-worker Byzantine-robust aggregation (Krum, Blanchard et al. NeurIPS'17; coordinate-wise median/trimmed-mean, Yin et al. ICML'18) has never been re-purposed onto the time axis of a single device's own adaptation history, and every single-device adaptation mechanism in the corpus (OASW, LE3D, ONLAD, AOC-IDS, CND-IDS) commits updates with zero robust-statistics gate. It also directly answers the FL-IoT-IDS paper's own finding that cross-client defenses fail under slow poisoning, by removing the cross-client assumption entirely.

candidates.name: Bounded-Drift IDS — Rate-Limited Trust-Region Adaptation with a Refreshing Trusted Anchor
candidates.problem_statement: Trusted-anchor mechanisms that exist in the corpus (AOC-IDS's Gaussian fit to fixed initial data X0, CND-IDS's held-out clean-normal subset Nc refit per experience) are either permanently frozen (AOC-IDS, so they cannot really track long-term benign drift) or refit with no bound on how far they may move per adaptation cycle (CND-IDS). Separately, the physical-sensor-acoustic-injection paper demonstrates a 100%-success single-shot attack against an undefended centroid-distance drift trigger (ONLAD) with zero proposed defense, and ADWIN's own theory proves gradual/linear-slope drift is detected only after a delay that scales as O(...)^{1/3} slower than abrupt drift — i.e. the exact mechanism a slow attacker would exploit is mathematically characterized but never turned into a safety bound anywhere in the corpus.
candidates.proposed_method_sketch: Implement an ESP32-feasible one-class/centroid detector (ONLAD-style multi-instance OS-ELM or a small autoencoder, sized per ArrythML/Manocchio et al.'s validated on-device budgets) whose 'normal' anchor is allowed to refresh over long timescales but whose per-cycle movement is capped by an explicit rate limit / cumulative drift budget: derive the budget from the variance of genuinely benign drift observed during a clean calibration period, and justify its necessity using ADWIN's own derived detection-delay bound for linear-slope drift. Maintain a cumulative-drift ledger over a sliding horizon; once the budget for that horizon is exhausted, require stronger corroboration (e.g., a longer dwell time or cross-feature agreement) before allowing further boundary movement. Evaluate on the exact undefended attack the physical-sensor paper demonstrated (extended from single-shot to a sustained multi-cycle 'boiling-frog' campaign against network-traffic features, e.g. CICIoT2023/TON_IoT), sweeping rate-limit tightness against (a) adaptation speed under real benign drift (new device type joining, as in N-BaIoT-style heterogeneity) and (b) cumulative poisoning-induced boundary shift after N cycles, plus ESP32 RAM/latency/energy cost of maintaining the ledger.
candidates.why_novel: No paper in the corpus couples a refreshing trusted anchor with an explicit, theoretically-motivated cumulative-drift rate limit; AOC-IDS/CND-IDS's anchors are static or unboundedly refit, and the one paper (physical-sensor injection) that shows an undefended centroid-trigger being poisoned 100% of the time proposes and evaluates zero defense, only a single deliberately-tuned injection rather than a sustained campaign.

candidates.name: Impact-CUSUM — Streaming, Label-Free RONI Analog via Accumulated Impact Statistics
candidates.problem_statement: RONI (Nelson et al. 2008) is the foundational impact-based poisoning defense, but it needs a full retrain-and-compare per candidate training sample (infeasible on MCU RAM/latency budgets) and its own authors explicitly name it blind to low-per-sample-impact, distributed poisoning — an 18-year-old, still-open problem never revisited with a streaming, resource-bounded, unsupervised reformulation.
candidates.proposed_method_sketch: Instead of a per-sample retrain-compare, define a cheap unsupervised 'impact' proxy for each admitted sample during on-device adaptation — e.g. the shift it induces in the detector's internal decision statistic (reconstruction-error distribution moment, centroid displacement, or gradient-alignment norm for a small linear/tree model) — and accumulate this impact signal with a Page-Hinkley/CUSUM-style running accumulator (reusing DDM/PHT's O(1)-memory sequential-test machinery, but tracking impact instead of labeled error). Many individually sub-threshold poisoned samples that a per-sample or per-window check would miss get caught once their accumulated impact crosses a bound, at which point the adaptation buffer is rolled back or flagged. Evaluate against a boiling-frog attacker deliberately tuned to inject impact below any single-sample or single-window threshold (stress-testing exactly RONI's named blind spot) on IoT traffic (CICIoT2023/N-BaIoT), comparing detection lag and false-alarm rate against (a) no defense, (b) naive per-sample thresholding, and (c) a small-scale RONI-lite retrain-compare baseline to quantify the accuracy/cost trade-off, with full ESP32 RAM/latency/energy accounting.
candidates.why_novel: RONI's own paper names low-visibility/distributed poisoning detection as an important, unsolved open problem and never revisits it; nothing in the corpus combines PHT/DDM's sequential-accumulation statistic with an IMPACT signal (rather than a labeled-error signal) for a genuinely unsupervised, MCU-feasible poisoning defense — this is the most exploratory of the three directions and should be scoped with a genuinely distinct signal (e.g. gradient-alignment) to avoid collapsing into the other two candidates.

merged.literature_map_summary: The corpus splits cleanly into three non-overlapping bodies of work that this project sits at the intersection of. (1) On-device/IoT NIDS papers (Kitsune, N-BaIoT, the ESP32/ESP32-S3 decision-tree and NN papers, ArrythML, the hardware-aware ML/DL IDS paper, CICIoT2023/TON_IoT dataset papers) establish that lightweight detectors (tree ensembles, small autoencoders, tiny NNs) can hit 96-99%+ accuracy at sub-30KB-to-few-hundred-KB footprints and microsecond-to-millisecond latency on real ESP32/ESP32-S3 hardware, with validated RAM/latency/energy measurement protocols (nested-if codegen + micros() timing, inline power-meter harnesses) — but every one of these is trained once and frozen, with zero post-deployment adaptation. (2) Drift-adaptation mechanisms (ADWIN, DDM, LE3D's ADWIN/PHT/KSWIN ensemble, OASW's threshold-gated retrain, ONLAD's centroid-trigger, AOC-IDS's periodic pseudo-label fine-tune, CND-IDS's per-experience PCA refit, the 2026 tinyFL survey's FedAvg loop) show how to track benign concept drift cheaply and even on constrained-ish hardware (mostly Raspberry Pi-class, not true MCU-class) — but every one of them commits adaptation updates unconditionally once a threshold is crossed, with no defense against manipulated input. (3) Poisoning-of-adaptation literature (the two ICS 'boiling frog' papers, Adversarial Concept Drift Detection/RRBM-DD, PACOL, the physical-sensor acoustic-injection paper against ONLAD, the FL-IoT-IDS poisoning workshop paper, RONI, Krum, and coordinate-wise median/trimmed-mean) demonstrates that gradual, alarm-avoiding poisoning of an online-retrained detector is a real, exploitable attack — but every poisoning DEFENSE that has actually been evaluated against this attack pattern (Krum, Multi-Krum, coordinate-wise median/trimmed-mean, FL clustering defenses, differential privacy) is structurally cross-worker/cross-client, requiring multiple simultaneous peer updates to compare against each other, and the one paper testing this in an IoT context shows these defenses already fail or cost accuracy under a slow attacker even with peers present. The clean, well-evidenced gap is therefore the intersection of all three bodies: no paper combines a genuine single-device temporal drift-adaptation mechanism with a poisoning defense that works with no peer devices to compare against, under real MCU-class (not Raspberry-Pi-class) RAM/latency/energy constraints, evaluated against a sustained multi-cycle (not single-shot) incremental poisoning campaign on IoT network-traffic features.
